en: Of the sacred tradition.

“Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; one approaches Vāyu alone with his own share [of the sacrifice]; he alone leads him to prosperity”—thus, through the first quarter [of the *Jaiminīya-sūtra*], the connection (*saṅgati*) of the subsequent three quarters is established both by way of *prasaṅga* (contextual relevance) and *ākṣepa* (implication).
And in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, just as the nature of *dharma* and *adharma* is the subject of the proposition (*pratijñā*), [so too is the nature of the means of knowledge].
Likewise, whatever collection of means of knowledge has been proposed is now first examined.

In this regard, the Veda— consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), prohibitions (*niṣedha*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names— as well as the *smṛtis* of Manu and others and the conduct of the virtuous (*śiṣṭācāra*), are the authorities for dharma and adharma.

In that regard, in the first chapter (*pūrvapāda*), having refuted— by means of its being established as non-personal in nature through previously stated arguments— the lack of authority (unreliability) that had accrued to the injunctions (*codanā*) because they are parts of the Veda as a whole and thus suspected of being personal in origin,

[the author] now addresses the injunctions, which are synonymous with prescriptions and prohibitions (*vidhi-niṣedha*) consisting of collections of words that convey the instigation or deterrence directed toward the object of the three-fold productive activity (*bhāvanā*).

Since the authority of Dharma and Adharma was established primarily in the *Codanāsūtra* (JS 1.1.2) regarding their origin from Vedic injunction (*codanā*), it follows that those elements present as its subordinate parts— namely, the portions of the Veda such as *arthavāda* and so forth distinct from *codanā*, as well as the *smṛtis* and other texts— are considered authoritative because they share the quality of being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*) and because their acceptance is firm and plausible; thus, what was promised in the first *sūtra* is now sought to be investigated.
It has been examined as a corollary whether or not the authority regarding dharma and adharma follows from the Vedic injunction.

Alternatively— even if the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) stated for the sake of the injunction (*codanā*) establishes that the validity of the entire Veda is almost proven, how can the aforementioned validity be tenable regarding those parts other than the injunction?

For while it may be maintained that the injunction— which consists of instigation (*pravartanā*) and dissuasion (*nivartanā*) that infer the status of being a means to what is desired or undesired and which generates activity toward the objects of dharma and adharma— is valid because it makes known an unapprehended object, such validity is clearly not perceived in those parts beyond it.
Having thus refuted the objection, the Great Sage began to establish the three-footed [Veda] by means of the following:
"Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal," and so forth (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1).
In this regard, after refuting the method of inquiry adopted in the *Śāstradīpikā*, the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* introduces the passage beginning with "Vāyur vai" as follows:

"Here, by means of both the previously mentioned *prasaṅga* and *ākṣepa* connections, the general lack of authority regarding all [scriptures] other than those containing injunctions— specifically concerning *dharma* and *adharma*— is established at once."

How can there be pointlessness—meaning a lack of a subject matter that culminates in human purpose, and a voidness of the utility consisting in the cognition of dharma and adharma—for those [Vedic passages] which do not have that as their object and do not have action as their object, such as arthavādas and the like? Because the Veda has action as its object; since it is a means of valid knowledge for dharma and adharma precisely insofar as it denotes an action in the form of a *bhāvanā* (productive operation) endowed with the three factors, those eternal injunctions and prohibitions do not constitute a means of knowing dharma and adharma in the manner described.
This is because it was understood in that very same way in the first sūtra—that arthavādas and so forth are distinct from the collection of words expressing obligatory rites (nityakriyā).

Therefore, having initially raised the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that all [Vedic portions] lack authority in general, [the siddhāntin] establishes that the entire Veda has as its purport a meaning culminating in human goals (puruṣārtha), in accordance with the requirement for the injunction to study (adhyayanavidhi) to have a visible purpose; consequently, those [arthavādas] are also objects of the injunction to study.

Since it would result in a lack of uniformity (vairūpya) to assume that for a single injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*), there is a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) in its injunctive portion while there is an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*) in its portions such as the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), one must establish the general conclusion (*siddhānta*) that they indeed possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding those matters, because they are intended to culminate in some human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that since the demonstration of the study injunction (*adhyayanavidhi*) having a visible purpose was already established in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, there is nothing further to be proven here; for, according to the maxim "its visible purpose is indeed the teaching of ritual action," that [visible purpose] is established only for the portions consisting of injunctions and prohibitions. And yet, even by that much, the sequence of study immediately following [the acquisition of the Veda]—which is denoted by the word *atha*—is justified in relation to the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). Therefore, in this very context, the general fact that all [portions of the Veda] other than injunctions and prohibitions have such a [visible] purpose must be established.
This must be established.

For it is not possible for explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) to have action as their purpose by way of praise or censure, nor for names and mantras to have that purpose except through the demonstration of specific means [of application] therein.

Therefore, having established that, even though study has a visible purpose, if there is no comprehension of a meaning that culminates in human welfare (*puruṣārtha*) arising from the explanatory passages—

Since even the status of having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), as taught by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), is not possible [for the Arthavādas], the opponent first establishes the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding the Arthavādas alone by repeating the word "of the sacred tradition" (*sāmnāyasya*) in the Sūtra; this is then proven by way of the specific distinction between praise and censure. In the same manner, through the means of the determination of Smṛti, the same applies to Mantras and Names. Thus, a general investigation into the authority or lack of authority of all elements other than the injunction (*vidhi*) must first be undertaken.
The view favored by Miśra appears in the *Śāstradīpikā*.

Likewise, since the Sūtra itself, through repetition, establishes two distinct investigations of different types of arguments, there would result— just as in the *Lokavedādhikaraṇa*— the designation of two separate *adhikaraṇas* here as well;

furthermore, because we observe that in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārtika*, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the general investigation is described as being intertwined with the prima facie argument concerning the specific investigation, and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the former is likewise intertwined with the conclusion of the latter, it follows by implication that the general investigation is established precisely through the specific investigation.

Since you yourself have already established the consistency of the meaning even upon a specific investigation of the Sūtra, there is no purpose in disregarding the general investigation. Rather, with reference to the mantras and so forth, and considering the proximity to the injunction (*codanā*) by way of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) within a single word and as a form of procedure (*itikartavyatā*), [the Sūtra states]:
"But because they are in syntactic unity with the injunction, they shall serve the purpose of praising the injunctions" (Jaimini 1.2.7).

Thus, since the author of the Sūtras has stated the very established doctrine regarding the subject matter of the *arthavāda*s, and since the author of the Bhāṣya has also conducted an investigation solely into the authority of dharma and adharma by citing only examples of *arthavāda*s, that very specific investigation [is presented as follows]: "The subject matter, the doubt, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and likewise the final conclusion (*uttara*)."
And they know that in this treatise, a formal topic (*adhikaraṇa*) consists of five members, including its purpose (*prayojana*).

Thus, formulating a five-membered *adhikaraṇa* consisting of the subject matter well-known among experts, doubt, prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), final conclusion (*siddhānta*), and purpose, he makes his declaration with the words "Vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā" and so forth:
"It is well known in the world that Vāyu is the swiftest—that is, the deity who moves most rapidly;
therefore, by means of the portion appropriate for Vāyu, namely the form of a white animal, the sacrificer gratifies the swift-moving deity Vāyu."

Furthermore, when Vāyu is pleased, he indeed causes this sacrificer, who has offered a portion, to attain sovereignty; such is the meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) through its connection with the particle *ava*.
[This refers to] such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as "The wind is indeed the swiftest" [which serves as a basis for the term *grahaṇa*], and "He wept" [which serves as an *upalakṣaṇa*].
By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it is indicated that not only those explanatory passages situated in proximity to an injunction (*vidhi*) that are of this nature should be understood, but others as well.

Furthermore, explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) such as, "He wept; because he wept, that is the origin of Rudra's name [rudratva]; what flowed from him became silver; therefore, they weep in his house before the year has passed," even though they are mentioned in conjunction with prohibitions such as, "Therefore, silver must not be given upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*"), are to be accepted as authoritative.
Because the discussion regarding the authority of the *adharma* concerning that subject will also occur later.
Here, by the word "that" (*saḥ*) in the pronoun *tat*, Agni, who was previously introduced in the passage "That Agni desired," is referred to.
The rest is clear in meaning.

By the statement "just as in the case of injunctions and prohibitions," it is indicated that in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, only the means of knowledge for dharma—including explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth—was introduced.

(B1) Just as in the case of injunctions and prohibitions, since the absence of a recollection of an author establishes their non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) by means of the preceding section, it is now considered whether or not they possess authority regarding dharma and adharma in that same manner.

In that regard, since positive and negative injunctions (vidhi-pratiṣedha) convey, by their own power, injunctions and prohibitions whose objects are *bhāvanās* qualified by the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it follows by implication that sacrifices and other acts— which are the objects of those injunctions and prohibitions— are the means to achieve the desirable and the undesirable; thus, it is logical that these two [injunctions and prohibitions] generate valid knowledge (*pramā*) regarding dharma and adharma, which consist in being the means to the desirable.

However, since explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) convey established facts—whether real or unreal—by their own expressive power (*śakti*), they cannot possibly possess authority regarding *dharma* and *adharma*.
Nor can they establish those [matters] through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), textual supplementation (*adhyāhāra*), and so forth, even if such [direct] expression is impossible;
for as long as the meaning is established by conveying the literal sense alone, there is no lack of syntactic compatibility (*anvaya*), and thus [indication and the like] are impossible.

Nor can that [intention] be postulated on the grounds of the failure of the intended meaning (tātparya-anupapatti), because such a failure itself is impossible due to the absence of any means for grasping the intended meaning.
For there is no proof for the restrictive rule that "verbal testimony is merely a means of valid cognition" or that "it must have only a purposeful object."
By this [reasoning], that very [study] might be suspected of being the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*);
for there is deviation, as purposeless [studies] are frequently observed.

Nor can it be argued that the injunction of Vedic study itself—namely, "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied"—in enjoining study with the aim of knowing the meaning, implies that the meaning must possess a purpose, because it is impossible for the knowledge of meaning to be the *bhāvya* (the result to be produced) if it were itself purposeless.

It must be said that [the objection] "it casts [aside]" is not valid; for study is not something to be enjoined, as it is already established in the world as being productive of the knowledge of meaning.

(B2) [The determination of the authority of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) through reasoning similar to that of injunctions, due to the absence of recollection of an author: "[Since it is] established... means:

And thus, since the lack of recollection of an author—the reason already stated for the Vedic injunction—is absent, the validity of the *arthavādas* and so forth is established by the same general logic as before; this is the meaning.

By this, the necessity [of the *arthavādas*] is refuted on the grounds that if their general validity were not stated, there would be no arising of an expectation for specific means such as praise (*stuti*).
Furthermore, by this, the two types of connection previously established—namely, those consisting of *prasaṅga* (logical consequence) and *ākṣepa* (objection)—are demonstrated.
"In relation to dharma and adharma" is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
"Of injunction and prohibition":
injunction and prohibition are synonyms for incitement (*pravartanā*) and dissuasion (*nivartanā*).

Regarding the phrase "by implication" (*arthāt*): since the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained through any other means, and since the understanding of "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and so forth is possible through inference alone, one need not postulate a direct denotative power (*śakti*) for it there, as the Naiyāyikas do.
The method of such inference has been demonstrated by the venerable [Śalikanātha] in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*.
(An explanation of the phrase *sadasadrūpa*): Regarding the term *sadasadrūpa*,

by this [the author] intends that since qualities such as being the swiftest mover of air (*vāyukṣepiṣṭhatva*) are already established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), they lack the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*) consisting in the capacity to apprehend an object not yet known (*anadhigatārthagantṛtva*).

In cases such as "The pressing-stones float," since even the criterion of correspondence with reality is impossible, it is all the more evident that the authority of the Veda regarding future dharma and adharma cannot be established by its capacity to convey accomplished facts— this is what has been indicated.

(An examination of the nature of the non-alteration of characteristics and so forth, with examples: [The phrase] "by means of the supply of characteristics and so forth" includes the alteration of characteristics, the attribution of qualities, and the like, by the word "and so forth."

As it has been said: "Supplying an ellipsis, implying what is not heard, transposition, intervention by words, modification— consisting of the alteration of a root or a suffix— and the alteration of a sentence, as well as the assumption of a restriction."
The term "cuts" (*chinatti*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. "Transposition" (*vyatyāsa*) refers to the conceptualization of a connection between words that are separated,
as for example in the mantra "yā te agne rajāśayā," where a connection is conceived with the word *tanūr varṣiṣṭhā* which stands at a distance.
Modification (*vipariṇāma*) is, for example, [the change from] "those desiring a firm foundation should approach the nights" (*pratitiṣṭhantīty atra pratiṣṭhākāmā rātrīr upeyuḥ*) and so forth.

The assumption of restriction (*vyavaccheda-kalpanā*) is, for example, [the change from] "as many horses as one might receive" (*yāvato 'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt*) to "one should cause [him] to receive [them]" (*pratigrāhayet*).
The assumption of a quality (*guṇa-kalpanā*) is, for example, [the statement] "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*).
The definitions and examples accepted by the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) are characterized by excellence (*prāśastya*) and lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*).
[This concerns] the justification of the definition of a sentence (*vākya-lakṣaṇa*): does that [sentence-meaning] reside in a single word?
Or [is it] in each of all [the causes] individually, or in them combined? Not the first.
Because there is no determining factor [to distinguish them],
and because otherwise the other names would result in meaninglessness;
nor is there another [possibility], since each individual word lacks a connection with either praise or censure.

And because it is not perceived [as such], the latter [alternative] is not tenable; for there is no single referent in the combined [words], since indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consists precisely in a possible relation [of the primary meaning]. Therefore, it must be admitted that indication occurs in a sentence; yet even there, it is impossible due to the absence of a cause and because a sentence lacks a single primary referent.

Thus he says: "according to the literal meaning" and "due to the absence of anything indicating the intended meaning. The sense is that the status of being intended as dharma or adharma is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Of that too" means because the intended purpose (tātparya) is untenable;
[it refers to] "a subject matter possessing a purpose."

The meaning is that [the subject matter] concerns objects suitable for the purpose of engaging in or desisting from action. This is because it is impossible for things that are purposeless, such as those in the form of mere narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), to be something that is to be brought about (*bhāvya*).

The meaning is that, because only that which constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is required as the objective (*bhāvya*) by the injunction, it is impossible for that which is not such [a goal] to be the objective.

(This establishes the view that the purpose of study is the knowledge of the meaning, in order to avoid the inconsistency arising from [the distinction between] being a subordinate action (*guṇakarman*) and a principal action (*pradhānakarman*)):
"The meaning possesses utility."

Furthermore, regarding the injunctive portion (*codanāṃśa*), the visible purpose of the cultivation of study (*adhyayanabhāvanā*) is simply the knowledge of the meaning. Likewise, even with respect to all other portions, that [cultivation] must have a visible purpose; otherwise, in the portion where there is a visible purpose, study would be a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*) toward that portion, whereas in the portion where there is an invisible purpose, it would be [a subordinate action] toward that [portion].

Because it would result in a lack of uniformity due to the [Veda] being a primary object (*pradhānakarma*), the opponent’s intention is as follows: in accordance with that [primary status], even in every respect, the fact that [the study] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) cannot be established without the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise and blame conducive to engagement and desistance. Thus, if the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*) were for the sake of the injunction for study itself, its fruit—whether visible or invisible—would have to be sought.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "That very [point] is untenable, because it is not something to be enjoined."
(Regarding the doubt and its resolution concerning the restrictive injunction of study for the purpose of knowing the meaning or for the purpose of the *apūrva* of the sacrifice:

Nor should it be argued that—since other means might optionally be available for the knowledge of the meaning, the injunction may still possess purposefulness in its aspect as a restriction regarding study;
for there is no clear utility of [the knowledge of meaning] in the act of study itself.

"For in the act of study, the visible result is the knowledge of meaning; therefore, it has no utility—either as the unseen merit (*apūrva*) produced by the ritual being performed, or in either of those two respects—as he says: 'And of that restriction' (*tanniyamasya ca*).

For the presentation of the *apūrva* produced by a sacrifice would occur either through the context (*prakaraṇa*), or through an invariable connection with the sacrifice, as in the case of [the quality of] being made of *parṇa-wood* and so forth.
In this regard, since the injunction for study is taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), the absence of a context is quite clear."

Since the knowledge of meaning can be utilized for the acquisition of wealth through means such as teaching even without a ritual sacrifice, an invariable connection with a sacrifice is not possible; therefore, the restriction cannot be an object of injunction, especially because a restriction has no utility in regard to prohibited actions.

Furthermore, because such a restriction is of no utility for the knowledge of meaning, and because it is impossible to assume that study extends as far as its utility in the sacrifice—given the absence of an invariable connection with the sacrifice—it cannot be the object of an injunction.
Therefore, by the injunction for the private recitation (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), study is enjoined solely for the sake of heaven and the like;
or, by acknowledging its prior occurrence in the world, it is for the sake of knowing the meaning exactly as it is heard in the text.
Alternatively, let study itself be the object to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) in the process of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Nor does it follow that activity would be untenable due to the absence of a desired object of cultivation; for even in the absence of such a desire, activity is established by the scriptural statement, "Those who do not study become outcasts (*vrātya*)," which makes known that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance.

Therefore, since the injunction regarding Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) does not, by virtue of its being delimited as "Veda-ness," necessitate that the subject matter must possess a purpose, there is no establishment of figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) on the strength of that injunction. Thus, it is argued that the *arthavādas* are not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma and adharma. To this, the following is stated:
the injunction regarding Vedic study does not enjoin study for the sake of heaven and the like; [rather, it enjoins it] for the sake of knowing the meaning.
Because it is improper to postulate an unseen result when a seen one is possible;

nor is it for the sake of knowing the meaning of the text as it is heard, because if that were the case, study would be mandatory by virtue of the sentence indicating the status of a *vrātya* for one who has already grasped the words and their mutual connections.

Furthermore, because of such statements as, "This [Vedic student] is a mere wooden post, a mere bearer of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning," knowledge is also indispensable; thus, even though the knowledge of the literal meaning arises as a necessary consequence,
it is for the sake of attaining heaven and other such goals.

The word "etc. (ādi) is used to indicate that, rather than postulating heaven as the result according to the principle of the *viśvajit* sacrifice, it is more appropriate—following the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the postulation of a Vedic source for the Smṛti rule "those who do not study become outcasts" (*vrātya*) in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), as in the case of the *rātrisatra*—to hold that this injunction is intended solely for the purpose of avoiding the state of being an outcast.
Furthermore, this does not entail the previously demonstrated defect of dual character (*vairūpya*) in the injunction to study.

Since you yourself must accept that the study of [Vedic texts] such as "Huṃ Phaṭ" and so forth has an invisible (transcendental) purpose, it is more appropriate to assume that this [study of the Veda] also serves that same purpose, in order to maintain consistency.

For even if the injunctions produce authority regarding Dharma by making known a purposeful object through their own inherent power, there is no contradiction in the study of the Veda having an invisible purpose.

(An examination of the purpose for excluding Śūdras from eligibility regarding the recitation of the Vedas (*pārāyaṇa*) and so forth, which precedes the commencement of the treatise from the perspective of worldly convention):
He states [the following] to counter the insistence that the injunction to study has only a visible purpose: "From the perspective of worldly convention" (*lokataḥ*).
The purpose of its prior operation from the perspective of worldly convention, however, is the establishment of the non-eligibility of Śūdras for the *pārāyaṇa*.

Otherwise, since recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) could occur even without formal study (*adhyayana*), if that [recitation] were to imply such study by means of its own injunction, it would follow that even a Śūdra would possess the entitlement [to perform it].

However, when this injunction exists, since an eligible person is obtained who already possesses the study established by this very injunction, there is no implication [of further study], and thus he has no entitlement.
And in this way, the complete recitation of a single Vedic branch (*ekaśākhā-pārāyaṇa*) is also logically justified.
"Or rather, it is study itself.

The meaning is that, with respect to the knowledge of the meaning as heard, since study is proximate to the productive operation (bhāvanā) by virtue of its being conveyed by the same word, it is logical that study alone should be the object to be accomplished (bhāvya).
The establishment of the characteristics and so forth.

And by the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), it is indicated that just as the definition is unestablished, so too the object to be defined— such as its excellence or lack thereof— is unestablished because it is difficult to determine.
(Refutation of the view that excellence and non-excellence consist merely in the presence of qualities and defects):
For that [excellence] is not merely the possession of qualities and defects;
because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can there be an excellence [in one] over the other;
for excellence is relative and thus lacks a fixed basis, and because virtues and defects— which are established merely through figurative praise (arthavāda)— cannot be definitively determined.

Since the fact that [an action] possesses distinguished desirable or undesirable results, the fact that it has a distinguished procedure (*itikartavyatā*), or the fact that it is the object of eternal, faultless Vedic injunctions and prohibitions, is understood through the injunctions and prohibitions themselves, there is no dependence upon explanatory passages (*arthavādas*).
Furthermore, excellence and defect do not consist in the possession of desirable or undesirable results;
for those two as well are understood solely through injunctions and prohibitions.

For even without [the action] being the means to a desired or undesired end, there is an absence of engagement or withdrawal for those who act without prior reflection unless it also possesses a result;
furthermore, this is untenable in the case of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the *śyena* sacrifice and others,
because since the *śyena* and such are themselves harmful, the desired result produced by them lacks any greater force than the undesired one.

Nor can it be maintained that the very qualities such as "quickness" (kṣepiṣṭhatva) propounded by those respective explanatory passages (arthavādas) constitute praise or censure in the form of merit or defect;

for this would lack consistency and would result in the impossibility of [the words] being used in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇika). Therefore, since such a status is difficult to establish, the explanatory passages do not serve as a means of valid knowledge regarding dharma and adharma even by virtue of making those qualities known.
(An exposition of the view that the injunction for study has the acquisition of syllables as its fruit:
By this very statement indicating the status of a *vrātya*, the injunction for study is obtained.

It might be argued as follows: if the knowledge of the meaning were the fruit of the injunction to study from the very beginning, then, because that [mere recitation] would otherwise result in futility, one would have to postulate an operation extending even to the implication of its purposefulness.
However, there is no evidence whatsoever for the postulation of such a thing.

Even under the view that the purpose [of study] is the knowledge of the meaning— since the attainment of the syllables, consisting in their mastery through one's own recitation, is required first as the means to accomplish that knowledge; and since this visible result can itself serve as the fruit for the recitation of the *stobha* sections (which are brought forward as the fruit by the cognition of the meaning of the karma to be performed), there is no futility of the injunction to study.

Because the causality residing in study, as defined by the knowledge of the meaning to be accomplished through reflection (*vicāra*), cannot be fulfilled without the acquisition of the syllables (*akṣara*).
Or, let it be that the knowledge of the meaning is the fruit;

even so, since the fact that [study] is for the sake of knowing the meaning is already established by other means, in order to avoid the redundancy of the injunction, one must conclude that only those who possess the knowledge of the Vedic meaning acquired through study perform the ritual acts, and such performance leads to prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and so forth.

If one accepts that the fruit of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) pertains solely to the form [of the action], then there would be a failure to produce the fruit from the performance of Vedic study, twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), and so forth;

for if those injunctions were known through other means prior to the study, there would arise the fault of transgressing the injunction of restriction regarding study, whereas if they were not known, there would follow the contingency of sin resulting from their non-performance due to a lack of engagement in the study and other such acts.
(An objection regarding the purpose of excluding Śūdras from the eligibility for the injunction of study which has the knowledge of meaning as its fruit, and its resolution:

Nor can it be argued that the result of the restrictive rule of study is not postulated as being that the performance [of rituals] by those who possess the knowledge of the Vedic meaning acquired through study alone leads to prosperity;
rather, its purpose is the establishment of the lack of eligibility for Śūdras.

For ritual injunctions, like the knowledge of the meaning of what is to be performed, require an eligible person (*adhikārin*). If the injunction for Vedic study has the knowledge of the meaning as its fruit, then since the performance is obtained through that injunction within the eligibility of the three castes who possess the knowledge of the meaning to be performed, they do not imply the knowledge [of the meaning] for Śūdras. However, if it does not have the knowledge of the meaning as its fruit, then the ritual injunctions themselves would imply their performance and include them as well as eligible persons.
Therefore, it should not be argued that the very establishment of the Śūdra’s lack of entitlement is itself the result when the purpose [of study] is the knowledge of the meaning;

for even if the rule of formal study (*adhyayana*) exists, the consequence of the Śūdra’s entitlement remains unavoidable, since even for the three higher castes there is only their own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*) transmitted through the lineage of fathers and grandfathers, according to the injunction: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied."

It should not be argued that, because study is enjoined, the ritual injunctions— by means of the synthesis of auxiliary mantras found in other recensions for the purpose of performing the rites— would, through the parsimony of implication (*ākṣepalāghava*), have as their scope only what is recorded in those other recensions, and thus would entitle only the three higher castes to perform the rituals and not a Śūdra.

If that were the case, then for whichever ritual action there is an injunction of many constituent parts (*aṅga*) in a particular recensional branch (*śākhā*), the primary action itself would also be enjoined therein according to the maxim "by virtue of the majority of scriptural statements" (*bhūyastvenobhayaśruti*);
whereas in another branch, there might be an injunction of only a few constituent parts.
Consequently, it would follow that only those who study that specific branch would have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform that ritual action.

Since for those of the three higher castes there is a necessary implication of the knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda], and since the Śūdra lacks eligibility [for Vedic study], the very reason for his prohibition from performing [Vedic rites] must be stated as his lack of entitlement to grasp the Veda and its meaning. Therefore, the prohibition against the Śūdra is not the result of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding study which has the knowledge of meaning as its fruit; rather, it is appropriate to maintain that the attainment of the syllables themselves is the fruit of that injunction.
Because [the Veda] would already be established [as authoritative], it would follow that the injunction for private study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) is purposeless.
By this, the position that the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) by study is [merely the act of recitation] is also refuted.
Therefore, in order to avoid this purposelessness, [the injunction must be understood] as aiming at the knowledge of the meaningful content.

(Refutation of the claim that the purposefulness of an utterance depends on its being intended for the comprehension of a specific meaning): Nor can it be argued that, since in all worldly cases it is established that the purposefulness (*arthaparatva*) of words depends on their being uttered with the intention of bringing about the cognition of a specific meaning,

one must therefore— in order to establish purposefulness in the Veda as well— imply an utterance intended for the comprehension of meaning, just as in the world, [an utterance] prompted by personal desire (*rāga*).

It should not be argued that—since such [recitation for its own sake] is impossible, since no injunction other than the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is observed, and since the recitation taught by the injunction of study—which consists in the repetition of what is uttered by the teacher—must necessarily be offered as having the knowledge of meaning as its root—the knowledge of meaning alone must be postulated as the fruit, and thus my own position is the correct one. For if the recitation aimed at the comprehension of a specific meaning were the factor that necessitates the text’s being "for the sake of the meaning" (*arthaparatva*), then in the case of a verse or similar text written down and given by a mute person, or when another person, upon seeing a single instance of writing, mentally reconstructs it; [in these cases, the recitation would fail to necessitate the text’s being for the sake of meaning].
Because, in the absence of utterance, there would be no attainment of the status of being intent upon meaning.
(The refutation that the state of being an activity aimed at the cognition of a qualified meaning is the determinant for being intent upon meaning.

Even so—if it were argued that the very state of being an activity aimed at the cognition of a qualified meaning is the determinant for determining the intentionality (*tātparya*) toward a meaning—[the response follows].
If it were argued that in the world of Mauniśrī, the activity of writing is itself the instigating cause of the act of giving,

whereas in the Veda— which is not of human origin— since there is no activity of an author, no activity conducive to it other than the utterance in the form of recitation is possible; therefore, in order to ensure its meaningfulness, one must necessarily accept that the injunction to study has the knowledge of meaning as its fruit.

If the knowledge of speaker’s intention (*tātparyajñāna*) were the cause for verbal cognition (*śabdabodha*) as delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition in general, then it would follow that such a cognition could not arise from the speech of parrots and the like, which are devoid of intention. Therefore, its causality does not reside solely in [verbal cognition] as delimited by being a verbal cognition produced by words that convey a single meaning.

Alternatively, if [verbal testimony] is a cause even with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then in cases such as the speech of parrots and the like, one must assume an intention residing solely in the word;
and since this is the same in the case of the Veda as well, there is no need for an operation established by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*);
for the fact that [the Veda] has the purpose of conveying meaning is established simply by inferring the intention through the very nature of the words.
(Conclusion on the fact that reflection (*vicāra*) is the determinant for the purposefulness of the meaning, preceded by the demonstration that the fruit of study is the acquisition of the syllables:
Let it be granted that being an activity aimed at the comprehension of meaning is the determinant for the determination of meaning;

nevertheless, let it be that reflection itself—which is distinct from mere study and which must be performed immediately after study with the aim of comprehending the meaning of the entire *svādhyāya*—is that very determinant.

For without inquiry (*vicāra*), it is not possible for anyone to determine the meaning of the Vedas as required for sacrifices (*kratu*) and meditations (*upāsanā*). Therefore, since inquiry itself is logically established as the primary cause for the Vedas having meaning as their purpose, there is no need to assume that the acquisition of knowledge of the meaning is also a result [of Vedic study], by bypassing the attainment of the syllables—which is obtained through the natural force of the *tavya* suffix—in order to justify study as the cause of that [meaning]. This [verse] is intended to remove such a doubt.
He explains the meaning of the sentence as accepted by the Siddhāntin: "Therefore, for the sake of avoiding futility...
(The fact that study has the purpose of being directed toward the meaning).

This is the sense: it is true that, like the case of the sentences of Śuka and others, one must admit that the intention (*tātparya*) resides in the word itself for the sake of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; yet—

Nevertheless, although the determination that such is the purport of the word—based on the consideration of the opening, the conclusion, and the internal consistency—is established in the Veda solely through its study and so forth, it is the injunction for that study itself which is the decisive factor therein;

for if one were to recite Vedic sentences according to one's own whim, one might even utter the word "fruit" (*phala*) in the subsidiary sentences, or derive the understanding of such meanings as: "He who is the Adhvaryu is the Hotṛ," or "Those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*)."
Nor is it the case that the inquiry performed immediately after study is itself the means of determining that [meaning],
because if study were not for the purpose of knowing the meaning, there would be no impetus for the necessity of inquiry, and thus inquiry itself would not even be established.
(Regarding the resolution of the doubt that *vicāra* is established by a *śruti* inferred from an *liṅga*):

Nor should it be argued that—when the *svādhyāya* sanctified by study requires an application, its application to the knowledge of meaning is postulated through a *śruti* inferred from the *liṅga* consisting in the fact that the *svādhyāya* generates the knowledge of meaning; and since that [application] is not possible without inquiry (*vicāra*), inquiry is thereby obtained. This is because:

Since the requirement for the application of the Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*)—which has been refined by study—for the purpose of knowing its meaning is already satisfied prior [to the consideration of the *liṅga*] by the injunctions regarding the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) and so forth, there is no scope for a *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) to be inferred from the *liṅga* (indicative power).

Furthermore, since *liṅga* is observed to produce knowledge of the meaning exactly as it is heard in the text, even the *śruti* inferred from that *liṅga* would result in that same meaning; thus, there would be no need for inquiry into that matter.
Moreover, because the Vedic recitation does not produce knowledge of meaning in parts such as "huṃ" and "phaṭ," the capacity to generate such knowledge is vitiated by inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, since the mere acquisition of syllables (*akṣara*) is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it cannot logically function as a fruit [of study]; therefore, its status as a fruit is established only by way of being a means for the knowledge of meaning.

However, since the knowledge of meaning likewise lacks intrinsic status as a human goal, it too can only be established as a fruit by way of being a means for the knowledge of meaning that is conducive to the performance of ritual acts (*karmānuṣṭhāna*).
Its status as a fruit must be accepted.

For it is not possible to understand, by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone, that the syllables of the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) culminate in the human goal through their utility for the performance of rituals via the knowledge of their meaning;
this is because no knowledge of meaning arises from syllables such as *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, or those found in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Furthermore, because there is deviation even when the knowledge of the meaning arises from certain syllables of the Veda,
and because in that case it depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes its general relationship [with the meaning],

therefore, ultimately, since the utility of grasping the syllables of one's own study (*svādhyāya*) must necessarily be postulated for the sake of the knowledge of the meaning conducive to the performance of rituals, it is simpler to postulate that very [grasping of syllables] as the fruit.
However, the attainment of the Imperishable does not follow merely from its being perceived immediately [after the injunction];

for it is only that which is known as being fit to be the fruit of what is enjoined— whether directly or through an indirect means— that serves to complete the understanding of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*),

whereas the knowledge of the meaning [of the Upaniṣads] cannot possibly lead to the performance of ritual action without that [attainment of the Imperishable], and thus [the Upaniṣadic teaching] is established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself.

Since it is logical that the knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth possesses the status of being an auxiliary to ritual action— just like the knowledge that [certain rites] have results pertaining to the next world— it is appropriate that this very knowledge, once known, constitutes the fruit; otherwise, if only the intermediate state of being freed from husks were the fruit, then even acts such as threshing would fail to have the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as their purpose.
(The manner in which the object to be realized, consisting of the knowledge of the meaning, is presented:
Nor should it be argued—how can the knowledge of the meaning, being unestablished, be connected as the object to be realized (*bhāvya*) within the cultivation of study (*adhyayanabhāvanā*)?

For, by means of the injunction (*vidhi*), there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) that its own object is a means to what is desired; and in common worldly practice, when activity occurs toward the utterance of words, [the knowledge of their meaning is required].

Since the knowledge of meaning useful for practical application (*vyavahāra*) alone is established as the intended goal of study, and since such [meaning] can be presented simply by virtue of the very nature of study— which consists in the utterance of words— for one who studies merely for the sake of acquiring the syllables, as indicated by the verse: "This man is like a pillar, a mere carrier of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning."

Furthermore, because it is clearly understood through the mention of its being a mere post (*sthāṇu*) that [the recitation] culminates in something that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*); and [this is done] precisely to demonstrate the utility [of the recitation] as a means (*dvāra*) for that very non-human goal, even though it was the first thing required.

Moreover, when there is an expectancy for a fruit regarding the study (*adhyayana*), there is a necessary consideration of its culminating in a human goal due to the force of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Since there is a lack of evidence for the sacrifice and so forth—which are either directly related or proximately adjacent to that [result]—and because they possess a requirement for a means (*sādhana*), it is logical that the knowledge of action (*karmajñāna*) alone, which is separated from it by only one intervening step, should be the end to be attained (*bhāvya*); this is because there is no reason to bypass it.
It is not, however, logical that the acquisition of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*), which is separated from it by a great distance, should be the end to be attained.

If that were the case, there would follow the consequence of an excessive mediation between the human goal and [the means] by means of those subsequent steps— such as the determination of the words— which would be independent [of knowledge];
for if knowledge is what is to be produced, then those [steps] are merely instrumental doors and thus do not constitute a mediation.

By this, the claim that the attainment of the syllable (*akṣara*) is the fruit because it is mentioned first is refuted; for the priority belonging to the object that serves as a means (*dvāra*) does not establish that the fruit culminates in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Otherwise, since an unaccomplished thing cannot function as an instrument, its status as something to be brought about (*bhāvyatva*) would necessarily require priority. Consequently, by virtue of its proximity to what is expressed in the same word (*samānapadopātta*), the sacrifice itself—serving as the means to heaven—would result in being the object to be brought about by the objective efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*).

Therefore, even for the first [result], which is not itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), its status as the "thing-to-be-produced" (*bhāvya*) must conform to the fact that it is understood through an injunction as a means to something desired; thus, just as with the sacrifice, the attainment of the syllables (*akṣarāvāpti*) is likewise [not the primary result].
Consequently, as long as possible, it is the knowledge of the meaning—which culminates in a human goal—that is postulated as the visible fruit, and not the attainment of the syllables.

(The study of the Veda for the sake of knowing its meaning is prompted by its own injunction, not by the injunctions of the sacrificial rites; furthermore, it does not entail the cognition of other branches of the Veda upon which one's own recitation depends.)
And thus, since the injunctions for sacrifices do not entail the necessity of knowing the meaning [of the entire Veda], it is established that even a Śūdra lacks eligibility for them.
Otherwise, because one would be unable to perform the ritual without knowledge of the meaning, it would follow that the injunctions must entail other means for the sake of acquiring that knowledge.
Nor should it be argued that the injunctions for sacrifices must indeed be assumed to entail the knowledge of the meanings of the subsidiary (aṅga) passages found in other recensions (śākhā); for...
Even in that case— namely, regarding the study of one's own and others' traditional branches— the injunction for study, in order to fulfill its own purpose as having a visible result (*dṛṣṭārtha*),

implies the study of at least that much [of the other branches] because the valid cognition of the meaning of the sentences contained in one's own branch depends upon the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences contained in other branches. Since this results in the attainment of knowledge of the meanings of the texts through that very [study] prompted by the injunction, there is no evidence for postulating that the ritual injunctions themselves imply such [study].

Therefore, even in a case where— by the principle "where both are heard, [the rite belongs to that which has] the greater number"— the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) in a particular recensional branch (*śākhā*) is established by the strength of many subsidiary elements (*aṅga*), while in one's own studied branch there is the injunction of only a few subsidiaries, the knowledge of the meaning of those subsidiary-injunctive sentences (which constitute the means of ascertaining the subsidiaries) is dependent upon the knowledge of the meaning of the primary injunctive sentence;

thus, for the sake of fulfilling its own purpose as seen through the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the knowledge of the meaning must be preceded by the study of that very primary injunctive sentence.
Since it is [the injunction] that is impelled, the injunctions regarding the seasons do not, in any case, have the capacity to impel the knowledge of their meaning.

(Conclusion of the position that the purpose of study is the knowledge of meaning, preceded by a description of the fault [in the view] that study aims at heaven or the acquisition of syllables, a description of the purpose of the injunctions regarding that [study] as being for the sake of knowing the meaning, and a description of the lack of eligibility for Śūdras.

Therefore, if study were for the sake of heaven and so forth, then—just like the threshing of all medicinal herbs—the purpose of the scripture would be accomplished even by a single recitation; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the status of study as a *saṃskāra-karman* (a preparatory rite), which is understood from the designation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) as the object (*karman*) of the action.

If, for the sake of fulfilling that [injunction], one were to accept the acquisition of the syllables (*akṣarāvāpti*) as the fruit, there would result the burden of implying the investigation into the knowledge of meaning within the injunctions of sacrifices;

furthermore, since it would be purposeless with respect to the nature of the *svādhyāya* itself, and because it is studied independently (*anārabhyādhīta*), the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by recitation (*pārāyaṇa*)—just like the sacrificial *apūrva*—cannot be indicated by the term *svādhyāya*. This is because, unlike the knowledge of meaning, the acquisition of syllables lacks an invariable connection (*avyabhicarita-sambandha*) with sacrifices, as it does not necessarily co-occur with ritual acts and the like.

Because the ritual act is not present [in the case of the mere recitation], it does not possess the status of being the fruit of that act; rather, it is the knowledge of the meaning and so forth that constitutes the fruit.
And that [knowledge] must be induced by the rituals through other means, such as reading from a book, expertise, observation, or the words of others.
Therefore, even prior to the commencement of the injunction for study, the cessation of that [injunction] is postulated as the result of the restrictive rule (*niyama*).

And its purpose is the restriction of eligibility to the three social classes (*traivarṇika*). For one who recognizes that the performance of sacrifices is impossible without the knowledge of their meaning, and thus understands that the ritual injunctions depend upon such knowledge, there arises the knowledge of the meaning characterized by the restrictive rule of studying the text along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-adhyayana*).

Furthermore, for a person who perceives the requirement of a purpose, once the understanding has been produced— either by means of an inference based on an indicative mark (*liṅga*) or by the scriptural statement "Whatever one performs with knowledge"— that such knowledge of the meaning is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice, it necessarily follows that only one possessing such knowledge is qualified (*adhikāra*) for the sacrifices.

(An exposition of the utility, as appropriate, of the rule of study—according to the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*—with respect to the sacrifice and the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of expiation): Let it be granted that, even though the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice, the fires characterized by the *apūrva* produced thereby are auxiliaries to the sacrifice; likewise, even though the study itself is not an auxiliary, the knowledge of the meaning characterized by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rule of study is understood to be an auxiliary to ritual action through a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) inferred from the previously mentioned indicative marks (*liṅga*). Thus, like the *āhavanīya* fire, the unseen merit of the rule [is also required].

According to the method stated by the author of the *Bhaṭṭālaṅkāra*, the restriction (*niyama*) serves the sacrifice (*kratu*) only through its indirect application to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the rite;

thus, since the restriction of study finds its purpose in prohibitions for the sake of the sacrifice, even regarding prohibitions for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), one learns— by means of the very prohibition acquired through study— that one’s own performed action produces a fault, and consequently, that fault is removed by performing the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) undertaken for the sake of its cessation.
Since the application [of the rite] is postulated as being for the sake of an unprecedented merit (*apūrva*) that serves as expiation in this manner, there is no contradiction.

(B1) The study of one’s own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is enjoined; this refers either to mere study directed toward the *svādhyāya* which serves as a means for attaining purposeful knowledge of the meaning and so forth, or—
(B2)— [it refers to] the refutation [of the view] that obligatory injunctions (*nityavidhi*) do not necessitate the knowledge of the meaning.

Nor should it be argued that, because there is no evidence for the compulsory performance of Vedic study, the compulsory injunctions would necessarily entail the requirement of knowing the meaning [of the texts];

for even in the case of compulsory ritual injunctions (*kratu-vidhi*), since it is established through parsimony (*lāghava*) that they depend on fire and knowledge acquired from others, there is eligibility for one who possesses the fire and knowledge established by their own injunctions.

Thus, although no transgression arises from the non-performance [of the ritual] for such a person, for one lacking those [fire and knowledge], a transgression does arise precisely because of his lack of eligibility.
Because, in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is untenable for [the knowledge of fire] to depend upon the injunction regarding fire;

and as for the statement of Pārthasārathi that, since the injunctions for sacrifices are eternal in this way, the injunctions for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and so forth are also effectively eternal—
that will be refuted by the Venerable Teacher himself in the section beginning with "of the Brāhmaṇa" in the sixth book.
By this, [the objection] that the performance of obligatory rites is impossible without the knowledge of the meaning established by the injunction to study is refuted.
As for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), its obligatoriness is to be inferred precisely from the scriptural prescription of penance for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

And thus, since eligibility for the obligatory rites belongs only to one who possesses the fire and knowledge established through study and fire-laying, there is no consequence of the injunctions for the obligatory sacrifices implying those [acts of study and fire-laying].
(An examination of how the injunctions regarding twilight prayers and other rites imply the teacher’s instruction and so forth:

For this very reason, for those for whom the injunctions for twilight prayers and the like have already commenced prior to the commencement of the injunction for Vedic study immediately after the instruction in the Gāyatrī, it is possible that the knowledge of the meaning is prompted by the injunction for study; therefore, even in cases not subject to restrictive rules (*niyama*), there certainly exists the implication of the teacher’s instruction and other means that serve as instruments for the knowledge of the meaning.
Just as in the case of the injunctions for the Niṣādasthapati sacrifice and others.

(Regarding the view that the purpose is the knowledge of the meaning, the justification for the suffix *tavya* in the phrase "it should be studied" [is as follows], according to the opinion of Miśra, Bhavadeva, and others):

Nor should it be argued—how can the suffix *tavya*, which indicates that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is the object (*karman*), be justified if the knowledge of the meaning is what is to be brought about (*bhāvya*)?
For its justification is possible by taking the knowledge of the meaning to be the intended object of refinement (*saṃskārya*).

For instance, regarding the injunction "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), the suffix *tavya* is prescribed in the sense of an injunction (*praiṣa*) by the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating, "The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the senses of injunction, permission, and [indicating] that the time has arrived. Furthermore, an injunction consists of a composite nature comprising both the reference to a matter already established (*prāptaviṣayakatva*) and the element of instigation (*pravartanātmakatva*); and since this composite nature is present in the Brāhmaṇa texts as well, [the injunction is established].

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the Brahmin to have already attained the object [of the action], even though the collective whole [of the agent and object] is not possible, the instigation (*pravartanā*) is expressed by the suffix *tavya* through a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a part of that whole.
As it has been said: "When [the object] is already attained, the recollection of instigation is called an injunction (*praiṣa*);
when the injunction concerns what is not yet attained, everything attains the status of a rule (*vidhi*)."

And since that [activity] consists of an operation conducive to engagement (*pravṛtti*), the objective productive activity (*arthībhāvanā*) whose form is engagement is also implied by that very [word].

And according to the principle of the sixth [book] and so forth, the knowledge of the purposeful meaning itself is accepted as the object to be produced (*bhāvya*), as far as possible. Then, when there is a requirement for an instrument (*karaṇa*), study (*adhyayana*) is the instrument due to its proximity, according to the principle of the section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*).

In this regard, since it is logically untenable for study (*adhyayana*) to be a means for knowing the meaning of words that are not [already] manifest as sound, it becomes such by way of the acquisition of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), in accordance with its capacity. Furthermore, since it would be impossible for study to be a means for that [knowledge of meaning] without the Vedic recitation itself being a means for knowing the meaning— and because [the acquisition] cannot serve as a medium unless it possesses that status— it follows by implication that the Vedic recitation also possesses the status of being a means for that [knowledge].
Just as [the Soma] is a means for you both in the case of the *sāman*s being the means of praise, so too [is the Veda].

Consequently, in the verbal cognition, by applying the "barley-grain" (*saktu*) maxim, one may postulate a displacement of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*); thus, even though the Veda is subordinate (*guṇatva*), because the acquisition of it serves as the door (*dvāra*), it also possesses the status of being the object (*karmatva*) to be attained through implication. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the objecthood expressed by the suffix *-tavya*.
In every respect, [the view that study is for its own sake] is untenable;

rather, the intention to express the oneness inherent in the Vedic text is established as something to be undertaken because of the necessity of study. Thus, according to the method established in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* and the perspective of Miśra, Bhavadeva, and others, study is indeed an action directed toward the meaning (*arthakarma*), being performed with the aim of attaining purposeful knowledge of the meaning and so forth.
The author of the root text has stated one position: that the study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāya-adhyayana) is enjoined.

As he said: "The status of the word as a subordinate factor for the cognition of an object—which is a constituent part of purposeful worldly activity—is determined by its fitness, given that [the word itself] is devoid of intrinsic fruit."

(The empirical purpose of the general study of all [Vedic texts], including *huṃ* and *phaṭ*): By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), even though the study of the *Sāmans* serves the purpose of knowing their meaning by means of manifesting the syllables, that which is impossible in every respect regarding the portions consisting of *stobha* elements such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ*— namely, the filling of the fixed duration— is also included as an empirical purpose.
Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the injunction for study,
nor is there a syntactical split; for its purpose is not merely the accomplishment of the comprehension of the meaning.

According to the method established by Miśra and others in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*— namely, "Whatever is seen to be capable of being accomplished is all intended as the fruit"— one takes "being seen" (*dṛṣṭatva*) as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, by means of a single syntactical turn, one obtains the sense that "one should bring about whatever can be brought about through the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) that is useful for other injunctions," and thereby all purposes are attained, so that no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) occurs.
Therefore—it will be stated in the fifth [book] that the order of recitation is indeed understood from the injunction for study.

For this very reason, even regarding those portions of the Veda which prescribe rites to be performed by Brāhmaṇas and others as agents, since the knowledge of the meaning produced by study leads one to realize that they are to be performed by an agent other than oneself, it is observed that the purpose [of such realization] is simply the non-engagement in those rites taught therein. Thus, it is not [the case that the Veda lacks a purpose].
In that case as well, there would be the fallacy of inconsistency (*vairūpyāpatti*).

As for what has been stated by some in the *Bhāṭṭabhāskara*, a commentary on the *Śāstradīpikā*, regarding such matters—that the visible purpose is merely the apprehension of syllables useful for recitation (*japa*), complete study (*pārāyaṇa*), and so forth;

that [view] should be disregarded, because if the apprehension of syllables must necessarily be postulated as a result in some instances, then by the principle of uniformity (*aikarūpya*) it would follow that it is the result in all cases, which renders its being the result of knowing the meaning untenable.
(An argument supporting the view of the ancient Mīmāṃsakas— that study is a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*)— without contradicting the position that it is for the purpose of knowing the meaning):

In reality, however, since the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text), which is denoted as the object (*karman*) by the suffix *-tavya*, would suffer a contradiction of its perceived primacy if it were construed as a subordinate factor (*guṇa*),

and since it is impossible for the *svādhyāya* to function as an object in any other way, its connection [with the act of study] is established through its status as an "object to be reached" (*prāpyakarman*).

When the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) appears to be purposeless in its literal form, since the act of study consists in the utterance of sounds and such utterance is conventionally understood to produce knowledge of meaning, one accepts—

on the basis of the capacity of the injunction and the suitability of the object of that injunction (*uddeśya*) to produce knowledge of meaning— that the *svādhyāya* is indeed capable of producing knowledge of meaning. Thus, because knowledge of meaning is present and because the study of one's own Veda is a means for attaining human goals such as that very knowledge, one adopts a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *svādhyāya* to denote "knowledge of meaning" and so forth.
It is appropriate that the injunction for study is directed toward that [Veda] alone;

therefore, in order to demonstrate that the view of the elder Mīmāṃsakas—that it is indeed a purificatory rite (saṃskārakarma)—is the correct one, he states the second position: "because it has a purpose" (*prayojanavat*).

(Refutation of the prima facie view regarding the meaning of the injunction for study: *adhyayanena svādhyāyaṃ bhāvayet*) As for the claim made by the authors of the *Bhāṭṭalaṅkāra* and other works— that the injunction for study, teaching at first sight that one should "bring about the Veda (*svādhyāya*) by means of study," then, upon the inquiry into the purpose of the Veda, [indicates] that "one should bring about the knowledge of a purposeful meaning by means of the Veda thus studied"— [this is refuted as follows].
It has been stated that [the injunction] makes one understand [the meaning] through modification, because the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is fit for use and thus differs from barley-gruel (*saktu*);

however, that is not correct. For if the attainment of the syllables were also a fruit, then—according to the method previously established—the fact that the Veda is a means for producing knowledge of the meaning would be established by the very *śruti* inferred from its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*), which consists in being a generator of knowledge of the meaning.

Even if one were to assume a modification (*vipariṇāma*) of the injunction under discussion, it would result in the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*), and the attainment of the very syllables spoken in the opponent's view would itself have to be considered the fruit [of the action].

Now, if it is argued that even in that case, while a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) capable of enjoining the act must be inferred based on the requirement for an injunction (*niyoga*), the requirement is already satisfied by the directly perceived injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) such as those found in the *Pārāyaṇa* and other texts.
Then, let the same scrutiny be applied to the present case as well;
for there too, once expectancy is satisfied by that [direct statement], there would be no room for the proliferation of assumptions regarding the application, the contrary sentence, or its meaning.
(Although the primary aim is the Veda itself, it ultimately results in the aim of knowing its meaning.

Therefore, in order to establish its status as the primary object— avoiding the consequence that it would be equivalent to injunctions for recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) and the like— the injunction for study is enjoined by a direct injunction with the very same figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) used for words such as *vrīhi* (rice), namely, the indication of being a means to the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and directed toward that [Veda] itself.

Therefore, just as the purport of the injunction regarding threshing and the like— which is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the husking of rice-grains that serve as the means for the *apūrva*— lies solely in its being for the sake of the *apūrva*, so too the purport of the injunction regarding study— which is a means for the refinement consisting of the grasping of the syllables of the Veda that serves as the means for the knowledge of meaning and so forth— lies solely in its being for the sake of the knowledge of meaning and the like. Thus,
it has already been explained previously that the status of being the fruit is fully realized in the knowledge of meaning, and not in the grasping of syllables which serves merely as a means.

(Justification for the restriction to the study of a single recension even under the view that the *svādhyāya* is the objective to be attained) Nor does this view entail a contradiction with the rule of studying a single recension (*eka-śākhā-adhyayana*)— as established in the *Śākhāntara-adhikaraṇa*— on the grounds that since the *svādhyāya* is the objective to be refined (*saṃskārya*), its qualifiers such as "singleness" (*ekatva*) would also have to be intended;

for even if singleness were not intended, the word *svādhyāya* contains the term *sva*, which denotes "one's own," referring to that [Veda] which has come down through the lineage of one's father and ancestors.

Since it is determined that a "branch" (*śākhā*) is denotable through its etymological derivation from the root *kṛ* (to act), the study of multiple branches would render the word "own" (*sva*) redundant; therefore, as stated in the *Nakṣatravādāvalī*, there is a restrictive rule for the study of a single branch. Consequently, when the injunction for the direct study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*)—which has the purpose of producing knowledge of the meaningful text—prescribes study within the scope of the sentence-meaning, the capacity of that *svādhyāya* to generate knowledge of the meaning exactly as heard is established.

In order to ensure that the injunction [to study] is purposeful, since the knowledge of the meaning—even though it culminates in human ends—is implied by the act of study, one must assume an injunction stating: "One should accomplish the knowledge of the meaning by means of the Veda (svādhyāya) acquired through study, so that it culminates precisely in a human end. Furthermore, because the status of the Veda as something to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*) is also perceived [in this context], and this perception of its being something to be undertaken arises through the assumption of an implied injunction.

It is not tenable for some to claim that, having first enjoined the repetition [of the Veda] for the purpose of purifying the *svādhyāya*, one should then— by a change of perspective— assume a different meaning of the sentence, namely that one should produce knowledge of the meaning by means of the *svādhyāya* as it has been studied through that very repetition; for this would result in the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), characterized by such a repetition.

And because there is a lack of evidence for the assumption of transformation (vipariṇāma), the Venerable Master [Śaṅkara] has demonstrated the presentation of the objective (uddeśya) by employing the compound expression "for the sake of the study of the Veda (svādhyāya) which serves as the means for the knowledge of purposeful meaning and so forth," in order to convey the understanding of the meaning.

(Regarding the difference between the term *svādhyāya*—which, like the word *vrīhi*, serves as the designatum—and [the word *svādhyāya*] when its own literal meaning is not intended to be expressed): Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of words such as *vrīhi*, if the *svādhyāya* (Veda) were the designatum by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because it is the means for attaining purposeful knowledge and so forth, then the *svādhyāya* itself would necessarily be unintended to be expressed just like the rice and other grains.

For, if that [literal sense] were not intended to be expressed, the status of being the designatum would be untenable, since there would be no other means of proof (*māna*) to present the knowledge of meaning as that which culminates in human welfare (*puruṣārtha*).
Furthermore, because injunctions such as "one should study all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights" would otherwise be rendered purposeless,
there is no obstacle to understanding that the status of being *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text) applies specifically to those [Vedas] which have fixed purposes.

Therefore, since the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) serve as means for knowing the meaning of the Veda by virtue of being auxiliaries, it is proper to maintain that just like the study of those [auxiliaries], the study of the Veda mentioned in conjunction with them likewise serves as a means for knowing the meaning.
The directions.
(An exposition of the view that the act of studying is prompted by the injunction to teach.
Therefore, by the phrase "for the sake of avoiding futility," it should be understood that the author of the root-text (*mūlakṛt*) has also refuted another opinion.

To explain: in the rule "one should initiate an eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa" (*aṣṭavarṣaṃ brāhmaṇam upanayīta*), the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule: "The middle voice is employed in the senses of honoring, elevating, acting as a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*), knowing, wages, counting, and spending."

From the sūtra *niyaḥ*, it is understood that the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) is prescribed as the result of the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*). When the question arises as to by what means this causality toward becoming a teacher—perceived in the rite of initiation (*upanayana*)—is realized, it is concluded that it occurs through the medium of study (*adhyayana*).

Since study is required for teaching, and since the act of teaching performed by the teacher can fulfill the requirement of study through its proximity to the student (*upaneyapratyāsatti*), it is postulated that teaching performed by the teacher serves as the means (*dvāra*) in that context. Thus, it is established that [initiation] leads to the status of a teacher by way of study.

Furthermore, that teaching is a primary act (pradhāna) which motivates its subsidiary (aṅga), namely initiation (upanayana), because it aims at the fruit consisting in the attainment of the status of an Ācārya. This is established by the inference of a Vedic text (*śruti*) from such Smṛti passages as: "But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the Rahasyas, him they call an Ācārya. Thus, one desiring the status of an Ācārya should initiate a pupil and teach him the Veda.

Since study (*adhyayana*) is also prompted by the activity of initiation (*upanayana*), when study is thus prompted by this very [initiation], one need not postulate that the injunction to study one’s own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*)—which pertains to those qualified by the revealed texts (*śruta-adhikārin*)—is the prompter of study by virtue of its independently producing knowledge of meaning; for that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
For this very reason, in the Smṛti text "having initiated," the suffix *ktvā* [indicates this sequence].

Because it is stated that there must be a single agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), and because this is untenable without a single performance (*prayogaikya*), the coordination between the acts of initiating [the student] (*upanayana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) is logically established only through a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*). Although the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*)—being of a supermundane excellence like the state of the *āhavanīya* fire produced by the *ādhāna* rite—is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), nevertheless, since there are traditional injunctions such as "A fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to the teacher," it indeed becomes a human goal by virtue of being the cause for the giving of fees and so forth; thus, it is the primary element.

Because of the connection of the initiated boy— referred to by the word "that" (*tat*) in the injunction "one should teach him"— with teaching, just as in the case of the statement "one pours curds into heated milk;
