that is the *āmikṣā* for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice," where the word "that" (*sā*) indicates that the milk processed by the pouring of curds is an auxiliary to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, so too, by the hearing of the word "that" (*tat*), it is understood according to the previously stated reasoning that initiation is an auxiliary to teaching.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the scriptural statement "he initiates" (*upanayīta*) can be explained as a mere connection of time—just like the injunction "having performed the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, one should sacrifice with Soma"—there is no evidence for a relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgi-bhāva*).

Furthermore, even if the force of that word (*tacchabda*) leads to the cognition that it is subordinate to the action mentioned in immediate proximity, there is still no evidence that initiation is subordinate specifically to teaching; rather, given that the causative verbal root (*ṇijanta-dhātu*) presents two operations—the activity of the prompted (the student) and the activity of the prompter (the teacher)—it would follow that initiation is equally subordinate to study as well.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to convey the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) by means of the middle voice (ātmanepada), which is prescribed for the act of acting as a teacher (ācāryakaraṇa).

Nor should it be argued that the indication of the teacher’s connection with the fruit of teaching—namely, instruction—in the rite of initiation (upanayana) implies its status as a subordinate element (aṅga) of that teaching; for we observe that even in the case of the Pūrṇāhuti, which is not a subordinate part of the Agnihotra, the Paurṇamāsa, and other rites, but is established by its own injunction as a benefactor to all those rites through the medium of the Ādhāna, there is the designation of the fruits of all those rites it benefits, namely: "By the Pūrṇāhuti, one obtains all desires. The same applies here as well.

If it is argued that this is also reasonable because the fruit of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study)—which is assisted by the initiation (*upanayana*)—is designated as belonging to the assistant through the medium of the study itself; we say no.

For, since the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the *Soma* sacrifice are understood from other scriptural passages to be independent means for achieving separate fruits, they possess distinct performances. Consequently, while the suffix *-ktvā*, which merely indicates sequence (*paurvāparya*), might somehow be justified by relying on the identity of the substratum of the agent (*kartṛkāraka*) even without a unity of performance, [the case here is different].

In the present case, just as in the instance "having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," it is appropriate to assume that the purport [of the text] lies solely in conveying the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*) in order to ensure the unity of performance;

for even though there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of two actions, the primary action is more venerable and thus it is proper that the connection occurs with that alone, and because this serves as authority for understanding [the teaching] as being subsidiary to instruction.

Since it can be asserted that the fruit of teaching— which is directly related [to the injunction]— is indicated in the act of initiation (*upanayana*) by virtue of its being a constituent part (*aṅga*), and since postulating an indirect relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) would render its justification purposeless,

they maintain that study is prompted solely by the injunction to teach, and not prompted by the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) as a means to the knowledge of meaning.

[The refutation of the view that study is prompted by the injunction for teaching: In that case, since initiation itself is not prompted by the injunction for teaching, it follows all the more that study is not prompted by it;

this is not so, because if that were the case, the act of study—which is the activity of the one being prompted—would be established solely through the necessity of otherwise accounting for the injunction for teaching, and thus the independent injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) would result in being purposeless.]

Furthermore, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), which is understood through injunctions such as "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the spring" to be for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa and others, must be established as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) only to their own duty of study (*adhyayana*),
and not as subsidiary to the duty of teaching (*adhyāpana*) belonging to another;

for when there arises a requirement for the application (*viniyoga*) of the visible refinement (*dṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) consisting of the teacher's satisfaction produced by the initiation, study— being inherent to the one initiated— is more proximate (*antaraṅga*).

For the sake of the initiate's entitlement to all ritual acts (*sarvakarmādhikāra*), just as the unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by initiation—which is of the nature of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*)—must necessarily be understood as being for the purpose of the initiate’s own end because it is produced by that [initiation], so too, since there is no difference in its being produced by that same rite, it is more appropriate that the unseen result in the form of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) to the teacher produced by initiation should also serve the purpose of the initiate’s end.

Furthermore, it is clearly established that initiation has the purpose of refining the student (*māṇavaka-saṃskārārthatva*) by way of removing the impurities arising from seed and womb (*bījagarbhasamudbhava-enas*): "By the rites pertaining to the womb, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle..."
"The sin pertaining to the seed and the sin pertaining to the womb are wiped away for the twice-born;
thus, the sin arising from the seed, the skin, and the womb quickly departs"—this is understood from such Smṛti texts.

For this very reason, some authorities declare that even for the mute and the insane, who are not entitled to perform ritual acts, initiation is mandatory for the purpose of destroying their sin, stating: "The mute and the insane are to be consecrated."

Manu has presented the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) as a possible position for some, stating: "And because they lack the right to perform rituals, these two [the Śūdra and the Vṛṣala] incur a fall from their status.

Therefore, since there is no evidence that initiation—which is intended for its own independent result—is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching, and since initiation itself is not prompted by the injunction to teach, it follows all the more clearly that study, which enters into the process through initiation, is likewise not prompted by that injunction.
(Just as the specific ages and so forth dependent upon the initiation ceremony [upanayana] serve the purpose of the one being initiated, so too does the initiation itself).

For this very reason, it is logical that the initiation— being the substratum for those qualities— is for the sake of that [initiate], because the qualities characterized by specific ages dependent upon the initiation, such as those prescribed by the injunctions of subordinate attributes (*guṇavidhi*) like "in the seventh year for one desiring spiritual luster" and "in the eighth year for one desiring long life," serve the purpose of the one being initiated.

This is because it is established as a general rule that the primary element, the quality, and the fruit must have a single substratum, and this has been demonstrated in the section beginning with *kāmo 'rthasaṃyogāt*.

For this very reason, in the statement "If one should desire that Parjanya be rainy," the desire is intended to belong to the sacrificer alone, setting aside the desire of the Adhvaryu priest who performs the measurement of the sacrificial ground; for [otherwise], since the *sāman*—which consists of the act of singing—is something to be refined, it would have to take as its medium the *ṛc* (verse) which is its primary constituent, and thus [the result] would become a means of praise consisting of the expression of qualities residing in the qualified object (*guṇin*), [rather than a fruit for the sacrificer].

Just as the fact that the *sāman* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the hymn of praise is understood from the injunction "one praises with the *sāman*," so too, in this case, there is no scriptural statement whatsoever that establishes the fact that initiation (*upanayana*), which is an auxiliary to Vedic study, is also an auxiliary to teaching by way of effecting the latter;
by virtue of which it could be an auxiliary to both.
(The passages beginning with "Having initiated... refer to the nature of the teacher himself, just as death is a cause for impurity, etc.
According to the Smṛti: "One who has initiated a disciple...
[is not a worthy recipient] by mere learning or even by austerity alone."

And because of the Smṛti text: "In whom both [the Veda and] conduct reside, him indeed they call a worthy recipient (pātra)," the statement regarding the status of being a recipient by means of these three is intended merely to define that status; for one does not become an Ācārya merely by teaching, but rather the intent is simply to state that one becomes so also through the rite of initiation (upanayana).

Just as the fruit of that [gift] depends upon the status of the recipient as a worthy vessel (*pātra*) in the case of giving and so forth, so too does the impurity (*āśauca*) resulting from one's own death and the like depend solely upon such a teacher; for it is precisely the non-transgression of that which is established by scripture—namely, that "the disciple must not overstep the teacher"—that serves as the cause.
Others [hold that]: "He who performs the rites beginning with the *niṣeka* according to the rule... [and so on].
"He who honors him with the final portion is called a guru;
he is a guru who, having performed the rites, bestows the Veda upon him."
By the force of such Smṛti texts, there would arise the consequence that the rites beginning with *niṣeka* and ending with *caula* are ancillary (*aṅga*) to the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*).

Just as this being the case, the status of these rites as ancillaries to study (*adhyayana*)—by way of purifying the student (*māṇavaka*) and others—is established through the very use of the *ātmanepada* prescribed by a specific sūtra with the intention of indicating that the fruit accrues to the agent, so too has it been demonstrated in the *Nakṣatravādāvalī* [under the heading: "The obligatory initiation (*upanayana*) is not prompted by optional teaching"].

In this manner, the venerable teacher will establish in the *Ādhānādhikaraṇa* that the qualification of the person to be enjoined—such as being seven or eight years old—is intended to be significant (*vivakṣā*).

Therefore, because the act of teaching (*adhyāpayīta*) connects only with the activity of studying (*adhyayana*), which is the prompted action (*prayojya*) referred to by the pronoun "him" (*tam*) in the phrase "one should teach him," and because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) can be justified even by the mere fact that studying assists the act of teaching; [the qualification is indeed intended].
"Thereafter, if these three [classes] remain uninitiated for the prescribed period,
they become *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī* and censured by the world.
That twice-born man who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other pursuits,"

"Even while living, he quickly falls to the status of a Śūdra along with his lineage"—by such Smṛti texts, since the compulsory initiation (*upanayana*) and study (*adhyayana*) cannot be prompted by the injunction for optional teaching (*kāmyādhyāpana*), study is prompted solely by the injunction for study for the sake of understanding the meaning.
In that very context, until the completion of the Veda, dependence upon the teacher is established [by the rule]: "By various specific austerities and vows enjoined by the Śruti..."

The connection [of the study of the Veda] with duties such as service to the teacher and others, as prescribed in the Smṛti— "The entire Veda, along with its secret portions (rahasya), must be mastered by the twice-born"— is by way of being the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) for the purpose of completing those duties without obstacle. As for what has been stated by some— that because such specific qualifications of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) cannot possibly serve a visible purpose consisting merely of the knowledge of the meaning, one must accept that "Vedic study" (*svādhyāyatva*) involves an extraordinary refinement (*alaukika-saṃskāra*), like the state of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatva*), and that its utility lies in that very refinement— [that is rejected].

This has been refuted by my venerable teacher in the *Kaustubha* under the section concerning the qualification of one who remains after [the study] (*tacchiṣṭāko-pādhikaraṇa*); it should be consulted therein.

For one who, until the completion of the Veda, remains under the authority of the teacher, intent upon his service according to the rules of attendance prescribed in the Smṛtis, and who—being naturally free from the loss of caste and other such defects—is engaged in that study which is accomplished through hardship, would not undertake it for the sake of a fruit consisting of making another person one's teacher.
It can be performed in some way or another;
therefore, just like receiving gifts and so forth, teaching is also established as a means for the acquisition of wealth.

In that very context, up until the completion of the Veda, there is the connection [of the study] with the state of being dependent upon the teacher, as well as with the duties prescribed by the Smṛti—such as service to the guru and others—as means for the unimpeded completion [of the study], according to the Smṛti passage: "The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born through various specific austerities and vows enjoined by the Śruti. As for the claim that, because such specific auxiliary elements cannot possibly serve a visible purpose consisting merely of the knowledge of the meaning, one must accept that the status of being "one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyatva*) involves an extraordinary refinement (*alaukika-saṃskāra*), like that of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and that its utility lies in that [refinement] alone—[this is rejected].
Thus it has been stated by some;

however, that was refuted by the venerable [author] in the *Kaustubha* under the section on "Non-contradiction with the Teachings of the Learned" (*śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa*), and should be examined therein.
(B3) F.N. Here, the authors of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti* state: "The injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) is solely for the purpose of grasping the syllables."
The comprehension of meaning, however, occurs spontaneously for one who has grasped the connection between words and their respective meanings;
the injunction to study has no operative function therein.
Otherwise, if its purpose were solely the comprehension of dharma, it would follow that there could be no study of the entire Veda.
For Brāhmaṇas and others who are ineligible for the Rājasūya and similar sacrifices, the study and comprehension of their meaning would serve no purpose;
therefore it has been stated in the Vedabhāṣya: "If [the Veda] ended with mere understanding, there would be no completeness of study.

Just as one possesses eligibility for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) and other rites through the knowledge of the meaning produced by the instruction of a father or other elders, [so too is the case here].
In this way, since it is established that [the same applies] to sacrifices as well, desire for them is not possible.

Furthermore, because the statements concerning the Agnihotra and other rites are infinite, it is impossible to designate their specific meanings individually; if they were designated in a general form, then knowledge in its general aspect would be the fruit of study, and thus the establishment of inquiry would be impossible.

The determination of the purport (*tātparya*) of Vedic sentences regarding their own literal meaning will occur through indicators such as the opening context (*upakrama*), and thus nothing is untenable.
Consequently, the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) has no purport toward the injunction for [mere] recitation of the *svādhyāya* for the sake of knowing the meaning.
For this very reason, the injunction for knowledge—“The Veda is to be studied and known by a Brahmin without [any other] motive”—is also logically consistent.
Otherwise, that [teaching] would be purposeless.
For there is no rule that everyone must necessarily have grasped the connection between words and their meanings;
this is contradicted by the frequent observation of those who are unlearned.

Granted that there is a restrictive rule (niyama), even so, since the meaning of the Veda— which is exceedingly profound— is not established without inquiry, the injunction for inquiry is indeed purposeful.
Precisely because the knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda is not prompted by the injunction for study, the composition of the Kalpasūtras and other such works is purposeful.

In the third and fourth chapters of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the view of Jaimini is presented as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) through the sūtra: “Because it is a subordinate element, it is a statement of human purpose, as in other cases; thus says Jaimini. According to this, the knowledge of the Self is subordinate to ritual action by way of the agent who performs that action; and the scriptural mention of the fruit—namely, “The knower of the Self overcomes grief”—is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), like the hearing of the verse concerning the absence of evil. Then, by means of another sūtra, “Because of the injunction for one who possesses that [knowledge],” [the sūtra] cites the passage: “Having studied the Veda from the family of a teacher...”

Furthermore, because the injunctions for ritual action apply even to one who possesses knowledge of the meaning of all the Vedas according to the Śruti, [the opponent] himself proposes another argument that the knowledge of the Self is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Having introduced the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words, "Because of the teaching of something more [than mere study], it is not so; for Bādarāyaṇa sees it thus," he states that since the Śruti mentions only the mere recitation (*adhyayana*), the qualification for ritual action belongs to one who has merely recited the text, and not to one who possesses knowledge of its meaning.
It is clearly understood that study is not undertaken for the sake of knowing the meaning;

the commentary of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya and other works, such as the statement, "We determine that eligibility for ritual action belongs to one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]," also serve as authority on this point.
Furthermore, this matter has been thoroughly established by Vācaspatimiśra and others, and may be seen from their works themselves.

And thus, since in the case of an *arthavāda* there is no attainment of a meaningful conclusion resulting in a fruit through the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), there arises no requirement for those [arthavādas] toward the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*). Consequently, there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the injunction and the *arthavāda* based on mutual expectancy; rather, as in the case of "the cloth becomes red" where there is an expectancy for the word "red" alone, the *arthavādas* have syntactic unity with the injunction solely through the latter's own expectancy. This is the easy path following the *Bhāṣya*, so they explain.

From the perspective of ultimate truth, however, what is intended here is precisely a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that "one should acquire knowledge of the meaning by means of the Vedic study one has already undertaken";
it is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*),
such that one might suspect the injunction for study would be rendered futile therein.
Even for Brāhmaṇas, the knowledge of the meaning of the Rājasūya and other rites acquired through study is useful for performing sacrifices and other priestly duties;

however, for others [the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas], the comprehension of rituals for which only Brāhmaṇas and others are eligible will serve an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose. Thus, there is no contingency of abandoning the study of the entire Veda. Furthermore, the scriptural passage cited in the Vedabhāṣya is not sufficient to undermine the final conclusion (siddhānta) of the proponent.
For it is clearly evident to those who perceive this that the purpose of Vedic study is indeed the knowledge of the meaning [of the texts] themselves;
however, the qualification for ritual performance (*kratv-adhikāra*) is not established by the knowledge of the meaning arising from the instruction of a father or others,
because of the reliance on restrictive injunctions (*niyama-vidhi*).
Indeed, it is even possible to aim for the specific knowledge of each respective meaning immediately upon the arising of the initial cognition following the study of each particular sentence.

And thus, in this context, study is enjoined solely for the purpose of knowing the meaningful content that possesses a purpose. Otherwise, the status of all Vedic sentences as authoritative means of knowing *dharma* would not be established.

In the case of the statement "by a Brahmin [it should be performed] without motive," however, there is no injunction regarding knowledge; for knowledge, being dependent on the nature of reality (*vastutantra*), is not something that can be enjoined.

Furthermore, according to the method you have established, the knowledge of the meaning [of the texts] arises even in the context of sacrifices through the instruction of a father or others, just as it does in the case of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and similar rites.

Since the study of the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is also enjoined by way of attainment (*prāpti*), it is necessary for everyone to have grasped the connection between the words and their meanings; furthermore, since even a determinate cognition such as "this is a post, a mere bearer of a burden" is already attained, the injunction for inquiry (*vicāra-vidhi*) would likewise be inapplicable. However, because its justification is possible through a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) even in the case of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) injunction, the operation of inquiry belongs precisely there.

Since this is already established by the statement, "Those who do not study become *vrātyas*," [the word] "and it is to be known" (*jñeyaśca*) serves solely to provide the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) required by the injunction for study; it does not, however, preclude the fact that study is motivated by the desire to know the meaning.
Alternatively, we see this as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

When the question "What is the use of that? arises, it follows from the connection [to the preceding] "whatever is possible" that the apprehension of the syllables results. Since even that is not a human goal in itself, the question "What is the use of that? leads to the determination of the words. From that comes the knowledge of the word-meanings; from that, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning; from that, the performance of the action; and from the performance, the attainment of fruits such as heaven—this much being the extent [of the process].

Indeed, through such statements as "one becomes free from expectancy," the authors of the Vārttika explicitly demonstrate that the purpose of Vedic study is the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*), and not the mere acquisition of syllables (*akṣarāvāpti*).

Furthermore, even under the view that the purpose is the knowledge of the meaning, the utility of the Kalpasūtras and similar texts is clearly established in the section concerning the Kalpasūtras (*kalpasūtrādhikaraṇa*) and elsewhere.

By stating that "because it is a remainder, it is an explanatory eulogy (*puruṣārthavāda*)," Bādarāyaṇa also lends his support here by restating the very position favored by Jaimini—that [the study of the Veda] is for the sake of knowing the meaning.

In the phrase "one who possesses merely the study," it is understood that there is no requirement for the knowledge of the meaning in the portion consisting solely of the Upaniṣads, but not that the comprehension of the meaning is absent;

this is quite clear. In that very sūtra, in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Bhāmatī*, and other works, the position that it is for the sake of knowing the meaning has been correctly established—alas, this is like cutting off one's own finger with one's own hand!
Thus, it is only the position that [the purpose of study] is the knowledge of the meaning that is accepted by all authoritative Mīmāṃsakas, not the position that it is the grasping of the syllables;
otherwise, since bathing occurs after the knowledge of the meaning, there would be a contradiction with the sequence [prescribed in the rule]: "Having studied, one should bathe.
Furthermore, otherwise, it would not be possible for arthavādas to indicate (lakṣaka) excellence (*prāśastya*).

The principle of the "red cloth" (raktapaṭa) is intended, as clarified in the Vārttika and other works, to dispel the suspicion that— just as in cases of meaningless explanatory passages (arthavāda)— the injunction itself might indicate its own excellence; thus, the heart of the authors of the Nyāyasudhā, Bhāṭṭadīpikā, and other such texts is that the injunction regarding one's own Vedic study (svādhyāyavidhi) teaches that study has the purpose of understanding the meaning.

By this, the established doctrine of the *Īśvara-mīmāṃsā* and others—that the injunction for study extends only as far as the acquisition of the syllables—is also refuted; for it contradicts the *Vārttika* and other texts, and it would entail the undesirable consequence that inquiry is not mandatory. This is how it should be understood. (B1)

Because the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is designated as the object of the injunction; and thus, when the purposefulness of the subject matter of the Vedic study is established as being inseparable from the act of inquiry (*jijñāsā*), there arises—by virtue of the factors that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). And the meaning indicated therein takes the form of praise or censure, because it is required by the proximate injunctions or prohibitions.
For instance: in common worldly usage, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is the intention of a person;
in the Veda, however, because such a person is absent, it is some property residing solely in the word itself, such as the optative suffix.
This is the delimitor of its denotability (*vācyatāvacchedaka*).
(Conclusion on the fact that study is prompted by its own injunction:

Since, as in the case of teaching, study would be impossible without an injunction because it lacks a prompter, it is established that for one who has been initiated, study is prompted by the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) for the sake of knowing the purposeful meaning; thus, taking the literal sense possible within the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), [the injunction is fulfilled].

In the absence of that [direct expression], for the sake of obtaining purposefulness as far as possible, one should—by means of elliptical implication (*lakṣaṇā*), ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and so forth—establish that [the Veda] is the motivator of dharma and adharma.

(Refutation of the claim that the impossibility of syntactic unity is the seed of metaphorical indication): Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the indicators of intended meaning" (*tātparyagrāhakavaśena*):

by this it is shown that when syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhi*) is impossible due to the connection of the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*), there occurs a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise (*prāśastya*) and so forth, in accordance with that [intended meaning].

The objection that this leads to a circular argument—namely, that the status of being a single sentence depends on that [intention], and that intention depends on the status of being a single sentence—is avoided;
for the meaning is that the non-occurrence of the status of being a single sentence is not the reason for accepting that [intention] by virtue of what grasps the intended meaning (tātparya).
(An argument for the fact that the *bhāvanā* denoted by the optative suffix resides in the intention of a person in worldly usage.

By means of the phrase beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*), [the author] demonstrates the requirement for the implied meaning by way of explaining the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions, in order to indicate the purpose required by the proximate injunctions and prohibitions.
To begin with, the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), and the gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes are indicators of a *bhāvanā* not previously known, and they are the instigators of its performance.

And *bhāvanā* (productive activity), according to its etymological derivation as "that by which something is brought into being," is an operation distinct from the meaning of the verbal root that is conducive to another state of existence;

for, immediately after hearing injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), there is the cognition of the instigation—also termed "performance"—which consists in making known what was previously unknown regarding the object of the *bhāvanā*, in the form: "one should perform an operation conducive to the sacrifice.
For this very reason, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others possess primary injunctive force (*vidhitva*) by virtue of enjoining the *bhāvanā*.

In sentences such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," which involve those [factors], there is the conventional designation of "injunction" (*vidhi*) because they make known the three unknown components of the *bhāvanā* and because they prompt the performance of that qualified *bhāvanā*. In this regard, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpodvāpa*), based on common usage such as "I am being impelled by my teacher" or "this person possesses an activity conducive to my engagement," the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others have their denotative power (*śakti*) residing in the activity conducive to engagement. Furthermore, since in worldly usage one says, "I have engaged in this action due to the teacher's wish, not out of my own wish," it is understood that this activity is indeed a wish; with this intention, he states: "In the world, it is the human intention (*puruṣāśaya*)."
(An exposition of the views of Maṇḍana and Pārthasārathi regarding *bhāvanā* as denoting the means to a desired end common to both worldly and Vedic contexts:
Even in the impersonal Veda, because of the conventional usage that "this injunction possesses an activity conducive to my engagement," and because such injunctions and the like,

being insentient, cannot possess such a desire, [the meaning of the suffix is] the status of being a means to a desired end residing in the sacrifice and so forth, by virtue of its conduciveness to engagement.
Maṇḍanamiśra maintains that because it is already known, the cognition [of the Veda] occurs in the form of being an instigation (*pravartanā*).

Pārthasārathi, however, states in the first section of the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya*) that in the Veda, the operation consisting of the communication of meaning by the word as its agent is itself the instigation (*pravartanatva*).

(The view of some that the knowledge of the injunction itself is the creative contemplation [bhāvanā]): In this view, when the question arises as to what that operation (*vyāpāra*) is, some say: it is an operation such as "impelling" (*pravartanā*) which is the cause of activity. And because the word of injunction, by virtue of its being a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), possesses the common attribute of the ten tenses and moods (*daśalakāra*), it [conveys] the objective creative contemplation (*arthabhāvanā*) consisting of human activity.
The capacity to signify means, in other words,
being the cause of the knowledge of that [object].

And since that [knowledge] can only be put into practice when it is known, the word— which is the cause of that knowledge— indeed possesses the status of being its cause through a mediated succession.

In this context, the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), which is the cause of the knowledge of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) consisting of a person's engagement, is its possession of the power to denote that [activity]; and that very operation, being the cause of engagement, receives the designation "incitement" (*pravartanā*). This is because a word produces engagement only through the mediation of knowledge, and there is no evidence for postulating an operation distinct from the operation that generates that knowledge.
And the operation that produces knowledge consists of its own cognition, the cognition of its capacity, and the cognition of itself as qualified by that capacity.
The distinction here is that one or the other of the first two constitutes the verbal bhāvanā, while the third functions as the instrument (karaṇa) therein.

This being the case, since one's own knowledge is produced by means of a rule according to a fixed procedure and is also designated as "instigation," it follows that the knowledge of the injunction itself is the verbal productive energy (*śābdabhāvanā*).
(The statement that *bhāvanā* has a desired fruit as its result is a capacity conducive to the expression of the objective *bhāvanā* (*arthabhāvanā*);
furthermore, the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śābdabhāvanā*) is indeed a transcendental property (*alaukikadharma*). This is the exposition of the views of Bhāṭṭabhāskara and others.
In the *Bhāṭṭabhāskara*, however, it is stated: "Its function is the presentation of the *bhāvanā* qualified by its three constituent parts."

In this regard, if the human goal (puruṣārtha) is brought forward as the objective to be realized (bhāvya), then the exposition of that [objective] becomes the cause for engagement, and nothing else; therefore, in order to establish that the operation consisting of the communication of meaning—which has the word as its agent—is of the nature of an instigation (pravartanā), it is determined that the productive urge (bhāvanā), which is the object of that [operation], has the human goal as its objective to be realized. This is according to the text of the *Śāstradīpikā* on that point.

Regarding the statement that the *bhāvanā* has a desirable result (*iṣṭaphala*) everywhere in the Veda: it is said that while the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabdabhāvanā*) is recognized in the Veda and the objective *bhāvanā* (*arthabhāvanā*), which consists of activity, is recognized in the world, the statement that this [objective *bhāvanā*] has a desirable result pertains to the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*). That very verbal *bhāvanā*, as the act of impelling (*pravartanā*), is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in the Veda. Thus it has been stated.

And since its function is stated to be the demonstration of a cultivation (bhāvanā) characterized by three factors, the venerable teachers (*pūjyapādāḥ*) and the authors of the *Prakāśa* maintain that in the Veda, the very capacity conducive to the expression of the objective cultivation (*arthabhāvanā*) is the meaning [of the optative suffix] as "instigation" (*pravartanā*). As it was said by the Teacher: "The optative suffixes and the like express a quite different [kind of] cultivation, namely, the cultivation of expression (*abhidhābhāvanā*)."
"Therefore, by implication, that cultivation is understood among them to be something distinct from all other objects."

In the view of all [authorities], since the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) between [the various options] is evident, and since that same state would result even in common worldly usage, it is logical—according to the maxim that "when there is an absence of a decisive criterion regarding established [entities], another [entity] must be postulated"—that an additional, non-worldly quality residing in the injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*), which is itself the *pravartanā* (the impelling force), is the meaning of the Veda. Intending to show that the opinion of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* alone is correct, he says: "some [quality]. (*kaścid iti*)
By this, its supramundane nature is stated;
and by the particle *eva*, the refutation of other doctrines is intended.

(B3) (1) Furthermore, since it is understood that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be refined by virtue of being the object (*karman*), and since the application of that refined Veda toward the knowledge of its meaning is established as a matter of fact, it is logical that the word *svādhyāya* indicates the Veda as the means for attaining the knowledge of meaning.

In the former position (*pakṣa*), the sentence-meaning should be understood as: "One should bring about the knowledge of meaning through a study qualified by the Veda," employing a transformation [of the case] like that of the *saktu* [grains] and a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
The suffix *-tavya*, however, indicates an objecthood that is merely figurative.
The ultimate meaning, however, is that one should cultivate the knowledge of the meaning through the recitation of the Veda one has studied.

This is clear from the *Nyāyaratnamālā*, which states that just as in the injunction "one should praise with the *sāman*," even though there is no application by another scriptural statement due to the *ṛc* being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) [of the *sāman*], its status as such a refinement is not lost by its very nature, so it is here as well. (2)

Bhavadeva holds that because the knowledge of *tātparya* (speaker’s intention) is the cause for [the production of] verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) as delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition, the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) itself is the grasper of the *tātparya* regarding the purposeful meaning of the entire Veda.

The authors of the *Kaustubha*, however, maintain that since the knowledge of *tātparya* is not a cause for verbal cognition as delimited by the property of being a verbal cognition— due to its deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sentences spoken by Śuka and others— the scripture functions prior to worldly experience to bring about the comprehension of a purposeful meaning.
The nature of being an operation (vyāpāratva) is common to both [positive and negative injunctions],
but it does not include the quality of being the motivator for engagement or withdrawal,
because that is obtainable from other sources.
In that context, in the absence of a negative particle (*nañ*), there is the property of being the motivator for the engagement with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*).
(B2) [This is the section on establishing the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) regarding non-worldly linguistic phenomena.

Now, according to the principle that "those very words which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic, and whatever is their meaning is the same as the meaning of these [Vedic] ones," the potency of an injunctive word (*vidhiśabda*) is apprehended in the world wherever it occurs.

In the Veda as well, it must have that same meaning. Since in common worldly usage it is established that [the term] denotes human attributes such as commanding (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, one might raise the objection: "In the absence of those [human attributes] in the Veda, there would be no apprehension of its primary power (*śakti*); how then could a non-worldly attribute be presented? To dispel this doubt, he says: "It is common to both," for instigation (*pravartanā*) is indeed an activity conducive to engagement (*pravṛtti*).

In that regard, since in the world the apprehension of the word-meaning occurs through the grasping of a power (*śakti*)— whether as a delimited or undelimited activity— by means of insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*udvāpa*), when a cognition produced by a word arises having a particular property as its qualifier (in accordance with the apprehension of the word’s power for that which is delimited by that property), and it is impossible for the individuals that are the substrata of that property to function as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), the cognition culminates only after projecting (*ākṣipya*) an individual not previously established [in the context].

The meaning is that this is established by applying—within the view that the meaning of an injunction is an effect consisting of an unprecedented entity (apūrva)—the well-known worldly "impelling" (nyāru), which must necessarily be transferred even to the verbal bhāvanā according to Pārthasārathi’s view; and within the view that maintains an extraordinary impulsion (alaukika-preraṇā), it is established by its application [to that bhāvanā].
Regarding the phrase "the occurrence of the meaning of the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārthapravṛtti*):

this demonstration—that the property of being a verbal suffix (*latva*), which consists in the nature of being a verbal suffix as it occurs across the ten tenses (*daśalakāra*), serves as the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*)—is intended according to the view of others (*paramata*), since its occurrence [as such] is established as being obtainable through other means. This is indicated by the expression "the meaning of the verbal suffix" (*ākhyātārtha*), [which implies] the refutation of *latva* as the delimitor of the expressive power and the establishment of the status of *tib* and so forth as such.
In that context, what is being demonstrated is not that [the meaning] is unobtainable from anything else due to a difference in the delimitors of capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*),
but rather simply by virtue of the distinct capacities of *ti* and so forth, which constitute the general meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) common to all ten tenses (*lakāra*).
For this very reason, the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) resides only in the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *ti* and the rest.
This is because it is understood that the term *ākhyāta* (verbal suffix) is applied precisely upon hearing that [suffix].

Since the instigation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth are presented by those very substitutes such as *tiP* and others, it is the status of being such a substitute itself that constitutes the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*), and not the nature of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) consisting in occurring in the ten tenses and moods (*daśalakāra*).

This is because it is established by experience that the respective meanings are presented even without the presentation of the *lakāra* through its substitutes (*ādeśa*s), and because there would otherwise result the undesirable consequence of understanding those meanings from a *lakāra* presented in any manner whatsoever.
Nor is it [the meaning] presented by the substitute (*ādeśa*).
For there would arise the undesirable consequence of understanding that [meaning] even from that which has undergone the substitution of the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*.
Nor is there any excessive complexity (gaurava) in accepting multiple delimiters for the capacity [of words];
for even complexity is authoritative when it conforms to the meaning as it is perceived.

Otherwise, the property of "substance-ness" (dravyatva), which is common to jars, cloths, and so forth, would itself—being the simpler entity—have to be accepted as the delimiter for the capacity of words to denote objects such as jars and cloths.

Just as in cases such as *rāmāu*, where the substitution of *au* for *vāriṇī* is established as having the capacity to convey meaning independently and thus serves as a reminder of the phoneme *au*, here [in the case of the verbal suffix], since the *lakāra* is not established as having the capacity to convey meaning independently, the status of being a substitute for that which is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇatadādeśatva*) alone is the delimiting factor of its expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).
For this very reason, in the co-occurrence with *pacati*, the mere element *ti* itself possesses multiple meanings, such as the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), the present tense, and singularity.

In the expression "one should cook" (*pacet*), there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) wherein the single form of the suffix possesses multiple meanings— such as instigation (*pravartanā*), bhāvanā, and oneness— and so it is in other cases as well.

This is according to the view that the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) consists of the triad of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

Just as there is the cognition of two word-meanings through the postulation of separate powers in the word *puṣpavant* despite its denoting three things, so too here there is the cognition of multiple meanings; however, this does not mean that the property of being a *liṅ* (optative suffix) and so forth is the delimitor of the power to incite action (*pravartanā*).
For, according to the previous reasoning, it is established by experience that cognition occurs even without the prior presentation of that [delimitor].
(An exposition of the Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra school’s view regarding the delimiting factor of the expressive power of being a verb):

As for the point raised by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*— namely, that if *bhāvanā* were denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), then since a genus called "verbal-root-ness" (*dhātutva*) cannot exist within verbal roots which consist of an aggregate of multiple phonemes, it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) if one were to accept each specific "root-ness" (*tattaddhātutva*) as the delimiting factor of the expressive power.

Since that [agent] would also result in being understood from words such as "sacrifice" (yāga) and "gift" (dāna), and since it is simpler to accept that it is denoted by the verbal suffix (ākhyāta), it is appropriate to maintain that it is denoted by the verbal suffix itself;
for the property of being a verbal suffix (ākhyātatva) does not always cause those [agents] to be cognized, nor are they presented by words such as "a" (akāra).

This is because, among those words, it is only the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by other words belonging to the *śrauta* scriptural tradition that serves as the delimiting condition for the result— the cognition of the respective meanings and their syntactic connection; likewise, although the apprehension of the primary power (*śakti*) occurs through the universal *latva* (the property of being the *l*-suffix) on the basis of rules such as *'laḥ karmaṇi'* which, being included within the Vedāṅgas, are the words of Pāṇini accepted in the Vedic tradition, it is nevertheless only the mental presentation produced by the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *tiP* that serves as the delimiting condition for the result.
It is not a fault that there is no cognition of *bhāvanā* from the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, or from the letter *l* when uttered with the *svarita* accent by its own nature.

Nor should it be suspected: "How could *asti* and other such verbs—which are themselves incapable [of denoting meaning], yet are employed for the purpose of conveying meaning by causing the recollection of other capable words, and which are treated by some as being 'born of incapacity' (*aśaktija*)—not be equivalent to corrupt forms like *gāvī*? This is because, while *gāvī* and the like are considered corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*) due to their being "born of incapacity" insofar as they convey meaning through the recollection of words like *go* (cow) without depending on the presentation of themselves within their own co-utterance (*svasamabhivyāhāra*), such a condition is impossible in the case of these [verbs].

For the letter *l* does not possess the capacity to convey meaning independently, without depending on the presentation of suffixes such as *tiP*, just as the word *gavya* and others do not convey the meaning of "cow" (*go*) without depending on the presentation of the word *go*.
If that were the case, one could claim that *tiP* and other suffixes are likewise produced by incapacity (*aśaktija*).
Although the diphthong *au* does indeed possess independent denotative power;

Nevertheless, in that context, within its own co-occurrence (*svasamabhivyāhāre*), it is only that which is recalled by means of a grammatical substitute (*ādeśa*) that possesses the capacity to convey meaning.

For this very reason, in the absence of the aforementioned corruption (*apabhraṣṭatva*), since the definition of correctness (*sādhutva*) exists— namely, "that word which conveys a particular meaning in its own co-occurrence, without depending on its own presentation and without the recollection of another word [as a substitute]," applies— it follows that words such as *go* and so forth are indeed correct, just like [the forms taught in grammar].
Since the correctness of *tib* and other suffixes is beyond dispute, *latva* alone is the common delimitor of the capacity for denoting a bhāvanā;
whereas *liṅtva*, being unique to the instigation (*pravartanā*), has been stated [to be its delimitor].
(B1) However, the distinction is that "relation" (*saṃsarga*) consists in being the cause for the absence of activity directed toward that object.

And here, "causality" refers to [the property] being the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*), which serves as the cause for both activity and its absence. (B2) [This concludes the refutation of the established doctrine of the *Bhaṭṭālaṅkāra* regarding the nature of the verbal suffix.]

That is not so. For, just as there is no evidence for the genus *dhātutva* (the nature of being a verbal root) consisting of a collection of multiple phonemes (*varṇa*), and thus [the action] is not denoted by the verbal root in its form as *dhātutva*, so too there is no evidence that *latva* (the nature of being the letter *l*) is a genus consisting of multiple [phonemes].

Furthermore, even in the view that it is denoted by a verbal root ending in a suffix, just as it is argued that it must be denoted by the suffix because of parsimony (*lāghava*), it would follow that it must be denoted by the *tib* suffix and others as well—this consequence applies to your own position as well.
If it is argued that *latva* exists as an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) because all ten *lakāra*s are subsumed under the term *latva* in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* and so forth:

Since "those beginning with *bhū* are verbal roots" (*bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*) includes even *bhū* and others within the category of verbal roots, there is no obstacle to accepting that this very [property of] being a verbal root—which is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—is the delimiting factor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). Consequently, there is likewise no obstacle to its being denotable. Furthermore, rather than postulating that the substitutes such as *tiP* and others are the cause for the presentation of the original element (*ādeśin*) *lṛK*, it is more parsimonious to postulate them as the cause for the presentation of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, because the postulation of their causality toward the infinite delusions regarding the substitutes such as *ti* and so forth is burdened by the fault of complexity (*gaurava*), it is simpler to postulate their causality only for the presentation of the *bhāvanā* and other meanings; moreover, since the status of being the delimitor of denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedakatva*) in the case of *la*— which is understood from grammar as being defined by its expressed meanings such as agent and object— is ultimately discarded even by you, [this view is superior].

Furthermore, because positing the property of being a *lat* (the letter *l*) as the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for the verbal suffix would render the citation of the grammatical rule "alaḥ karmaṇi" as an authority contradictory to all preceding and subsequent texts— and thus a source of ridicule—

and because the definitions of corruption and correctness previously established by you are beset by the defects of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of words such as *dvirepha*,
the property of being a *lat* is not the delimitor of expressive power.
Rather, it is simply the state of being the respective object of those [verbal suffixes];

for when these very [suffixes] are glossed as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), there is the cognition of a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that is perceived as distinct from the meaning of the verbal root.

Furthermore, because this [activity] is glossed by the verb *karoti*, which signifies either effort (*yatna*) or general operation (*vyāpāra-sāmānya*), there is a difference of opinion as to whether it is of the nature of effort or of the nature of general operation; this distinction should be examined in works such as the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*.

(An exposition on the necessity of postulating distinct potencies for the *laṭ* and other suffixes with respect to the factor of *bhāvanā*, and a description of the venerable author’s statement regarding "attainability elsewhere" as being intended to refer to mere syntactic relation.

Nor should it be argued: "If there is no distinct delimitor of potency (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for *pravartanā* (incitement) and *bhāva* (existence), how can the venerable author’s statement regarding 'attainability elsewhere' be justified?
For, with respect to the factor of *bhāvanā*, it is necessary to postulate a distinct potency for the substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *laṭ*.

Likewise, since comprehension can arise even from the substitutes for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth through their individual powers, it would be cumbersome to postulate a power for the qualified [sentence] as a whole; furthermore, the fact that [the meaning] is obtainable elsewhere must be established precisely with reference to the intended relation of being the prompter (*prayojakatva*) and so forth.

Otherwise, if one were to establish that the lack of being obtainable from other means is due to a disparity— namely, that while the aspect of "liṅ-ness" (the *liṅ* suffix itself) in the *liṅ*, etc., expresses instigation (*pravartanā*), it is only those specific substitutes (*ādeśa*) such as *tib* that directly express the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)—

then, instead, one should take the status of being a substitute (*ādeśatva*) as the delimiting factor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) for all [suffixes] alike, based on their uniform nature as instigation, just as they are presented by their respective substitutes.

Since it is more cumbersome to establish that *latva* (the property of being a *la*-suffix) is the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*)— as this would entail the possibility of expressing the sense of "bhāvanā" through suffixes alone—

the view established in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya* and elsewhere, as well as in the present *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, that specific substitutes (*ādeśaviśeṣa*) are the delimiters of expressive power would be rendered devoid of justification.

Therefore, since that [meaning] is obtained through a distinct expressive power common to *laṭ* and other suffixes, the cumbersome property of being an operation that motivates activity (*pravṛttiprayojakavyāpāratva*) need not be posited.

It is more reasonable to assume that the capacity for the qualified meaning is based on the acceptance of the delimitor of capability (śakyatāvacchedaka); thus, it is appropriate to establish that the relational component alone is obtainable from other means.

(The demonstration that there is no contradiction in taking *bhāvanā* as the primary qualificand [of the sentence], based on the statement from the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*: "The relation is the state of being the motivator for the activity [denoted] by the meaning of the verb.
Regarding the term "relation" (*saṃsarga*):

this demonstration of the relation is made in accordance with the single causal relationship between the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), such as desire, and [the meanings of] time and so forth.

Since the author of the root-text has demonstrated in various places that there is an occurrence of [the word] as a qualifier through the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence caused by an inference produced by a cognition of its own object— which is itself produced by a cognition [of the word]— one should understand this by taking up that which, by virtue of being cognized in the same act of consciousness (*samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatva*),

functions as the causal factor for activity and cessation with respect to the meaning consisting of "prompting to act" and so forth, and which thus arrives [in the cognition] as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga*).
However, this does not mean that the Venerable Teacher’s intention was to treat the instigation as the qualificand with respect to the activity.

(Establishing that *bhāvanā* is the primary qualificand): In response to the inquiry as to which among the various meanings of a verb is the primary one—given the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the finite verb has *bhāva* as its principal meaning"—the [definition] is applied for the purpose of restrictive determination (*parisaṃkhyā*).

It is established, with the assistance of the principle of parsimony regarding the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), that *bhāvanā* alone is the primary qualificand, a status common to all verbal suffixes such as the present indicative (*laṭ*) and others.

For it is most reasonable that the object of the cognition [of the injunction] is precisely its qualificand (*viśeṣya*); furthermore, since there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating merely the state of being defined by the instigation (*pravartanā*) once the state of being the qualificand of the activity defined by the instrument and the result is already established.
As they say: "When the stem and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together..."
"Because of its predominance, the efficient force (bhāvanā) is understood as the meaning of the suffix;
likewise, between the two parts— the base and the suffix— which always occur in a fixed sequence,
the nature of the efficient force is understood at the moment the suffix is heard."
(An exposition of the view that *pravartanā* is the primary qualificand):

As for the view established by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*, who maintains that—in order for the *prakṛti* (verbal root) to be construed as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—the status of being the object of a power delimited by "optativeness" (*liṅtva*) is necessarily required for *pravartanā*;

otherwise, if it were the object of a power delimited by "verbality" (*ākhyātatva*), it would result in its being the primary element, just as it is in the case of the present tense (*laṭ*) and other such suffixes.

Because it would be excessively cumbersome to state that there is a double *bhāvanā* within a single suffix, and because the traditional Smṛti is justified by the statement that in all verbal forms (*ākhyāta*) the *bhāvanā*—as determined by the meaning of the root—is predominant;

and because, when injunction (*vidhi*) and *bhāvanā*—both possessing independent denotative capacity—are presented simultaneously by a single word, they must necessarily share a single common substratum (the agent) according to the logic of number and case-role (*kāraka*);

and because, following the cognition presented in the original source, it is more appropriate for the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) to function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅartha*).

For it cannot be said that the denotative capacity (śakyatā) of the two—prescription (vidhi) and productive urge (bhāvanā)—resides in them as conjoined, like the sun and moon in the word *puṣpavant* and others; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence that the productive urge is not perceived in the present tense (*laṭ*) and other such suffixes. Nor does the suffix produce the cognition of both successively, like the word *akṣa* which has multiple meanings.

Nor is it accompanied by multiple elided words in the manner of the *ekaśeṣa* (grammatical retention of one from a class), whereby the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related) would apply to those two through their respective examples; thus, this [position] has been refuted.
(B1) [It is] the state of being the object of a cognition that generates the knowledge of something being a means to what is desired or undesired.
Furthermore, the causality of non-existence (*abhāva*) is common to both *yoga* and *kṣema*;
and its nature consists in being a factor that disrupts the causal complex for activity (*pravṛtti*), as is explained in detail elsewhere.
(B2) (Refutation of the claim that [the word] is primarily the subject of the operation): That is incorrect;

for there is no obstacle to a word denoting [its object] twice even when the delimitors of its expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) are identical, just as there is no obstacle to it denoting [its object] twice when the delimiters of its expressive power differ, by virtue of a single cognition.

On the contrary, in your own view, there would result the fault of excessive complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) in postulating a causal relationship for each individual case, based on the dependence upon the simultaneous presentation of multiple properties—such as *la*-ness, singular number, and so forth—residing in their respective positions for those multiple meanings perceived at the same time.

Furthermore, since even *laṭ*-ness cannot be of the nature of a universal (*jāti*), one must ultimately resort to defining it as being "any one of the ten [suffixes] beginning with *la*"; thus, for the sake of conveying the present tense and other such meanings, [the definition remains unnecessarily complex].

Since the presence of *laṭ* (the present tense marker) as a form is necessary for the presentation of *laṭ* through its substitutes such as *ti*, the presentation of the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) from that very source— which is established by experience— is unavoidable;

furthermore, it would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate that *latva* (the property of being *laṭ*) other than that [present tense marker] is the delimitor of the denotative power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

Although words such as *divākara* (sun) and *niśākara* (moon), when used individually, convey their respective meanings independently and thus denote distinct objects— just like the word "flower" [which denotes a single object]— nevertheless, because those two meanings are perceived together from the word *puṣpavat* (possessing flowers), that word denotes a combined meaning. Similarly, although in the case of the *laṭ* suffix and others, there is only the cognition of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), in the case of the *liṅ* suffix and others, there is the cognition of both meanings.
Furthermore, there is no obstacle to postulating that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others also denote such meanings;

for the Logicians (*tārkika*) and others, by means of a single capacity delimited by a single delimitor, maintain that the optative suffix expresses each of the meanings—such as being connected with an undesirable result, being a means to a desired end, and being achievable through effort—individually.

They justify the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verb-root is predominant" by taking the predominance relative to the meaning of the root, and thus such a meaning [of the optative] is [expressed] just like the meaning of a case-ending (*sub-artha*).
Since this is already established by the traditional rule (*smṛti*) itself— "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, but between them, the suffix is predominant"—

it would be redundant to state the predominance of *bhāvanā* specifically by prioritizing the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, [the opponent's position] would result in the absurdity that one would have to think, "I possess an activity produced by an operation residing in the Teacher," just as one thinks, "This person possesses an operation conducive to my own activity."

Since even the cognition [of the injunction] does not establish the commencement [of activity]— because it is no different from the original cognition— and since there is no evidence for postulating that the object of the instigation (*pravartanā*) is the primary qualificandum based merely on the cognition of an instigation qualified by the activity (in accordance with that original cognition),

it is more appropriate that the status of being the qualificandum of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)— which is established elsewhere and conforms to the well-known causal relationship common to its own co-occurrence— is what is logical. Therefore, in that [productive urge], the instigation itself is the qualifier.

Furthermore, whether the negative particle (*nañ*) is present or absent, its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is respectively with "instigation" (*pravṛtti*) alone, through the two relations of being produced by an inference generated by a cognition whose object is itself, and being the counter-positive of an absence prompted by such an inference.
And the word "self" (*sva*) refers to the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

The method for inferring that [causal efficacy], which constitutes the essence of that [injunction], should be consulted in works such as the *Bhāṭṭarahasya*; it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "and being the motivator" (*prayojakatvaṃ cātra*), the root text establishes that [the injunction] is not obtainable from any other source by taking up the sense of being the motivator of instigation (*pravartanā-prayojakatva*), which is established by implication;
it is not, however, a statement made because [that efficacy] is useful for the verbal cognition that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This is the direction of the argument.
Regarding "acquisition and security" (*yogakṣema*):
acquisition (*yoga*) is the obtaining of what has not yet been obtained;
security (*kṣema*) is the preservation of what has already been obtained.

And thus, by means of the inference that [the action] is a means to an undesirable end, the causal complex for activity is disrupted; having brought about this, the non-existence of activity is maintained, which is precisely what is meant by its being a cause of negation (*abhāva*).

However, when—according to the view of Bhaṭṭa Someśvara—it is accepted that activity is indeed distinct from the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the resolve "this must be done by me," and that through that [activity] alone the productive urge possesses the status of being the object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) by the injunction, then such [activity] would not be perceived in other verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*).
Thus it has been stated by the great Maudgalya Bhaṭṭas in the *Bhāvanāviveka*:

"If, even when a separate potency is postulated for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) itself, there is a requirement for a qualificand in the case of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal suffix—just as there is a requirement for a result such as heaven (*svarga*)—then let that which consists of the instigation (*pravartanā*) serve as the qualificand; and let it be granted that this [instigation] is obtainable from another source."

(An examination of the ways in which cessation is understood in the case of the locus of cessation): Now, one might object: "Since activity (*pravṛtti*) is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), even if it is obtainable from other sources, cessation (*nivṛtti*) is not perceived elsewhere; therefore, it is necessary to postulate a specific expressive power (*śakti*) for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth with respect to that aspect [of cessation]. How, then, can it be said that [cessation] is obtainable from other sources? To dispel this doubt, he says: "And its nature... (*tattvañca*).

The meaning is as follows: in such injunctions as "One should not eat *kalañja*," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) heard in the text does not denote a prohibition (*nivartanā*) in the same way it denotes an instigation (*pravartanā*); rather, it does so only when co-occurring with the negative particle (*nañ*), because the latter is indicative.
Thus, the capacity to denote a prohibition resides in the optative suffix only when the negative particle, which serves to indicate its intended meaning, is present.

Alternatively—the denotative power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) resides in mere operation (*vyāpāra*) in its generality, being common to both instigation (*pravartanā*) and dissuasion (*nivartanā*). In this case, the negative particle (*nañ*) serves as an indicator of the intended specific relation (*saṃsarga-viśeṣa*), namely that it is the cause of the non-occurrence of activity. Alternatively, its denotative power resides in instigation alone, specifically by way of the universal property of instigation (*pravartanātva*).
When a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed in conjunction [with a verb], it should be understood as having an indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward cessation (*nivartanā*).

Thus, with reference to the inclination toward eating *kalañja*—which takes the form of a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the verbal suffix and is prompted by passion—the optative suffix (*liṅ*) enjoins a "prohibition" (*nivartanā*), which is an activity whose result is an activity consisting of the cessation of that [inclination]. This is because a mere inclination cannot be the object of reference (*uddeśya*); according to the logic of the *Havirārti* [sacrifice], the meaning of the verbal root, its factors (*kāraka*), and so forth, do not fall within the scope of the object of reference.

Since being a qualifier of the agent is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), even when [the agent] is intended to be expressed, the non-intentional expression (*avivakṣā*) of qualifiers such as gender and number residing in the factors of action (*kāraka*)—namely the agent, the object, and so forth—is justified because they serve as qualifiers of the objective (*uddeśya*). (This concludes the refutation of the views of the *atat* and its proponents regarding the fact that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the sense of exclusion.

As for the claim made by some that the negative particle (*nañ*), although denoting absence, conveys the sense of "exhortation to desist" (*nivartanā*) when it occurs in syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*) with verbal suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like:

But it cannot be the optative suffix (*liṅ*); for since the optative is already established as denoting "incitement" (*pravartanā*), to assume a further expressive power (*śakti*) for it in that context would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Thus, the description of the sentence-meaning—namely, that the optative and so forth point toward the incitement to eat *kalañja* (which is already prompted by passion and the like), and the negative particle (*nañ*) enjoins the cessation thereof—is incorrect. This is because the optative’s denotation of incitement residing in passion and the like is not established either in common worldly usage or in the Veda, and thus it cannot be the object of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, since incitement residing in the optative itself is not [otherwise] established, it cannot be the object of a restatement by the optative; rather, it must be something enjoined.
This is because it would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) and other such fallacies.

By this [argument], it is shown that when there is a misconception regarding the injunctive force (*pravartanātva*) of the desirability as a means (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) inherent in eating—which is apprehended as being followed by an undesirable result—the optative suffix (*liṅ*) expresses a prohibition by restating (*anūdya*) that very desirability.
Thus, just as in the case of eating food, the fact that eating *kalañja* is also known as a cause of desired results by virtue of its being an instigator is negated; that is not so.

The statement by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*— that the meaning of the sentence [of the prohibition] is that the desired result obtainable from eating *kalañja* is followed by an undesirable consequence— is refuted; for in the Mīmāṃsaka view, since there is no apprehension of the injunctive force (*pravartanā*) in the form of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) residing in the act of eating as derived from the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is not cognized in any way, and thus the postulation of an additional power would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, the previously stated meaning of the sentence alone is logical.

When, through that prohibition, there arises an understanding of desisting (*nivartanā*), and when— as established in the *Bhaṭṭarahasya*— there also occurs an inferential cognition (*anumiti*) of its being a producer of the undesired (*aniṣṭajanakatva*) by virtue of being the object of a [prohibitive] injunction (*pravartanā*), then, by way of producing the cognition that obstructs inclination (*pravṛtti*), namely the cognition consisting in the knowledge of its being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānubandhitvajñāna*), [the prohibition functions].

Even in cases where there is an inference of the absence of being a means to the desired object (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) due to the disruption of the causal complex for activity— which consists in the absence of such an obstructing factor— there occurs an absence of activity by way of both ascertaining the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of the previously grasped cognition of being a means to the desired object and by disrupting the causal complex for activity.
The state of being its counter-positive (*tatpratiyogitva*) is understood in relation to the activity (*pravṛtti*).

Thus, when the cessation (*nivartanā*) is connected with the activity, the object of the term "cessation" is precisely that absence of activity which appears as a relation— in the manner of a relational qualifier (*saṃsargavidhayā*)— within the relation of being the counter-positive of an absence, which is itself prompted by an inference produced by a cognition having that [activity] as its object.
So that it may not be something obtainable through other means.
And that meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is, in an injunctive sentence, synonymous with instigation (*pravartanā*), incitement (*preraṇā*), and injunction (*vidhi*);
whereas in a prohibitive sentence, it is synonymous with desisting (*nivartanā*), warding off (*nivāraṇā*), negation (*niṣedha*), and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).
And this twofold [meaning] is the verbal productive energy (*śābdī bhāvanā*).
And its result (bhāvya) is, as appropriate, engagement and desistance.
The knowledge of the verbal productive energy (śābdabhāvanā) is the instrument (karaṇa).
And here, being an instrument consists in the production of the result of the productive energy.
Thus— (B2) [An analysis of the nature of instigation, entreaty, and permission]:

For instigation (*pravartanā*), which is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, when directed by a superior toward an inferior, is called "command" (*ājñā*) or "instigation" (*preṣaṇā*).
That [request] directed toward a superior by one who is inferior is *adhyeṣaṇā* (solicitation);

that [request] directed toward an equal by one who is equal, characterized by indifference toward superiority or inferiority, is called *anujñā* (permission) and is also designated as *anumiti* (inference).

Since such specific distinctions are not useful for the present context, the author sets aside those distinctions and demonstrates the relevant conventional usage of their difference, beginning with "And that... (*sa ca*).
The verbal productive energy (śābdībhāvanā).

(An examination of the dependence on the three factors of the verbal *bhāvanā*): Since that [verbal *bhāvanā*], which consists of a non-worldly dharma, resides in words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) within the injunctive and prohibitive sentences of the Veda,

although both types of verbal *bhāvanā*— [the objective and the verbal]— are present in injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and in prohibitions as well, because there is no other instigation (*pravartanā*) directed toward them;
There is no cognition of something as "to be done" (kartavyatā),

by virtue of which their connection could be stated through an expectation of an instrument, a procedure, and an object of realization— as is the case with objective productive activity (arthabhāvanā).
Nevertheless, from the injunction to study, it follows that the Veda, once studied, should produce whatever benefit it is capable of producing for a person.
Upon examining the capacity of those respective portions of the Veda through such understanding, the following realization arises regarding the portions consisting of injunctions and prohibitions:

"The optative suffix (*liṅ*) in expressions such as *yajeta* (‘one should sacrifice’), which has been the object of study by a male agent, should— by means of either the recollection of the relationship [between word and meaning] or by cognition itself acting as the instrument within the verbal element (*ākhyāta*)— produce a knowledge of the sentence-meaning in the form of an efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) qualified by a desired end, and thereby effect the activity of the person."
