Furthermore, although in this section of the *Vārttika* it was demonstrated that the words (*liṅ*) refined by study should make known the object as a means to a desired end through the knowledge of the injunction, that statement regarding the "extent of activity" (i.e., ending with the initiation of action) is because there is no requirement for either the "thing to be brought about" (*bhāvya*)—which is the means—or for the "excellence" (*prāśastya*) within that very [injunction], since they are useful only in relation to it. In that context, the injunction and prohibition must be performed with the specific qualification of the three factors: by whom, in what manner, and with reference to what.

Among the three parts being presented—namely, the injunction to perform the cultivation of the word "bodhi" (awakening), the objective to be realized, and the requirement for the means—the excellence (*prāśastya*) required as the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) in the present context is defined; thus, the [author] restates the objective and the instrument in the commentary with the words "And of that... (*tasyāśca*).

The sense is that it is logical for the very *bhāvanā* understood through the direct statement of a common verbal expression (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*) to possess the status of the objective (*bhāvya*).

(An exposition on the fact that the status of the verbal *bhāvanā* as the instrument does not depend on the word being known for its semantic meaning, but rather on the knowledge of the instigation [to act]:
Here, the status of the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*)—known as possessing the power to denote human activity—is that of the instrument;

this refers to the knowledge of the relationship [between the word and its meaning], which is the primary and foundational basis for all cognitions produced by the optative suffix (*liṅ*), namely: "this optative suffix denotes instigation."

The meaning is as follows: in order to refute the view that the word itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is argued that since words, their meanings, and their relations lack the status of being instruments with respect to the activity [of prompting], it is more logical for the cognition of the object—which is proximate compared to the remote word and so forth—to be the instrument.

This is because such a cognition cannot be an instrument in its own right with respect to the instigation (*pravartanā*), even though [the word] is an instrument in the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) of sacrifices and the like.

He states— “And the status of being an instrument (karaṇatva)” — that here too, the status of being an instrument must be understood in exactly the same way as that which is conventionally designated [in grammar] as the producer of the essential nature of heaven and so forth.
“Bhāvanā” refers to verbal bhāvanā (śābdībhāvanā).
Its "being" (bhāvya) means the activity of the person, that is to say, its state of being the producer thereof.
(The view that even that which is not presented through a mental mode [vṛtti], such as the knowledge of commendability, can be an object of verbal cognition):

In this regard, some describe it thus—that in verbal cognition, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) not only between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), but also between the knowledge of injunctions and prohibitions and their respective commendability or lack thereof.
First, the injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*) is presented through hearing;
its capacity to denote human activity is also presented through recollection;

and the "knownness" (*jñātatā*) residing in both of these is apprehended by the mind. Thus, the injunctive word is indeed presented as being known for its possession of the denotative power residing therein.

And because of the purport of the injunction for Vedic study— that "one should meditate upon whatever one is able"— even that which is presented by means other than the word itself appears in the verbal cognition,
just as, for example, the name *jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth,
or as a mantra to be applied by its indicative power (*liṅga*).
This has been stated by the Teacher in the *Udbhidadhikaraṇa*:
"A cognition of a qualified object does not arise when its qualifier is not present, but it does arise even when the qualifier is not explicitly expressed."

Thus, the presentation of the explanatory passages (arthavādas) occurs through the sense of hearing; their excellence, however, is apprehended through them by means of indication (lakṣaṇā); and the "cognizedness" (jñātatā) residing in both [the injunction and the arthavāda] is apprehended by the mind. Therefore, the connection with the procedure (itikartavyatā)—in the form "having known [the act] as praiseworthy through the arthavādas"—is indeed logically established.
(The established tenet is that the instrument (*karaṇa*) lacks syntactic connection (*ananvaya*), whereas the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) possesses it.

In reality, however, since—in all cases such as *ūha* and so forth—it is accepted that the postulation of words occurs precisely through the force of connection with the meaning of another word, just like an object presented by a verbal function (*vṛtti*), there is no possibility of connection for that which is not denoted by a word (*aśābda*). Therefore, the instrument is connected as an instrument, and not as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in any other respect.

Thus, since praise (*prāśastya*) and blame (*aprāśastya*), which are characterized by *arthavāda* and the like, are presented through their function (*vṛtti*), they connect elsewhere [in the injunction] by way of cognition;
and so, with the intention that praise and blame themselves constitute the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*) in their own form, he says: "Praise and blame.

Now, one might object: since activity is established simply from the injunction itself through the cognition that [the act] is a means to a desired end, and cessation is established simply from the prohibition itself through the cognition that it is a means to an undesired end, what is the use of praise and blame?
And so, since both of these are established by these two alone, those two would be useless; thus he says: "For [the knowledge] of praise and blame... and so forth.
And "oughtness" (*kartavyatā*) consists, as the case may be, in praise and blame.

For it is established in common worldly experience that the knowledge of praise and blame acts as an auxiliary cause for the instigation of activity and cessation by way of generating desire and aversion.

These [qualities] are expressed by the words "praise" and "blame," and are synonymous with "excellence" (*prāśastya*) and "non-excellence" (*aprāśastya*), consisting respectively in the fitness for being connected with or not being connected to a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavad-aniṣṭa*).
And these [two], praise and blame, as appropriate, serve as a means for activity through the medium of knowledge. For instance,

although the purchase of a cow is made attractive by the understanding that "this cow is to be bought" because it is a means to achieve a desired end, a person who wishes to prevent activity from it— due to perceiving the expenditure and effort involved— experiences a state of hesitation.

However, that [objection] is removed by describing qualities such as "abundant milk" and so forth; thus, the utility of that knowledge lies in its producing the cessation of the perceived obstruction. As it has been said: "In neither the world nor the Veda is there any such instrument for an action to be accomplished through a procedure (itikartavyatā) that does not require the assistance of such [knowledge]."
And thus, since both of these [affirmation and negation] act as auxiliaries in generating engagement and withdrawal through injunctions and prohibitions, they are not purposeless; this is the sense.
It has been stated that the object of that knowledge which is useful for engagement and withdrawal by way of producing desire and aversion is difficult to define.

To avoid that [objection], others have stated that neither excellence (*prāśastya*) nor non-excellence (*aprāśastya*) is possible; demonstrating this, [the author] himself says by way of defining their essential nature with the words "that which is intensely undesirable" (*balavadaniṣṭa*), etc.

For, since injunctions and prohibitions imply being a means to the desired and the undesired, even when the production of the desired and undesired—which serve as the causes for the engagement and withdrawal of those to be prompted—occurs, there would follow the impossibility of engagement and withdrawal due to the occurrence of aversion and enthusiasm, because the state of being a means to immediate pleasure and pain is also apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

When there is an expectation for something that can remove that [defect], it is because she possesses the capacity to remove it in the world that she is described as "having much milk," "having good offspring," and "having a living calf.
Therefore, in the context of the statement "This cow is for sale," one postulates that these descriptions serve to support the cognition of praise or blame already understood;
and it is established by direct perception that praise and blame produce desire and aversion, respectively.

Furthermore, when there is a requirement for a means of expression for those two [the injunction and the prohibition], it would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to assume that words containing the term "fruit" (*phala*)—which have already ceased their expectancy by functioning as expressers of the fruit and so forth—are the means of expression for them. Rather than that, it is more reasonable to assume that the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) themselves, which require a purpose, serve as the indicators (*lakṣakas*) of those two.
And these are indeed praise and censure, which are synonymous with excellence (*prāśastya*) and non-excellence (*aprāśastya*).
(An investigation into the nature of excellence and defect as being respectively the state of being praiseworthy and the state of being blameworthy:
That [excellence] consists in the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) and that [defect] in the possession of faults (*doṣavattva*).

For instance, regarding sound, which has the inherent nature of producing cognition, those who hold other views describe as a "quality" such properties as being uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*), which serve as the cause for the excellence consisting in the truthfulness (*yāthārthya*) residing in the cognition.

Thus, that which is intended by the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is a factor such as having a swift deity, which resides in the injunction and serves as the cause for excellence regarding the swiftness of the result and so forth.
In that very form, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) makes known each respective quality residing in the injunction.

And it can be said that wood characterized by being made of *udumbara* wood or having leaves of *parṇa* grass produces a sacrificial fruit characterized by not hearing evil words and so forth; thus some have said.
(Refutation of the previous view: That is incorrect;
for if that were the case, such qualities would be conveyed by primary denotation (*śakti*) itself, and thus it would be impossible for them to be secondary (*lākṣaṇika*).
Furthermore, because such qualities are impossible in explanatory passages (arthavāda) such as, "These indeed are the ten sacrificial implements," and "He chooses one."
(An alternative determination of the nature of excellence and defect as being respectively praiseworthy and blameworthy):

Some, however, maintain that the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that serves as the cause for breaking through aversion and laziness which obstruct engagement (*pravṛtti*); likewise, the state of being a defect (*doṣatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that serves as the cause for breaking through attachment which obstructs withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
And this is merely illustrative;

for in cognition, the state of being an object (*viṣayatā*) consists in its being the determinant of the respective causes for the destruction [of that cognition], and this occurs according to each specific case through its own particular form.
For this very reason, their subsistence in the performer is also required.
Because for those things known as being for the sake of that [purpose], there is no absence of being such;

likewise, it should be understood that the status of being a quality or a defect is established relative to a person, at a particular time, and with respect to a specific purpose for which one engages in activity or desists from it.

Therefore, in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others, there is authority for both injunctions and prohibitions as well as for the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) that serve as their supplements.
Consequently, it is precisely the merits and defects propounded by those respective *arthavādas* that constitute the nature of praise and blame.
And since the knowledge of merits and defects as they truly are is the very cause of purposeful engagement or withdrawal, [the *arthavādas*] by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*)...
Furthermore, since the things described— such as the hearing of evil reports from the world and weeping for up to a year— are unreal due to a lack of authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*),

the study of the *lakṣaṇas* is for the purpose of establishing real qualities and defects. Nor is it the case that, in this instance, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding prosperity (*bhūti*) is redundant because its capacity to indicate [prosperity] pertains to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), is real, and because activity is established through the Vedic text and the knowledge thereof alone, rendering the element of "swiftness" (*kṣipratva*) useless.
It should not be said that this refers to the meditation on that [wind];
for, by the statement "it is most swift," the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in that which is qualified by swiftness.

Otherwise, since it would be useless in the context of the Vedic sense, it would result in its own pointlessness; therefore, metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is required for the sake of that comprehension.
However, they say that this is the distinction: here, only an exaggeration of that very [quality] is intended as the mark, whereas elsewhere, it is indeed another actual quality.
(An argument establishing that the knowledge of qualities and defects as they truly are does not consist in the knowledge of what is praiseworthy and what is blameworthy):

Here it should be noted— if only the knowledge of qualities and defects as they truly are were the cause of purposeful engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), then how could the knowledge of excellence such as "swiftness" residing in the result indicated by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) like "Vāyu is the swiftest deity" be conducive to engagement, given that such knowledge lacks [the status of] being a knowledge of things as they truly are?

For just as the cognition of the literal meaning regarding the *parṇa-wood* [used for the ladle] is not considered false simply because the hearing of the "world of sin" (*pāpaśloka*) and so forth does not arise at that time when the *parṇatā* is being performed, so too here, it cannot be said that the cognition of excellence— which is the indicated sense of the *arthavāda*— cannot be true simply because the fruit of prosperity (*bhūti*) does not arise immediately following the performance of the ritual action.

Because the production of such a result in another birth is equal in both cases; furthermore, since it is universally acknowledged that even from a cognition consisting of error— such as the cognition that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence— one engages in activity that is in accordance with reality, it is indeed difficult to establish that only a true cognition (yathārthajñāna) is the cause of activity that accords with reality.

Or, even if that were the case, since it is generally observed that a cause imparts to its effect qualities corresponding to its own nature, the air—which serves as the instrument (*sādhana*) for the action—is characterized by rapidity; therefore, the action to be accomplished by it is also rapid. Consequently, in accordance with the cognition that "this praiseworthy sacrifice should be performed," [the excellence of the sacrifice] is understood in relation to an excellence of time consisting of rapidity.

It is understood that it is praise (*prāśastya*) alone—distinct from the mere hearing of the report of a world free from evil—that serves as the cause for engagement. Furthermore, since the qualities known through which laziness (which is an obstacle to engagement) is removed vary for each individual according to their specific type of laziness, they lack uniformity; consequently, because it is impossible to consistently indicate them as the primary meaning, it is untenable for the *arthavādas* to form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive word.
It is indeed manifest.

(B3) (1) For a person who has developed an inclination toward the performance of that [Vedic] action or its cessation, there is an absence of the quality of producing such an inclination—which is conditioned by the fruit—[in the case of the action itself]; therefore, the factor of "fitness" (*yogyatva*) is present.
(B2) [The nature of] excellence (*prāśastya*) and non-excellence (*aprāśastya*) consists in being the means to what is desired or undesired beyond the pleasure and pain produced by the action itself.
It is precisely with the intention that such excellence and non-excellence as described are not possible [in this context] that some have said this.
Excellence (*prāśastya*) consists in being a means to a desired end that is greater than the suffering produced by the performance of the action.
The resulting benefit (*artha*) is established from another source,
since injunctions and prohibitions merely imply that something is a means to a desired or undesired end.
Therefore, where an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not recited, it is necessarily implied by the injunction itself.
Even though such knowledge of praise or censure cannot possibly be the cause of engagement or desistance through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*);
Nevertheless, that knowledge certainly possesses utility solely in terms of promoting engagement or withdrawal by way of generating attraction or aversion.

(Refutation of the aforementioned view) That too is not correct; for in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning permissions and prohibitions— such as "When the omentum has been offered, one may eat the food of the initiated" and "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*"— there is an excess of satisfaction and suffering relative to the pleasure and pain understood from the injunctions and prohibitions themselves.

Because it is impossible to define it with a single uniform nature due to its being inexpressible; for it is not the case that the superiority of the fruit of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) over immediate suffering must be made known, since at that time, the prohibition "one shall not kill" makes the production of an undesirable result known therein, and because action would be impossible given the presence of a collection of factors that obstruct such activity, how could knowledge of that [superiority] be of any use?
The new [interpretation] does not involve the cognition of a greater degree [of suffering] in comparison to the sufferings of hell and so forth that result from employing the Śyena sacrifice;

for even in comparison to those, the prohibition "one shall not injure" (na hiṃsyāt) has already made known a greater degree [of suffering] in hell and so forth. Therefore, neither of these two types [of undesirable consequences] applies here.

However, it is more appropriate to define "praiseworthiness" (prāśastya) as the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, and "unpraiseworthiness" (aprāśastya) as the state of producing such a consequence; this is the definition accepted by the venerable Dīkṣita Madhusūdana Svāmin.
(Refutation of all previously mentioned objections by defining the "strength" of the desirable and the undesirable as consisting in their being objects of intense attachment and aversion:
Here, the strength of the undesirable consists in its being the object of intense aversion, and not in its numerical superiority.
Because, due to the power of past karma, an intense aversion arises toward even a slight suffering in heaven that occurs at that moment;
for this very reason, one does not engage in sacrifices and the like at that time.
Likewise, because an intense attachment arises toward even a slight pleasure in hell that occurs at that moment, due to the power of past karma.
For this very reason, one indeed engages in malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like.

For this very reason, in the case of sacrifices and the like, it is only at certain times—by virtue of previous auspicious karma—that there is the state of being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*);
whereas in prohibitions, there is the production of such a consequence. Thus, "excellence" (*prāśastya*) consists in the fitness for being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence.
The capacity to produce that [action], as well as its lack of praiseworthiness, is of a single form everywhere.

And for that person who has always understood, in the case of sacrifices and the like, that they are not followed by a powerful undesirable result, the knowledge of that [lack of praiseworthiness] is useful for initiating action by producing the realization of the invalidity of the [Vedic] injunction; for [only] a cognition of non-connection with a powerful undesirable result that is not overridden by a cognition of invalidity [motivates action].
Because it acts as an obstacle to activity:

where there is an absence of both types of knowledge due merely to the understanding of injunction and prohibition by their own nature in both cases, since the obstacle itself is absent, even if that knowledge is of no use, the authority of the *arthavāda* is indeed established simply by its being useful for a particular person.
Therefore, when an obstacle exists, the [knowledge of] the non-existence of that obstacle merely serves as a means for engaging in or desisting from action;

it does not, however, function as their (action and desistance) cause through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as a rule. With this very intention, the venerable [author] in the *Bhāṭṭarahasya* refuted the view of the Logicians (*Tārkika*), who hold that because the property of "not being connected with a powerful undesirable result" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) is absent in sacrifices and the like by necessity, the verbal suffixes (*liṅgadi*) do not possess denotative power (*śakti*) toward them as a rule.
And such praise is possible in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning a permissive injunction (*abhyanujñā-vidhi*);

for it makes known that the eating of food by the consecrated (*dīkṣita*) after the offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) is not followed by the undesirable consequences entailed by the prohibition [of such eating].

This is because, although the injunction produces an absence of aversion and thereby implies that [absence], the cognition of its fitness to produce that absence of aversion depends upon the explanatory passage.
Thus, even in the case of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) prohibiting the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, there is a lack of excellence (*aprāśastya*);

for it conveys a sense of "strength" characterized by being the object of intense aversion, based on the co-referentiality with even a slight, temporary suffering produced by the act of taking the cup.

Similarly, in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice as well, since the capacity to not be followed by a powerful undesirable consequence exists according to the method of establishing its status as dharma, it is likewise easy to convey that [lack of excellence] through its explanatory passage as well.
Otherwise, activity would never be possible.

Therefore, since the quality of being characterized by *tamas* is established, there is also the possibility of "non-praise" (*aprāśastya*)— consisting in the fitness for not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence— and thus even the non-praise indicated by the prohibitory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not at all contradictory.
(Regarding the view that the injunction itself implies commendation:

By this, the aforementioned arguments by some who rejected both commendation and non-commendation are refuted— namely, [the claim] that it would lead to the consequence of inconsistency for the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) which are subordinate to injunctions of harmful acts such as the *śyena* sacrifice, and because the specific implication can be achieved by the injunctions themselves.

This [objection] is refuted by the following: since only such [an action] can be the object of an intentional agent's engagement, even in the case of prohibitions, the fact that they produce an undesirable result is established by the very principle that "painful action [is to be avoided]"; for prohibitions function by implying the production of a powerful undesirable result, and thus it is untenable for them to depend on [external factors] such as the Arthavāda passages. Therefore, [the objection] is discarded.
(Refutation of the injunction’s implication of commendation:

Just as injunctions imply that [an action] is a means to a desired end qualified by not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, it is possible for those same injunctions to imply even non-commendability; thus, according to your own view, since prohibitions function independently of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), there is independence from explanatory passages.

Furthermore, because it is difficult to avoid [the charge of redundancy], and because there is no evidence for assuming that the function of prohibitions extends as far as implying their powerful nature— even when one merely implies that they produce hellish rebirths in order to avoid the futility of conveying to worldly people that they produce undesirable results; and because...

Because that [excellence or deficiency] is obtained everywhere through the very injunctions, prohibitions, and explanatory passages (arthavādas) present there; because it would be cumbersome to assume that each respective injunction or prohibition extends only as far as those [arthavādas];

and because, since the cognition of excellence or deficiency must necessarily be admitted to occur even before the injunctions or prohibitions inferred from the arthavādas, it is impossible for those injunctions or prohibitions to invariably imply them by necessity.

Therefore, where explanatory passages (arthavādas) are recited in proximity [to an injunction], since the knowledge of praise or censure can be obtained there through the requirement for a purpose, it should not be assumed that they have that as their primary aim along with the injunctions or prohibitions; this is because of the principle of parsimony (gaurava).

(B1) Because they are required by injunctions and prohibitions, [these meanings] are conveyed through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) associated with them.

In that regard, in cases such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," the metaphorical indication occurs precisely through qualities such as swiftness, which are directly denotable by the word itself. However, in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*)," there is the capacity to perform one's own function, which is understood through secondary indication (*gauṇī*). (B2)

(Admission that an injunction devoid of an explanatory statement (arthavāda) implies such a statement): However, in cases where there are injunctions lacking explanatory statements, such as "One should sacrifice kapiñjala birds for the sake of spring," one must, out of necessity, admit that they too have that [explanatory statement] as their intended purpose.

Furthermore, just as in those cases [of *atideśa*], because the excellence (*prāśastya*) is obtained through the extension of the verbal statement (*vacana-atideśa*) or the extension of the name (*nāma-atideśa*), there is no assumption of the operation of an injunction (*vidhi-vyāpāra-kalpana*),

but rather the assumption of the operation of an injunction occurs only where both direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extension (*atideśa*) are absent— as in the case of the *darvihoma* and similar rites—
this has been established by my venerable teacher in the *Kaustubha*; it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.

Thus it is established that "praiseworthiness" (prāśastya) is the fitness for not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence, while "unpraiseworthiness" (aprāśastya) is the fitness for producing such a consequence.
(An examination of the mutual expectancy between injunctions and explanatory passages: "Because they are required by injunctions and prohibitions.
This is also an illustration of the requirement for explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Just as injunctions and prohibitions, in the manner previously established, require the assistance provided by explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)— by way of removing obstacles— to produce their results in the form of engagement and withdrawal, so too do the *arthavādas* themselves, even while expressing a factual matter through either primary or secondary figurative function (*vṛtti*), require the assistance of an injunction in order to obtain the status of having a visible purpose brought about by the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-vidhi*).

Furthermore, since the knowledge of commendation (*prāśastya*) required by the injunction is provided by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and that [knowledge] provided by the explanatory passages is required by the injunction, such knowledge is easily obtained through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the explanatory passages. Moreover, the relationship constituting this secondary function—consisting in being the object of a cognition produced by the cognition of its own primary meaning—is indeed composed of cognition itself. By the phrase "co-uttered with those [injunctions]," the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the injunction and the explanatory passage is indicated; it takes the form: "Because it is commendable, it ought to be performed," based on the mutual expectancy previously established.

And thus the Siddhānta-sūtra states: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, the [Arthavādas] should serve the purpose of praising the injunctions. Because the Arthavādas—which possess a requirement for a purpose—form a single syntactical unit with an injunction that requires praise, the injunctions (i.e., the things to be enjoined) [are understood] through the purpose of praising, namely, by means of the figurative sense consisting of praise; thus, the Arthavādas do not lack meaning.
The meaning of that is: "There should be means of valid cognition regarding the Dharma."
The three words beginning with "vidhinā" (by injunction) are also indicative of prohibitions and so forth.
(Justification for the definition of sentence-meaning as figurative indication:
For this very reason, this figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in the sentence, not in a single word.

Because otherwise the other words would result in being redundant; because, if those words were merely intended to indicate the purport (*tātparya*), there would be no decisive criterion for determining which one does so; and because all the words are understood to serve as a means of establishing praise (*stuti*) in the form: "Since the effect conforms to its cause, an action accomplished through a swift deity will grant its fruit very quickly."
Therefore, indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs only in a sentence, which consists of a collection of words;

for although, according to the method stated in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning "that which has come into being" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*), a sentence possesses no additional power (*śakti*) toward the sentence-meaning such that indication in this sentence would be appropriate by virtue of its connection with a related meaning.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that it is not improper to establish the presence of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a sentence by accepting its very nature as indication based merely on the connection with its own primary meaning; for experience itself is the authority (*pramāṇa*).

(There is a necessity for even those [words] which by their own power bring about the presentation of an unreal object to necessarily bring about the presentation of a real object through some basis whatsoever.
Furthermore, among the *arthavādas*, some bring about the presentation of a real object by their very power, while others bring about the presentation of an unreal object by that same power.
Where this literal meaning is possible and true, there metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs because of the connection with the primary meaning as it truly is;
where the meaning is not true, [it does not].

In this regard, even though the cognition of praise or blame arises from an unreal object, its validity is indeed established because it conveys a real object in the form of praise or blame which is the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*). However, since the reality of an object is impossible without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since the correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) is the natural rule for all cognitions, even if the Arthavāda does not depend on the reality of the object for the sake of establishing the praise or blame, it nonetheless depends on it for the sake of establishing the denotation itself.

Having established the reality of the object (*arthasatyatva*) in some way or another by means of any [suitable] objective support (*ālambana*), he demonstrates the distinction that it is a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) due to its connection with that object, by showing various examples beginning with the words "tatra" and so forth.

For it is generally observed that a cause imparts to its effect properties corresponding to its own properties; thus, from the knowledge that the wind—which serves as the means for the ritual act—is characterized by swiftness, there arises a cognition of the meaning of the truthful statement regarding its capacity to produce swift results within the action to be accomplished by it.

It is precisely through this objectified meaning of the statement that there occurs, in passages such as "Vāyu is the swiftest mover" (*vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhaḥ*), the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of excellence (*prāśastya*).
In the statement "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), by determining the meaning of the basis (*ālambana*), the sense results in a form of censure.

In these explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He wept," the pronoun "he" (*saḥ*) refers back to Agni, who was previously introduced in the passage "That Agni desired this" (*tad agnir nyakāmayata*).
In the phrase "that silver" (*tad rajatam*), the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers to the tears.

In this context, the passage "Before a year has passed for him" is a censure of the gift of silver; its justification is provided by the statement "He wept. Since the effect conforms to its cause, the gift of silver—which originates from tears—results in weeping; thus, the lack of excellence in the form of censure consists in the fact that it is produced by tears born of weeping.

Because it possesses the nature of defects such as causing the weeping produced by that [object], Rudra is indicated by its own meanings; however, since there is a lack of evidence for weeping and its origin in silver, this is untenable and must be established through some other basis.
The manner of doing so should be seen elsewhere.
(An examination of the statement "The sacrificer is the *prastara*"):
Thus, in cases such as "The sacrificer is the *prastara*," because there exists a certainty of incompatibility (*ayogyatā*), the initial sentence-meaning does not reach its final conclusion;

for the non-difference of the sacrificer from the *prastara* is sublated (*bādhita*). Therefore, in that context, the word "sacrificer" [is applied] by virtue of the connection with a quality consisting in the performance of a similar type of action, namely, the performance of the duties of the sacrificer.

Having accepted the secondary sense (*gauṇa*) with respect to the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), it will be stated in the *Tatsiddhi* and subsequent sūtras that after the cognition produced by the sentence "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle," there occurs subsequently a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by that same sentence, on the basis of the relationship between the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning consisting in the sacrificer's being the performer of his own duties.
(Water is indeed peaceful;
[the discussion of explanatory passages such as] "one should sprinkle with *gavīdhuka* barley-gruel," etc.

Thus, just as in some cases there is a direct praise of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), in other cases, through the praise of something else related to the object of the injunction, a praise of that which is connected to the thing to be enjoined is indicated by implication (*lakṣyate*).

Just as in the case of the injunction, "One should drag the fire with a cane branch and *avakā* grass," there are explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) in proximity to that injunction, such as, "Water is indeed peaceful; by means of these peaceful [substances], he pacifies his impurity.
In that context, through the praise of water, the praise of the cane and *avakā* grass—which are born from water—is understood by means of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
Sometimes, even the praise of something unrelated and not itself enjoined, when accompanied by a censure of another, indicates the superior excellence of that which is actually enjoined.

Just as there is praise for the *gavīdhuka* grain regarding milk, so they deliberate: "Should the *tryambaka* cakes be sprinkled with clarified butter, or should they not? If one were to sprinkle them, he would place the cattle in the mouth of Rudra; if he were not to sprinkle them, he would not place the cattle in the mouth of Rudra. However, they also say: "They should indeed be sprinkled."

Thus, the censure of the enjoined sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), accompanied by the praise of its opposite— non-sprinkling— and functioning as a single syntactical unit with the injunction for sprinkling, indicates a praise of the sprinkling that does not result in the censure of Rudra, who is the deity of the Tryambaka sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
In some cases, it indicates the excellence of another thing to be enjoined through a censure of what has been stated, as follows.
(B1) It will be stated [later] that [the Veda possesses authority] "by means of qualities such as being composed by [an omniscient author].

Therefore, it is established that because they generate valid cognition regarding objects of praise and censure associated with *bhāvanā*, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) contribute to [the knowledge of] *dharma* and *adharma*.
(B2) [This concludes the determination that certain explanatory passages serve both the purpose of praise and the purpose of the fruit.]

Furthermore, because [the mantra] possesses the form of a consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, it is first understood merely by virtue of its occurring when that [act] occurs; since it is not understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it lacks the status of a real quality (*guṇa*). Thus, according to the logic stated in the *Vārttika*—"This is untrue; I shall obtain something else"—it indicates excellence (*prāśastya*). Having thus been utilized through syntactic unity with some revealed injunction (*śruta-vidhi*) or as an indicator of some injunction, it is again [connected] by way of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
It also serves for the sake of the result:

the praise of the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth is intended to establish that [the injunction] has a basis by providing a justification through the description of qualities such as purity.

In this way, the "various modes" found in other explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) associated with injunctions or prohibitions should be understood as being subsumed under the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the root text.
(An examination of the laudatory nature of the verse beginning with "That which is not mixed with suffering...

And thus, since there is a natural liking or aversion toward results such as heaven or hell, there is no purpose [in teaching them]; therefore, regarding those [results] that are taught [as goals], [the text says]: "That which is not mixed with suffering, nor seized by it immediately..."
And such passages as "That happiness brought about by desire is the locus of the state of heaven" do not have the function of indicating praise or blame;
rather, they are solely intent upon defining the nature of heaven, hell, and so forth, as required by injunctions and prohibitions.
(An exposition on the respective utility of the Upaniṣads in relation to ritual action):

Thus, even for the Upaniṣads—which, though situated at a distance [from the ritual context], establish the Self as an eternal agent and enjoyer distinct from the perishable body—their purpose is precisely to convey such a Self as required by the injunctions for rituals whose fruits lie in the next world.

This is so even according to the view of Miśra, who holds that although the knowledge described above is studied outside of any specific ritual context (*anārabhyādhīta*), it serves a purpose through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the absence of any other means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for establishing a general connection [with the ritual].

Furthermore, because they serve as means of application (*viniyojaka*), according to the view of the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, these [texts] possess the status of being subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*) based on the statement: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that becomes more powerful.

It should be understood that the Upanishads, which establish the nature of the Self as both possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*) and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) for those who are not subject to transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*), have their own intrinsic purpose (*svārthaparatva*) alone, as they are required by the injunctions for both types of meditation (*upāsanā*).
Now, one might ask: even if explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) function as indicators of praise or dispraise, how can they be considered exponents of *dharma* and *adharma*?
To this, he says: "Therefore, it is established."

And thus, since the authoritative cognition of Dharma in the form of a qualified productive urge (*bhāvanā*) is produced by the injunctions (*vidhi*), it is logical that even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), like words denoting substances and deities, serve as causes for that authoritative cognition by means of conveying a specific qualification in the form of praise (*prāśastya*).
This is the meaning: the same applies to explanatory passages concerning prohibitions (*niṣedha*).

(An Examination of the Syntactic Unity of Arthavādas with Injunctions) In this regard, according to the method stated in the *Vārttika* on the *Aktādhikaraṇa*, since injunctions (*vidhi*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack the capacity to convey their respective meanings independently, they possess only syntactic unity at the level of the word (*padaikavākyatā*).

For it is a rule that when a sentence has completed its own meaning through dependence on another sense, its syntactic unity with another sentence-meaning constitutes "syntactic unity of sentences" (*vākyaikavākyatā*), just as between the injunctions for the subsidiary and the principal acts.
Thus it has been said in the *Aktādhikaraṇavārttika*:

"Sentences that are complete in their own meaning attain the status of a single sentence again by being combined, through the requirement of the relationship between principal and subordinate elements."
By this, the statement in the *Adhikaraṇamālā* and other works that there is syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) between an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and an injunction (*vidhi*) is refuted.
(On the absence of the expectancy for *itikartavyatā* [the manner of performance] in the verbal productive energy):

Although, because commendation (*prāśastya*) constitutes the *itikartavyatā* of the verbal productive energy—just as it does for the objective productive energy—it is possible for the connection with the *itikartavyatā* "in this way" (*ittham*) to follow the expectancy "how? (*katham*); nevertheless, there is no such cognition of the *itikartavyatā* for the verbal productive energy for every individual injunction (*vidhi*).
Because no other instigation (pravartanā) directed toward that [study] is perceived, but rather it resides in the objective productive urge (arthabhāvanā) itself;
for it is from the injunction to study (adhyayanavidhi) alone that the necessity of performing that [objective urge] is understood by implication.
The stage of practice following thorough penetration.
(According to the view of some, the excellence [prāśastya] is construed with the verbal efficient force [śābdabhāvanā]):

In that context, since it is impossible for an unknown excellence to function as a causal factor (*kāraka*) toward activity, it is logical that its construction be precisely as "because of being excellent" (*praśastatvāt*), which depends upon a cause.

However, according to the view of some, even in that form, it is construed with the verbal efficient force itself through the relation of being the object of a cognition that generates the activity or cessation produced by a cognition of its own object.
(On one's own view, the connection of excellence and so forth with the efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*) occurs through a mediated relation.

On our own view, however, in accordance with the parsimony of a single causal relationship— as in the case of the meaning of other nominal stems— excellence (*prāśastya*) is connected [to the efficient-force] by way of the relation "being produced by an intense desire directed toward a desired object, which is itself produced by a cognition whose object is that [excellence]," and non-excellence (*aprāśastya*) is connected by way of the relation "being produced by an intense aversion directed toward an undesired object, which is itself produced by a cognition whose object is that [non-excellence]."

To indicate the difference between these views—that the connection [of praise and blame] occurs only with the efficient-force directed toward the object (*arthabhāvanā*)—it was stated in a general manner that "praise and blame are connected with the efficient-force.
By this, it should be understood that the view held by some—that those two are connected to the root-meaning itself through a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*)—is utterly refuted;
for the requirement of an auxiliary factor, which is the very basis of such a connection, is satisfied simply by their connection to either the cause or the effect.
(Conclusion on the utility of *arthavādas* for *dharma* by way of establishing their excellence:

Therefore, since the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) makes it known that even the *arthavāda* culminates in human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), and since the postulation of heaven and so forth is untenable when a visible fruit is obtained— even if indirectly— the mere statement of a factual matter (*bhūtārtha*) being devoid of purpose, [the *arthavāda*] must have as its primary aim praise (*prāśastya*) or censure (*aprāśastya*).

By resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is established that, through their respective connection with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) conveyed by injunctions and prohibitions, these two have as their purpose the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) consisting in a qualified productive urge.
(B1) Regarding the term "venerable" (*mānya*):

the purpose [of this discussion] is as follows. According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even if one acts upon the basis of a knowledge of commendation (*prāśastya*) that is not presented by an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the attainment of the result is established.

However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since it is a rule that explanatory passages alone—just like mantras—are what incite action (*prarocaka*), the attainment of the result should be understood to occur only when one acts upon the basis of a knowledge of commendation that is presented by those very explanatory passages. // 1 //
Thus ends the first section concerning explanatory passages (arthavāda).
(Section 2: Or rather, it is an injunction.

In explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) such as, “The sacrificial post is made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is strength (*ūrj*), and cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains strength and cattle for him, for the sake of securing strength,” there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of praise.
This is because its authority is established precisely through its own literal power (*śakti*) in enjoining a connection with a fruit in the form of cattle.

Since the attainment of cattle is understood either by the accusative case in “cattle” (*paśūn*) or by the dative-like purpose clause “for the sake of securing strength” (*ūrjo ’varudhyai*), the quality of being made of *udumbara* [is enjoined] because of the requirement for a means (*sādhana*).
(An exposition of the two purposes— general and specific— of the investigation into the authority of *arthavādas*):
Since the specific purpose of establishing the authority of *arthavādas*, namely the accomplishment of results such as the determination of doubtful meanings,
will be understood from each respective *arthavāda* in its own particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the author sets that aside and states the general purpose.

Regarding the "purpose" (*prayojana*): [this is] the definition of the nature of the various types of connection (*saṃgati*), such as the introductory connection (*ākṣepikī*) and so forth. Now, connection is fourfold by way of the treatise (*śāstra*), the chapter (*adhyāya*), the section (*pāda*), and the topical discussion (*adhikaraṇa*).
Furthermore, among those, the connection between topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa-saṃgati*) is sixfold or sevenfold through the method of grouping (*rāśīkaraṇa*).
Where something is projected first, that is considered "projective" (ākṣepikī);
where there is a departure from the previous reasoning, that is the "counter-example" (pratyudāharaṇā).

That which is considered incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) is that which is contemplated in connection with another topic; however, when it is contemplated while remaining within the scope of the primary subject, it is essentially not distinct from that subject. Furthermore, where an excessive doubt has arisen, it is indicated by way of extension (*atideśa*) even before the main discussion.

"In that regard, those who know the logic [of the *Nyāya*] have declared the connection (*saṃgati*) to be of two kinds: the extended application (*atideśikī*) and the introductory inquiry (*upodghāta*), which is for the purpose of establishing the subject matter under consideration (*prakṛti-siddhyartham*).
Thus it is said.
When there are six types of *saṅgati*, it should be understood that *upodghāta* (introduction) is included within *prasaṅga* (occasion).

Thus, since wise men are certainly capable of inferring such forms of *saṅgati* and so forth for each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), the venerable author did not demonstrate them out of fear of prolixity; for that reason, I too shall not demonstrate them in detail here.
This concludes the first topical section concerning *arthavāda* (explanatory passages).
(An exposition of the connection with the preceding section:

In the preceding section, it was established that all explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are not purposeless because they serve the purpose of praise; now, however, since in certain explanatory passages that lack of purposelessness can be accounted for in another way as well, one need not resort to the view that they are primarily intended for praise that is almost useless.
Having thus raised an objection, it will be resolved; in this way, the "objection-based" (ākṣepikī) connection will be indicated at the conclusion of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

To that end, he shows an example of a specific explanatory passage (arthavāda) found within the context of a modified sacrifice: "One desiring cattle should offer a three-year-old goat to Soma and Pūṣan"—namely, the passage beginning with "audumbara."
(An exposition of the meaning of the subject sentence: "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood" is the injunction (*vidhi*);
"The Udumbara is indeed strength" is the portion that is the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
The word *vā* has the sense of *vai*.
By the word *udumbara*, food is meant;
for the *udumbara* tree consists of food by way of its ripe fruit.
It is well known in the world that "animals consist of food.

Therefore, the meaning of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is that the Adhvaryu priest who meditates upon the sacrificial post as being of the nature of Udumbara wood maintains animals for the sacrificer;
such is the sense of the phrase "and so forth."

By the phrase "and so forth," there is an inclusion of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) for injunctions such as "he does not hear evil report," which concern the use of *parṇa*-wood and similar matters.

And in this present example, according to the final position (*siddhānta*), the explanatory passage ending with "for the attainment of vigor" (*ūrjo 'varudhyai*) has the fruit of the sacrifice itself as its fruit.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, the statement "He obtains vigor and cattle for the sake of securing vigor" functions as an indicator of the fruit (*phala*) and thus does not possess the nature of a glorification (*stāvaka*).

The distinction is that the Vedic passage "The Udumbara tree is indeed vigor" serves the purpose of praise by demonstrating the appropriateness of the relationship between the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*).
"By means of power alone."

And therefore, because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is weaker due to its dependence on other means for grasping the intended meaning (*tātparya*), it follows that an indication of excellence (*prāśastya-lakṣaṇā*) should not be accepted; this is the meaning.
[The phrase] "by way of being injunctive" (*vidhāyakatvena*)...

Although, since activity regarding the portion of the result proceeds from desire alone, an injunction in the form of "instigating one who has not yet acted" is not possible; nevertheless, it is called "injunctional" insofar as it makes known what was previously unknown.

Now, one might ask: in the absence of words such as "kāma" (desire), how is there a cognition of the cattle as the result, by virtue of which its authority is asserted through that cognition? To this, he says: "paśūn" (the cattle).

The meaning is that although only the aspect of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is understood through the accusative case in the word *paśūn* (animals), the status of being the objective (*bhāvyatva*) is established because the state of being desired (*īpsitatva*) is also understood by virtue of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*). This occurs when the state of being something to be accomplished has been understood.

(B3) (1) Since the connection with the sacrifice is established by the statement "whatever one does through knowledge" for the sake of understanding a purposeful meaning, study—even when prompted by the desire for knowledge of the meaning—culminates in the sacrifice itself; thus, its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is justified. Consequently, it is a restrictive injunction whose result is the exclusion of other means, according to the *Kaustubha*.

In the *Nyāyaratnamālā*, however, it is established that the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is meaningful because such injunctions are observed even regarding human goals (*puruṣārtha*), such as the acquisition of wealth; thus, it is not the case that a restrictive injunction applies only to ritual purposes (*kratvartha*). [Verse 1: "In the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, there would be stability (*pratiṣṭhā*); in ignorance, there is the persistence of clarified butter (*ghṛtasaṃsthiti*);
likewise, the status of being a name (*nāmatā*) for sentences concerning the Śyena and other rites is a cause of differentiation."
Likewise, the gift in the Vāruṇī sacrifice, the Vedic emetic, and that which pertains to the Soma sacrifice—namely, the status of the term *jyotiṣṭoma* [as referring to the Soma sacrifice]. (2)
And there is the insertion of the *dhāyyā* verses; the middle verse is recited after the *ṛc*;
there is the displacement of the *iḍā* and other elements; and even in the case of Rudra, who is denoted by the word "weeping" (*rodana*), [the same applies]. // 3 //
The superiority of the [last] three is threefold; the officiating priest should be a Brāhmaṇa;
and the eternality of Soma, Vedic knowledge, progeny, and so forth is established in the sixth [chapter]. (4)
In the seventh [chapter], the carrying forward of the two fires at the middle parvans is declared;
likewise, in the eighth, the status of being the archetype (prakṛti) is established by means of indicative marks found in explanatory passages (arthavāda).
Thus, in the Kaustubha:
[the means] is the proof,
because of proximity.

Since the third case ending is heard in the word *ūrjā* ("with vigor"), and since the verbal suffix in *bhavati* denotes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or by its primary power (*śakti*), and since the root *bhū* merely restates the cutting and other acts that produce the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), it is determined to be in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood because its meaning is not already established; thus, the objection arises that this [sentence] must enjoin an efficient force qualified by both [the material and the purpose]. To this, the reply is given: when the efficient force having the sacrificial post as its agent is already implied...

In the context of the meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), since it is appropriate for the sacrificial post (yūpa) alone to be the object to be realized (bhāvya), and because of its proximity, the injunction regarding the quality of being made of Udumbara wood is intended solely for the sake of the sacrificial post,
not for the sake of a fruit; for, in the absence of words such as "kāma" (desire), the status of [the fruit] is not presented in that manner.
Furthermore, according to your view, this would be a relationship between a quality (guṇa) and its fruit (phala);
yet that is not possible, because no substratum (āśraya) can be found.

For if the sacrifice under discussion—“One desiring cattle should offer a three-year-old animal to Soma and Pūṣan”—were the substratum, then the mention of the *yūpa* (sacrificial post) would be untenable.
Furthermore, since the *yūpa* itself is not part of the context (*aprakṛta*), it cannot be the substratum.

Even if its presence were established through extended application (*atideśa*), that presence would be common to other vessels such as the *juhū*; thus, if those too were the substrata, the mention of the *yūpa* would likewise be purposeless.
Furthermore, if the substrate were provided by a separate sentence, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). [Note:

*Audumbara* is established otherwise as a derivative suffix denoting a modification; thus, the status of the animal as the fruit is determined by the direct hearing of the accusative and dative cases.

By this [argument]—namely, that because the word *audumbara* is a taddhita suffix denoting a modification, it expresses a specific form in the shape of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) due to the force of the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), and because of the proximity conveyed by the word *yūpa*, it must serve the purpose of the post itself—it is refuted.

The meaning is as follows: since the second and fourth *śruti*s (direct and syntactical indications), which are stronger than that [context], convey that the [udumbara wood] is for the sake of the animal (*paśvarthatā*), the formation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is justified by its producing the substrate in the form of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is obtained as an inseparable consequence (*nāntarīyakatayā*). Thus, the *śruti* within the same word is established otherwise.
(Just as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," etc., the determination of the *udumbara* as the means [of the post] arises from proximity.
This is what is meant by "from proximity" (*sannidhānāt*).

The meaning is as follows: just as in cases such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*yajeta svargakāmaḥ*) or "the Jyotiṣṭoma [is prescribed] for all [desires]," even in the absence of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth, the sacrifice is understood to possess the required status of being a means simply through its proximity (*sannidhāna*), because the state of being an end (*sādhyatva*) residing in heaven and the like is perceived; so it is here as well.
Although in this instance the status of being a means is easily understood even by the instrumental suffix in the word *ūrjā*;
Nevertheless, since that [causal efficiency] is absent in the case of the *parṇatā* (leafiness) and so forth, it is stated that mere proximity alone is the cause of that [result].

(The body of this present section consists of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the injunction is redundant because activity is established by the very fact that the means to the desired end is understood through proximity.

Here, the ancient [commentators] have formulated a prima facie argument extending as far as: "Since the status of *audumbara* wood as a means is understood from proximity alone, and since activity is established by that mere knowledge of it being a means to the desired end, there is no need for an injunction. [The refutation continues: In the absence of an injunction, [the status of] being a means consisting of *audumbara* wood would be...
That very [meditation] would be the object to be cultivated through cultivation,
not the fruit; because it is remote, and because when there is an injunction, its nature consists in the instigation of the person.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to incite a person toward that which is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), one must set aside the status of the *audumbara* quality as the end to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)—as if it were merely incidental—and instead establish that the fruit itself, being a human goal, is the *bhāvya*.

Therefore, the injunctive force (*vidhitva*), which is necessarily required because there is a rule that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) must serve to praise that which is enjoined, must be inferred through the assumption of the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, as it would otherwise be untenable.
Moreover, if the passage is intent upon the fruit, its status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is no longer possible.
For it is not possible that, having generated the power of an injunction by means of being a praise, one could then again postulate a fruit by that very same [praise];
this would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) in the form of a repetition of the sentence. Therefore, it was concluded that these are indeed *arthavādas* (explanatory passages).
(Refutation of the prima facie view by refuting the ancient opinion and accepting the status of an injunction:
That is incorrect;

for, without syntactical unity with an injunction, there can be no certainty that it is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), and thus it is impossible for it to establish the existence of an injunction. To the spring...

Just as the determination that [the suffix] is *leṭ* occurs here even in the absence of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because the meaning is not otherwise established—just as in the case of the rule regarding *kapiñjalān*—so too is it appropriate here; for even if the determination is grasped solely from the explanatory passage, the status of being a glorification (*stāvaka*) is accepted by the opponent even up to the end of the section beginning with "The udumbara is strength; verily by strength he provides him with strength," and thus that [determination] is also established thereby. This is done in order to refute the position that extends to the total removal of the injunction (*vidhi-utkhāta-paryanta-pakṣa*) and to establish the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Intending that there is an absence of purpose, and thus accepting the status of [the passage] as an injunction, the author states the meaning of the sentence in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of the verb "it comes to be" (bhavati).
(According to different views, the expression *bhavati* denotes *bhāvanā* either through metaphorical indication or by its own primary power).

Since the relationship between the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) has action as its core, and because if there were a connection to action alone— as in "a pot comes into being by means of a stick"— the injunction would be rendered purposeless as it would not have the instigation of a person as its object, there must necessarily be something residing in the person [that serves as the basis for the injunction].
The operation (vyāpāra) to be accomplished by instigation (pravartanā) is the expressed meaning [of the optative suffix].
Although its cognition can occur through implication (ākṣepa) in the case of verbal roots whose meanings consist of the operation of the person to be prompted (prayojya),

nevertheless, since it must be stated that this [instigation] possesses verbal status (śābdatva) in order to connect with the injunction (vidhi), for those who hold that the tip-ness (tiptva) and so forth— which are the explications of the root *kṛ*— are the delimiters of the expressive power (śaktatāvacchedaka), in their view, [instigation] is not cognized here from the optative suffix (ākhyāta) by means of its primary expressive power (śakti).
The manifestation [of the meaning] occurs through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
However, for those whose view is that it is merely the suffix -tiP and so forth, the denotation of that [meaning] occurs through primary power (śakti) itself; this is the distinction.

And thus, when there arises the expectation, "How should one meditate on [the sacrificial post] as an udumbara tree?", the fruit consisting of cattle, mentioned in the explanatory passage (arthavāda), connects with that expectation. Therefore, the sense is that the activity— characterized by having cattle as its object and the udumbara tree as its instrument— is understood as being to be accomplished through the instigation (pravartanā).

The meaning is that even though the operation of the instigator has been mentioned, because it is not understood to be accomplished by instigation (*pravartanā*), there is no certainty regarding its having a desired end as its objective (*iṣṭabhāvyakatva*); consequently, there is no cognition of it being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*).
(Refutation of the view that "he obtains cattle" functions as the presentation of a fruit, because the *rātrisatra* principle does not apply due to the absence of words denoting desire and so forth:
"Because it is not thus presented."

The meaning is as follows: because the second case ending merely denotes the state of being produced (*janyatva*), the state of being something to be brought about (*bhāvyatva*) that is co-located with the state of being desired (*īpsitatva*) is not presented by the word *kāma*, just as it is not by the word *iṣṭa*.

Even if it were somehow possible [to derive such a meaning], nevertheless, since there is a reference to the present in the phrase "he obtains cattle" (*paśūn āpnoti*), this is sublated by the non-perception of a present result; thus, there would be the necessity of resorting to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a future time.

For this very reason—because there is no further expectancy since the purpose is already fulfilled by the fact that [the act] is desired as a means to an unseen result (*apūrva*)—even the principle of the *rātrisatra* does not apply; this will be explained in the *parṇamayī-adhikaraṇa*.
(This section provides the resolution of the charge of redundancy with the *parṇamayyadhikaraṇa*.

Thus, by refuting here the view that [the passage] is solely intent upon a result, its status as being intent upon praise is established; in that case, just as in the *rātrisatra*, the fact that it is merely an *arthavāda* will necessarily preclude its being intent upon a result.

Furthermore, even if the dative case were intent upon a result, there would be no requirement for it to be intent upon a result mentioned within its own sentence, because its expectancy is satisfied by its purpose being the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) mentioned in its own context.
The intention is that even for a powerful [word], if there is an absence of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), it is impossible for it to function as the motivator of syntactic connection (anvaya).
He states another refutation: "Furthermore," etc.
This is clear in meaning.
"Of the state of being an udumbara tree."

The meaning is that since the fruit which is primary takes the form of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*), the quality of being made of *udumbara* wood is appropriate as something that assists it—as expressed in passages such as "the cow is the *udumbara"—and thus its status as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) consists in its function of effecting praise by declaring that this *udumbara*-ness is commendable.
This concludes the second section, the *vidhivannigada-adhikaraṇa*.
Therefore, it is established that the passage beginning with "The Udumbara is indeed strength" is merely an *arthavāda* for the purpose of the Udumbara wood.

The practical application (*prayojana*) is as follows: if there is a desire for a result other than the fruit of the sacrifice, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of Udumbara wood according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is to be made of Udumbara wood alone. // 2 //
Thus ends the second section concerning injunctions expressed by direct statement.
(Section 3: Or it is the reason (*hetu*).

In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, after enjoining a sacrifice performed with a winnowing basket (śūrpa) through the statement "He offers with a winnowing basket," the explanatory passage (arthavāda) heard as "For by that food is prepared" does not function as a mere figurative praise; rather, with the capacity to be the instrument of the sacrifice being the probandum, the fact of its being the means for preparing food is enjoined as the reason.
For in this case, there is nothing that needs to be inferred, as there was in the previous instance where [the status of] being the end to be accomplished had to be supplied.

Because the word *hi* itself expresses the state of being a reason (*hetutva*) by its very sound; and since a reason is untenable without pervasion (*vyāpti*), the statement of pervasion—namely, "whatever is used as food, by that [fire] one must offer"—is either the pervasion itself or the reason.
"At the Cāturmāsya" means within that [sacrificial session], specifically at the Varuṇapraghāsa.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa).
The sense is that [it is established] by the Taittirīya passage, "He offers the *karambha* vessels.
Even though the statement "He offers the *karambha* vessels" was not written in the Bhāṣya, there is confidence in its authority because it is recorded in the Kaustubha.
Thus, in this context, it follows as a matter of course that [the offering] has the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) as its instrument.
The meaning is that, by way of the result, it enjoins the state of being a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*).
This has been stated for the purpose of determining its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) on the grounds that its meaning was not already established [by another means].

By this, the objection—that because the passage "for by that [winnowing basket] food [is prepared]" lacks the status of an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), its status as an injunction is uncertain, and thus the logical reason (*hetu*) is devoid of a subject—has been refuted.
For this very reason— namely, that by the word "tena" (by that), only that which is intended as a means of praise is here taken as the example—

it should also be understood that this [example] serves to demonstrate the probandum (*sādhya*) in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it serves to demonstrate the praise (*stuti*).
It is prescribed.
(The determination of the postulation of pervasion based on the impossibility otherwise of the causality understood from the word *hi*:
The meaning is that what is unknown is made known here, unlike in cases such as "there are no after-offerings" (*nānūyājāḥ*).

Now, one might object: since in the world it is observed that the understanding of a reason occurs only through a prior comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), how can such an understanding occur here in the absence of that [pervasion]? To this, he says: "And the reason... (*hetuśca*).

Just as the inference of pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises from the authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) that "smoke is the producer of the cognition of fire," so too here, by the impossibility otherwise of the causality known from the Veda, the status of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) as an instrument of the oblation—which is a part of the heard word—is established through the principle that "a postulation [is justified] because it is a part of the same unit. Therefore, since the reason is its being a means of preparing food, one must offer with whatever is a means of preparing food, whether it be the winnowing basket or something else; thus, [the conclusion follows] from both the heard and the inferred.
The meaning is that an injunctive sentence is inferred as being composed of its parts, namely a single portion and a constituent element.
The statement of pervasion (vyāpti).
The meaning is: a statement preceded by pervasion (vyāpti).

[Objection: But surely, since the connection with the *śūrpa* (winnowing basket) and the *homa* (oblation) can be established by an injunction that does not depend on a reason (*hetu*), there is futility even in making known its status as a reason—just as there is when it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). To this, he says: "And therefore... (*tataśca*).
The word *piṭhara* means an earthen vessel.

Therefore, the meaning is that by the rule formulated—"whatever is an implement for preparing food, with that [implement] one should offer"—the purpose is that all such things obtain the status of being instruments for the oblation (*homa*).
(An examination of the relative nature of "most effective instrumentality" [sādhakatamatva], which is common to the ladle, the pot, and so forth):

Nor is it correct to argue that only cooking is the "most effective instrument" for the production of food, and thus the status of being the "instrument of food" belongs to cooking alone and not to the ladle and other such tools;
for in relation to the plow, the harrow, and so forth, it is logical for cooking to be considered the most effective instrument.
Otherwise, since that [quality] would also be absent in the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), it would be impossible for it to be mentioned as the basis for the praise of that [basket].

[Objection: If all [vessels] are means for the *homa*, then the injunction of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) alone here would be purposeless; and to avoid that, if one were to assume that it alone is the primary substratum, then—since the requirement is satisfied by the directly heard scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) itself—there would be no occasion to postulate its status as a means through inference. To this, he says: "The word 'winnowing basket'... [and so forth].

The word *śūrpa* (winnowing basket) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in order to conform to its being the means for the oblation (*homa*), which functions solely as the instrument for preparing food as understood from the *arthavāda*.
However, the word *juhoti* (he offers) is not redundant; rather, by demonstrating the indication of the goal to be accomplished, it serves to imply the injunction "it should be offered" (*hotavyam*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that it is indeed injunctive, having attained syntactic unity with the injunction: "Whatever is an instrument for preparing food, with each of those one should offer."
Or it is a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*).
The meaning is that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), like saying "he chooses one" after many have already been obtained, having distinguished one from the others;
for [otherwise] these two faults would arise. He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in another way, beginning with "Or rather" (*yadvā*).

(B3) (1) The suspicion of redundancy regarding this section (*adhikaraṇa*) based on the principle of the *parṇamayī-adhikaraṇa* has been refuted by the author of the *Vārttika* in many ways as follows: (1) the suspicion might arise that "this [section] is redundant because its meaning is already covered by that [previous section]," but not that "this [section] itself is redundant"; (2) here, there is the demonstration that [the previous statement] is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
In that [previous case], there was merely a refutation of the status of being an injunction for a result;

(3) here, however, the scope includes injunctions of substance, quality, action, and so forth without distinction, whereas in that [previous] case it concerned only those resembling injunctions for results;
(4) here, the status of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is established for all things resembling injunctions simply by refuting their status as injunctions.
In that regard, however, there is the further doubt (*adhikāśaṅkā*) that even for that which is merely an *arthavāda*, there may be a connection with a specific result;
