(5) therefore, the subject matter here is cases where, within a prescription of a result itself, words of praise and words denoting the result exist separately, whereas those cases where the result or the praise must be expressed by that alone fall under the scope of the fourth [book]. (6)

Alternatively, it may mean that those things whose purpose for another has been understood, and which are not of such a nature [as to be self-evident], possess the status of being objects (*viṣaya*) therein;

or else, it means that disregarding the investigation of the probans (*sādhana*), one accepts and investigates only the probandum (*sādhya*), or conversely, disregarding the investigation of the probandum, one accepts and investigates only the probans—thus [it is said]. As for the author of the *Kaustubha*, however:

They say that another section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced for the sake of clarifying the intellect of the students. However, the authors of the *Seśvaramīmāṃsā* explain that there is not even a suspicion of redundancy, because here the status of being a mere eulogy (*stāvaka*) is established by refuting the idea that passages such as "The Udumbara tree is strength" enjoin a perceptible object, whereas in that [other] case, only the capacity of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to bestow a fruit is denied while its status as an *arthavāda* remains. Thus, they describe it as follows.
Many scholars consider that since this matter has already been resolved by the *arthavāda* section (*adhikaraṇa*), the formal structure of this particular section is not appropriate;
nevertheless, it should be understood that this section is by no means redundant.
Thus he explains:

Furthermore, since other implements such as the ladle (*darvī*) and the cooking pot (*piṭhara*) are also perceived to be means for preparing the oblation (*hema*), the word "winnowing basket" (*śūrpa*) in the injunction must be taken either as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) or as a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*).
Alternatively, since the pronoun "that" (*tat*) refers specifically to the winnowing basket, the reason (*hetu*) is simply its capacity to produce food (*annakaraṇatva*).

Thus, because the logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) is conceived as being restricted [to the winnowing basket], even though the winnowing basket’s incapacity to produce food is excluded, the word "winnowing basket" situated in the injunction is not to be interpreted otherwise; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: because of the instruction ending in the present tense marker *laṭ* in the expression "it is made" (*kriyate*), the state of being a means of preparing food must be expressed as a reason for the present time.
Yet, the state of being a means of preparing food is not possible at the time of the oblation (*homakāla*).
Therefore, in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*), there is necessarily a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the *laṭ* of another time, namely the past or the future.
Although this [present tense] is also necessary for me, as it constitutes a quality that serves as a mark of excellence (*prāśastya-lakṣaṇa*);
nevertheless, because it occurs within a restatement (*anuvāda*) and because it nourishes that excellence, it is not a fault,
since that excellence would not be perceived without the mention of the present tense.
Furthermore, since it is possible for [the passage] to have as its purpose the praise that is required, it is not proper to accept that its purpose is to state a reason that is not so required.
Therefore, it is established that all explanatory passages (arthavādas) possess authority by virtue of being commendatory. // 3 //
Thus ends the third section, *Hetuvannigadādhikaraṇa*.

(B2) [The presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by refuting the opinion of the *Nyāyasudhā*, even while intending to show that the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) residing in the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) alone—which is capable of producing food—is what is intended to be expressed:

As for the point that, in this case, since the instrumentality expressed by the instrumental case-ending is the object to be qualified (*uddeśya*) when there is an injunction of the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) conveyed by the word *hi*—and since...

The *Nyāyasudhā* suggests that because it is impossible to qualify the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) by means of what is expressed by the agent (*pratipādaka*), the capacity for producing food (*annakaraṇatva*) residing therein cannot be the probans (*hetu*). However, this is incorrect; for since the word "winnowing basket" (*śūrpa*)—the referent of the respective term—is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*), its instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is understood through the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). Consequently, there is no possibility of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) resulting from a qualified connection (*viśiṣṭānvaya*), as the grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) allows for the connection [of the quality] with that which is already expressed as the instrument.
Since the pervasion is specifically conceived as "whatever is an instrument for preparing food, by that [instrument] one must offer," this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is indeed appropriate.
(An examination of the natural appropriateness [svārasya] in the realization of praise regarding the word "tenahi":
it is because that [praise] is not realized.)

Under the view that this is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), even though the act of preparing food is not currently occurring, it is expressed as if it were present through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of generating delight. For there is no such pleasure in what has already occurred or what is yet to come as there is in what is present; nor is the potency in the present such as that which resides in the result. Therefore, in our position, the mention [of the action] is justified, as it is performed in order to praise that which possesses present potency, whether it be something already done or something yet to be done.

In the view that [the Veda] is a source of knowledge (*hetuvidhipakṣa*), since there is an absence of mere restatement of an object already established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), the meaning is that imagining this [Vedic injunction] to be otherwise than as it is heard would indeed be a fault.
(Indeed, in this case [of the phrase] "nahyatrānūyājāḥ," the word *hi* has the sense of a reason.

For this very reason, where there is no occurrence of such defects as the aforementioned [loss of] definition (*lakṣaṇa*), in that instance—namely, in the phrase "nahyatrānūyājānī"—the sense of a reason is indeed present.
For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there are two *caturgṛhīta* portions for both the *prayāja* and the *anuyāja*.

Regarding the *upabhṛt* [ladle], although the scriptural injunction "he takes eight [spoonfuls] in the *upabhṛt*" establishes the number eight, one should not perform two sets of eight spoonfuls—or even a single set of eight—for the purpose of providing the means for both the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. Rather, one should take two sets of four spoonfuls, such that one set of four is for the *prayāja* and the other set of four is for the *anuyāja*. This is because the term "eight" refers to two groups of four.
Why? Because in the *ātithyā* sacrifice, there are clarified butter portions taken four times (*caturgṛhīta*).
For here, it is not prescribed that there are after-offerings (*anūyāja*s).
And since the plural form "four-times-taken portions" (*caturgṛhītāni*) is heard here, the absence of after-offerings is stated as the reason for enjoining three four-times-taken portions.
Therefore, the injunction of the number three— which has as its result the accomplishment of four *caturgṛhīta* portions by means of the absence of the commonality of *anuyāja* offerings—

is only logical if there were an injunction of two sets of four in the archetype (*prakṛti*) regarding the word "eight"; otherwise, since even the two *caturgṛhīta* portions would not be obtained [in the archetype], that injunction would be untenable.

Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing this purpose, there is no possibility whatsoever of [the application of] indication (lakṣaṇā) or the like here, even when the status of being a reason (hetutva) is being conveyed.
"Not without dependence."

(Conclusion of the established doctrine by refuting the prima facie view through the understanding of independent causality derived from the third [type of statement], which contradicts [the previous position]):

If it were a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), there would be a connection with the injunction because it is required by it; however, in the case of a statement expressing a reason (*hetuvidhi*), since the injunction’s capacity to enjoin is established by its own inherent independence, there is no requirement for such a connection.

On the contrary, since there would be the contingency of option (*vikalpa*) regarding the ladle (*darvī*) and other implements as means, and because in the case of their combination (*samuccaya*), there would be the contingency of subverting the independent causality understood from the instrumental suffix (*tṛtīyā*), the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of that [instrumental case] would be destroyed; this is the intended meaning.
How the instrumental suffixes and others denote independent causality and so forth should be seen in the *Kaustubha* and other works.
The purpose (*prayojana*) is not stated here because it is obvious.
Thus ends the third section, concerning the explanatory statement containing a reason (*hetumannigadādhikaraṇa*).

(B3) (1) Even if the word *tat* refers to the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), there is no fault because it is impossible for the qualified status of being its instrument to be the object of reference; rather, according to the principle of the section on gender and number (*liṅga-saṃkhyā-adhikaraṇa*), the mere connection with the oblation (*homa*) is what constitutes the object of reference. (2) Since the rule "a grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they are semantically capable" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*) must necessarily apply even to the prescription of case-endings such as the accusative, the case-ending would be untenable for the other items as well, due to their lack of semantic capacity characterized by mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), just as it is for the winnowing basket.
(B1) (Section 4:
Because there is an explanatory teaching for that purpose.
In the inquiry as to whether mantras possess authority regarding dharma and adharma or not, they do not first have authority by way of being injunctions (*vidhi*),
because that will be refuted in the second [chapter].
Nor do they have authority by way of being commendatory (*stāvaka*), like an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

For in the case of those [injunctions], because they form a single syntactical unit with the word [of the injunction] through proximity, it is logical that they generate a verbal cognition whose object is the *bhāvanā* (productive urge) as connected with the excellence (*prāśastya*) presented by themselves.

However, in the case of mantras, since they are situated at a distance, the formation of a single syntactical unit with a word is untenable; thus, their status as a means of valid knowledge cannot arise through that [proximate] rule.
Nor can excellence be the meaning of the sentence independently.
Because it is presented as a category of object (*padārtha*),
nor does it possess validity as a reminder of an object, since that is impossible due to the absence of the capacity to make known an object not previously apprehended.
Furthermore, because the Sāman mantras lack referential meaning, even their literal correspondence [to reality] is untenable.
Nor can it be accepted that they have a purpose merely as reminders despite lacking authority;
for since remembrance could be achieved through other means such as meditation, the mandatory recitation of the mantras would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, because memory would be redundant in the case of those [mantras] which remind one of matters already connected with the ritual performance (*prayoga*), the mere recitation of those mantras—whose status as subsidiaries to specific sacrifices has been removed by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) known as "qualification" (*adhikāra*) and so forth—is enjoined for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). And since the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) prescribes study only for the purpose of attaining proficiency in the performance that utilizes such recitation, there is no fault whatsoever. This being the position reached—(B2)
(Regarding "of the mantras," this is the introduction to the root [topic]:

Having established the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the *codanās*—which constitute parts of the Vedas—with respect to *dharma* by means of the first quarter [of the first chapter], [the author now addresses] the *arthavādas* and *mantras* which present themselves as constituent parts of those [*codanās*]; since the *arthavādas* are more intimately related (*antaraṅga*) than the *mantras*, they are treated here in the first topic (*adhikaraṇa*) of this quarter. In that regard:

Having stated the authority [of the Veda] through both objection and resolution, he says "of the mantras" with the intention that the authority of the mantras present therein is now being considered in the same manner.

(An examination of the justification for the operation of the section on explanatory passages [arthavāda] prior to the section on names [nāmadheya]): Even though a name is more closely related to an injunction than an explanatory passage, how much more so must it be said of mantras? Therefore, it is appropriate to conduct the investigation into their authority before that [section on names].

Nevertheless, since the status of terms such as *śyena* and *agnihotra* as names depends upon the similes found in the *arthavādas* and upon the principle of *tatprakhyanyāya* (the naming after a mantra), it is understood that they depend for their authority on those [other sources]; therefore, the proof of this [present] authority prior to them is indeed appropriate—this is the sense.
Thus, the authority of those parts that constitute limbs of the Veda has been established by way of two methods.

And because that [perception] is impossible here, and because no other mode of apprehension observed elsewhere is possible, he establishes the impossibility of the two aforementioned modes in order to argue for invalidity in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—starting with the words "Not first... and so forth.
The second [verse] says: "Thus."

The meaning is that, because in those [passages] containing the word *yat*, the vocative case, and the first person (uttama-puruṣa), the injunctive power is obstructed by the word *yat* and others, they lack injunctive force; thus, this will be refuted in the second section on the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha-pāda*), in the section titled "The mantra and the injunction have the same purpose because they consist of the same words" (*vidhimantrayoraikārthyam ekaśabdyāt*).
Its status as a means of valid cognition by way of praise is twofold:
either through syntactic unity with a single word or through syntactic unity with an entire sentence.
Therein, he refutes the first [position] with the words: "Of those..."

And by this—namely, by formulating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) on the grounds that no reason exists to establish the authority of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—the connection (*saṃgati*) consisting of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) has been indicated.
Since it is a different context, there is no fault even in the absence of an immediate connection.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "Nor also... (nāpi).
(An examination of the absence of syntactic unity through presentation by way of word-meanings):
"By way of word-meanings" means as follows.
For the meaning of a sentence consists in a single qualificandum (viśeṣya) which is endowed with multiple meanings (padārtha).
When sentences, each complete in its own sense, are connected with another sentence within that [larger] sense, there occurs "sentence-sentential unity" (vākyaikavākyatā),
as in the case of sentences concerning subsidiary and principal rites.

In the present case, however, although excellence (*prāśastya*) is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is not possible [to derive the injunction] because that excellence is not understood as being connected with other factors (*itarānvitatva*), and because the sentence has not reached completion (*samāpti*) regarding that meaning.
Having restated the argument of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he refutes it with "Nor also... (*nāpi*).
Because the traditional transmission of the mantras would otherwise be rendered purposeless.
The meaning is that the recollection of the words of the expressive mantra depends upon the recollection of their meaning;
and [the word] "not inherent in the performance" (prayogāsamavetā) [is used].

The point is that although mantras such as those for encouragement (*protsāhana*) and authorization (*anumantraṇa*) express meanings connected with the ritual action, since they serve a purpose related to what is to be performed during the actual performance, there is no utility for their recollection [at the time of learning]; thus, it is not logical that they should be the motivators [of the study].
(An exposition on the utility of mantras in the sacrifice by way of their recitation:

Therefore, since their utility as mere reminders is impossible, and because there is a need for the utility of these [mantras] which have been refined through study, those mantras— whether read within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*) or studied outside of any context (*anārabhyādhīta*)— are understood, as far as possible, to be subsidiary elements of the primary sacrifice (*pradhānāṅga*) through the means of direct statement (*śruti*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), contextual requirement (*adhikāra*), context (*prakaraṇa*), order of sequence (*krama*), and name (*samākhyā*).
By the primary injunction, only the very form of the mantra is accepted,
and not its meaning as well— as is the case with Brāhmaṇa passages—
because [the latter] is of no utility.

Although it is not possible for a mantra to assist the primary ritual act by its own inherent form, nevertheless, in order to fulfill its status as an auxiliary whose nature is known through authoritative means, it is accepted as such by way of the act of recitation and as an instrumental factor (*kāraka*).
For it is not possible for the communication of meaning— which cannot be accomplished by human effort— to function as a ritual operation (*vyāpāra*).
Therefore, the mere utterance itself is the function.

And since no visible purpose for it can be established, its purpose must ultimately be invisible (adṛṣṭa), just as in the final conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the restrictive rule of mantras. With this in mind, he states the result of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa): "Therefore... [ata iti].
He avoids the contradiction of the perceived utility (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) understood from the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*) by stating: "svādhyāya... [etc.].

(The commencement of the final conclusion [siddhānta]: since mere utterance—which is not required by the ritual and does not reside in the mantra—cannot constitute an operation (*vyāpāra*), it is established that the communication of meaning alone constitutes such an operation.

Although utterance may indeed be an operation because it is produced by the mantras through the relation of being its object (*viṣayatā-sambandha*), nevertheless, since that utterance is not required by the ritual, rather than postulating an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), it is more reasonable—given that the denotation of word-meanings is already a visible fact—to accept the denotation of the sentence-meaning, since the former lacks the capacity to serve as a means for the performance of the rite.
It is appropriate to conceive [the act] as an activity (*vyāpāra*);
for, since utterance is an activity of the person, it does not reside in the mantra. With this intention, he states the final position (*siddhānta*) with the words: "In the visible... (*dṛṣṭe*).

Regarding the mantras that convey the meaning of what is to be performed, since they produce the memory that serves as the cause for performance, they assist the primary ritual action by means of expressing that meaning; thus he says: "those which are connected with the performance" and "as far as possible."

(B3) (1) Because it is not connected [with other words], it is the object of a cognition dependent on the word’s own power (*svarūpa*) alone. (B1) It is denoted; for when a visible purpose is possible, it is illogical to postulate an invisible one. Therefore, the purpose of mantras that are possible [to function] is simply the recollection of the objects inherent in their ritual application.
Granted that, in the absence of any other possibility, an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭa) may be assumed;
nevertheless, even in that case, it can be asserted that mantras exist for the purpose of revealing meaning, and that this revelation itself serves an unseen purpose.
In the case of the *sāman*, the manifestation of syllables is indeed its perceived purpose, and this remains unimpeded even in the absence of a visible external object;
however, for the *ṛc* and *sāman* that do not consist of [perceptible] words, their purpose is exclusively transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*), as is explained at length elsewhere.
Nevertheless, it does not follow from this that everything everywhere has only a transcendental purpose.
Nor is the recitation of mantras rendered useless by such a restriction;
for one may postulate a restrictive rule that "one must remember [the object] by means of the mantras alone through their power.
And there is no fault even if that [recollection] has an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) as its fruit.

And it should not be argued that—since the application (*viniyoga*) of mantras in various contexts is established by this very capacity (*sāmarthya*), their further application in some instances would be redundant; (B2) [this is not so] because [the purpose is] to demonstrate the integration of the performance (*prayogasamavāya*) of those mantras applied by means of the particle *iti*—that is, the mantras used as instruments (*karaṇamantra*)—as a visible method (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*) for the sake of the fruit of the subsequent consecration (*anumantraṇa*). This is the meaning.
Even in cases where the meaning to be performed is not understood from the mantra by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*),

and the mantra is applied through the particle *iti* and so forth— as in "With 'iṣe tvā', he cuts the branch"— there too, since it is impossible for it to be a cause through any other means in a visible manner (*dṛṣṭavidhayā*) without the expression of meaning, the function of expressing the meaning itself must occur even through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the like.

In the case of *anuvāda* mantras such as "yuvā suvāsāḥ" and others recited while an action is being performed, the expression of meaning is not required by the injunction regarding the ritual act (*karma-vidhi*);
for since the act has already been commenced, its [meaning] is already remembered, making such expression redundant.

Nevertheless, because acts such as the encircling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-parivyāṇa*) extend over many moments, there may at times be an interruption of mental awareness even in the midst of the performance; therefore, since the requirement for those mantras is justified for the sake of strengthening memory, they serve a purpose through a visible means (*dṛṣṭa-vidhayā*).
It is not difficult to find [a solution].

Even in cases where there is a combination of mantras, such as in the case of the *abhryādāna* (taking up the spade) and so forth, the redundancy of the others is avoided by the fact that the result is accomplished through the recollection of just one, as will be explained in the twelfth [chapter] regarding the method for *japa* mantras and the like.

As for those *protsāhana-mantras* (encouraging mantras) such as "aganma suvaḥ" (*we have gone to heaven*), which express matters not inherent in the ritual action to be performed, their purpose is to generate faith; since even though the matter is not to be performed, the recollection of the fruit inherent in the ritual action produces an excellence of faith, it should be understood that they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) by having that [faith] as their aim.

For it is entirely appropriate that the *anumantraṇa-mantras* depend upon such recollection in order to strengthen the memory and dispel any doubt regarding the performance of the act. Thus, their purpose is indeed established.

As for the statement in the *Tantraratna* on the fifth [section] that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the mantras used for consecration (*anumantraṇa*) because they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), that is incorrect; this will be explained in that very same place. Furthermore, it should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.
(Admission that those whose visible purpose is impossible must have an invisible purpose):

Regarding the recitation mantras such as *dhuṅśca* and *pūṅśca*, since a visible purpose is impossible, he states that they have an invisible purpose with the words, "of those [whose purpose] is impossible."

Since it is observed in such scriptural indications as, "A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, or wrongly employed, does not convey that meaning," it is understood that even mantras used for recitation (*japa*) and the like— which involve specific accents— denote meaning just like *karaṇa*-mantras; furthermore, because their capacity to convey meaning is established through etymology (*nirukta*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and so forth, and since mere illumination is not useful for the performance of ritual acts, it is impossible for them to have a purpose consisting solely of visible or traditional (Smṛti) effects.
He states another position—that even the purpose may be unperceived—with the words: "But it can be... (śakyate tu).

This being the case, the point is that when it was stated in the twelfth [chapter] that mantras such as those for recitation have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), this was intended with reference to the fact that the expression of the object to be accomplished by the mantra has an unseen purpose.

(An examination of the visible purpose of the Sāmans: Since Sāman mantras consist of singing, they lack a [literal] meaning; thus, even though their utility cannot be established through the expression of that meaning, the fact that they serve to manifest the syllables of the Ṛk verses—which will be demonstrated in the ninth book—is precisely their visible purpose. Thus he says: "But as for the Sāmans..."
(An investigation into the invisible purpose of the *anu-sāmans*):
As for those [syllables] which are superimposed upon the *stobha* syllables, because they lack the purpose of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛc*, their purpose is exclusively invisible (*adṛṣṭa*).
For this very reason, it should also be understood that the *rathantara* and other *sāmans* function as the substrates for ritual actions.

However, regarding those [mantras] that are not Ṛk or Sāman, such as the *Prajāpatihṛdaya* and others, because they are based upon the *stobha* syllables and because it will be stated in the ninth [book] that *stobhas* are devoid of meaning, they cannot function as hymns (*stotra*) consisting of the expression of meaning;

therefore, as there is no other alternative, he says "but as for the non-Ṛk and non-Sāman [mantras]," [meaning] their purpose is solely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) by way of mere recitation, in accordance with the application of the Sāmans.

(Refutation of the utility of non-Ṛgvedic and non-Sāmavedic texts for the sake of conveying the performance [of rituals]): As for what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṭṭālaṅkāra*— namely, that even non-Ṛgvedic and non-Sāmavedic texts serve the purpose of conveying meaning because they also accomplish the communication of the performance through the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), characterized by their own specific features, which is required by the *apūrva* of that ritual in which those texts are employed— [we respond as follows].
The venerable teacher has disregarded that very point, because by adopting that same form [of reasoning], it would follow that the same purpose applies elsewhere as well.

(Regarding the view that mantras serve as reminders of what is involved in the ritual performance, the demonstration that [the mantra] "imām agṛbhṇan" and "uru prathasva" would otherwise be useless: There is no fault.

Nor should it be argued that the postulation of a necessary unseen result (adṛṣṭa) is justified by the mere fact of utterance due to its primacy or necessity; for the point is that when a requirement is already satisfied by what is perceived (dṛṣṭa), there is an absence of the expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) that serves as the cause for postulating an unseen result, and thus primacy and such factors alone are not determinative.
In some cases, this constitutes the means of application (viniyoga).

The meaning is that there would be the futility of injunctions of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), such as: "He takes it with four [mantras]," "He takes the horse's halter," and "With 'O wide-expanding one,' he spreads out the sacrificial cake. Regarding the first [example], the taking of the spade—which is already established as necessary for the purpose of obtaining the bricks used in the fire-altar construction—is [governed] by the very Vedic text (śruti) inferred from the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in the manifestation of the meaning of the four mantras recited, beginning with "Of the god Savitṛ... (*devasya tvā savituḥ...*), in relation to the taking of the spade, which serves as the means of digging.

If the application of the mantra were already established [by other means], the injunction for it would be redundant. In the second case, since the taking up of the reins for the purpose of bringing that clay upon the horse and the donkey— and for the purpose of binding them— is already established by the context (*artha*), the mantra "imām agr̥bhṇan" (RV 10.85.46), through a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) inferred from its indicative power (*liṅga*), would apply to the taking up of the donkey's rein just as it does to the taking up of the horse's rein.
Even so, the injunction [of the mantra] would be purposeless because its application is already established by the very nature of the case.

In the third alternative, since the spreading [of the dough] on eight potsherds for the sake of preparing the *puroḍāśa* is already established, and since the application of the mantra to that spreading is already established by a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) inferred from its indicative power (*liṅga*), the injunction of it would be purposeless. However, if the mantras were intended for an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then since their recitation could occur anywhere, the injunction would have a purpose: it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for recitation by ensuring the application of those mantras which would otherwise not be applied due to a lack of indicative power. This is the meaning of the passage expressing this doubt.
(B1) It should not be said that the injunction is purposeless;

for it possesses utility as a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the qualities. To explain: although the taking up of the spade (*abhri*) is already established by the purpose, and four mantras would otherwise be applicable to it by virtue of their indicative power (*liṅga*), [the injunction serves to restrict them].

When, by the statement "he takes it with four," an efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) of taking— qualified by both the number and the mantra— is enjoined even prior to the means-of-proof (*pramāṇa*) that would otherwise establish it, and when there arises a desire to know the result of the operation of this statement, it is determined that the result is the acquisition of the quality consisting of the number four, which has conjunction as its fruit. Similarly, regarding the taking of the horse's halter as a subsidiary of the fire-piling (*agnicayana*), although a mantra would be obtained from the indicative power (*liṅga*) itself, [the rule applies] because of what precedes it.

By the injunction, "With the mantra *imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya*, he takes up the horse's halter," the taking [of the halter] qualified by the mantra is prescribed as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the horse's halter.
As in the previous cases, when there is a desire to know the result, the result is an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of the donkey's halter, which serves as the counter-positive (*śeṣin*).

Nor does this entail the threefold defect of an exclusion—namely, the abandonment of one's own meaning, the assumption of a foreign meaning, and the sublation of what was already established—since the exclusion is here a matter of the result.
Because it is the very nature of its own meaning—the connection with the horse’s bridle—that is to be enjoined;

because the exclusion of others, which constitutes a secondary meaning, need not be postulated as it is established by implication; and because there is no sublation of what has been obtained, since the means of knowledge that would establish such a sublation has not yet operated.

Therefore, that [exclusionary injunction] applies only in cases where the operation of the exclusionary scripture (*parisaṅkhyā-śāstra*) occurs precisely after the operation of the means of knowledge that establishes [the possibility of the action],

such as in "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten" and the like; for there, since the eating of five-nailed animals is already established through passion (*rāga*), the scripture effects an exclusion of those other than the five.

Furthermore, regarding the explicit scriptural statement (*śrautī*), which involves the necessary determination that the injunction concerns the act of taking qualified by the fourfold number and qualified by the mantras—

here, there are three sūtras intended to resolve these doubts: "Or rather, the repetition is for the sake of a subordinate quality (*guṇārthā*)," "It is an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*)," and "Or it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)."
Having investigated that matter, he refutes it with the words "guṇa" etc.

And here, since the injunction of the number four—by means of delimiting the mantra obtained through its indicative power (*liṅga*) with reference to the taking up of the stone already established by the sense—is not an injunction of both the mental act of taking up (*ādāna-bhāvanā*) and the mantras, it is impossible for them to be governed by a single action, as in the case of the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow). Consequently, if the mantras were also enjoined, there would result a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) caused by enjoining two things; therefore, prior to that [injunction], there is the scriptural text (*śruti*) inferred from the indicative power (*liṅga*).

Even though there is an injunction of a mantra qualified by the number four as expressed by the four words, since a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) cannot be avoided in any way when there is a qualified objective (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*), it is logical that the taking up (*ādāna*) is also enjoined by implication (*ākṣepataḥ*) through its prior occurrence, just like the injunction of the mantra; for it is proper to enjoin the meaning of the verbal root even by resorting to the complexity of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi-gaurava*). Thus, as in the opinion of the author of the *Vārttika* regarding the passage "the horse's halter" (*aśvābhidhānīm*), here too there is indeed an injunction of a qualified productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Intending that, because it is logical, the prescription of a qualified *bhāvanā* is appropriate here as well—just as in the case of the Vārttikakāra’s view regarding the passage "the horse's halter"—he says: "For thus... (*tathā hi*).
"It is ascertained."
Although this [result] is the fruit of merely enjoining both types of mantras numbered four, and not of the injunction regarding their taking up,
nevertheless, the meaning is as follows: for here the word "four" (catuḥ) refers solely to the quality (guṇa), just like the word "aruṇā" and so forth.

The qualificand (*viśeṣya*), although not obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*), is supplied by the very word *mantraiḥ* (by means of mantras) which is supplied as an ellipsis for the sake of its connection with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).

Since a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*paricchedya-paricchedaka-bhāva*) between those two [the mantra and the deity] is untenable due to their lack of mutual syntactic connection, it is necessary to enjoin a qualified efficient force (*viśiṣṭa-bhāvanā-vidhāna*) by connecting both of them with the efficient force.
And the understanding of the relationship of qualifier and qualified between those two occurs only subsequently (*pārṣṭhika*).

Therefore, it is not unreasonable that the result of the injunction regarding the taking [of the vows] is the attainment of the quality consisting of the number four, which serves to delimit the mantras that yield the combined fruit.

And thus, the meaning of the statement in the Sūtra, "for the sake of the qualities," is that the status of being "for the sake of the qualities" should be explained as resulting from the injunction of a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) qualified by those qualities. This is the intended sense.

(The resolution of the lack of contradiction between the *Bhāṣya*, which states that the injunction of the mantra is for the purpose of being an auxiliary to the taking up of the horse's reins, and the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, which states that the taking up qualified by the mantra is enjoined as an auxiliary to the horse's bridle:
"In the case of the taking up qualified by the mantra.")

Bhāṣya 5: Although the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that the injunction of the mantra is solely for the purpose of taking up the horse’s reins (*aśvābhidhānī*), nevertheless, as before, it should be understood that the "qualified taking" (*viśiṣṭādāna*) is mentioned according to the intention of the author of the Vārttika.

By the phrase "as a subordinate element of the horse’s reins," it is indicated that in the Vārttikakāra’s view—where the position is that there is an injunction for the qualified taking—the word *aśvābhidhānī* [also functions as a qualifier].

By demonstrating that [the word "soma"] is included within a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it is shown that it does not have a non-subordinate element as its referent; thus, there is no necessity for a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being for the sake of the *apūrva*" in that word.

This refutes the claim established in the second verse of the *Udāharaṇākṣepa* section of the *Vidhirasāyana*—that the subordinate element is not included within the injunction—and indicates that such a position cannot withstand logical scrutiny, while also showing that the syntactical directness of the accusative case (*dvitīyāśruti*) sublates the indicative power (*liṅga*).

Although some hold the view that there is a conflict between *liṅga* (indicative power) and *vākya* (syntactic connection) in the context of the cause (*kāraṇa*), because it takes the form of a sentence;

nevertheless, since this [text] is a Brāhmaṇa passage, it possesses greater authority than *liṅga*, just as the text "even if dedicated to another deity" does, and thus its sublation of *liṅga* is logically established.
By this, the objection stated in the *Nyāyaprakāśa*—that under the theory of application based on *vākya*, the *vākya* itself would necessarily be sublated by *liṅga*—is refuted.
In that very context, [it is said]:

"O Rāghava, by means of the *brahmakṣatra* [mantra] here... [This is the justification for the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) regarding the meaning of the statement: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten."]
"The porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the hare, and the tortoise as the fifth"— this latter three-line verse from the *Rāmāyaṇa* is to be understood as the speech of Vālin.
And in this context, eating is not something to be enjoined,
because it is already established by natural inclination (*rāga*).

Nor can it be enjoined by way of a preliminary activity for the attainment of passion, because that would entail the assumption of a separate result and would contradict the context concerning forbidden foods.
Nor can it be enjoined as a collective performance together with the eating of the five five-toed animals.
Because attainment is not occasional,

and because even if attainment were occasionally possible, it would result in a contradiction with the context concerning what is unfit to be eaten; therefore, this is indeed a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*).

Likewise, the meaning is that by indirect indication (lakṣaṇā), there is an injunction for the very cessation of eating five-nailed animals other than the five [permitted ones]; thus, there are three faults, beginning with the abandonment of one's own [literal] meaning (svārtha-hāni).
Here, the distinction is that two of these faults reside in the word (śabda-niṣṭha), while the last resides in the meaning (artha-niṣṭha).
(An investigation into the nature of verbal *parisaṅkhyā* specifically in instances involving a sentence containing a negative particle [nañ]:
Since the previously mentioned *parisaṅkhyā* is based on indication (*lakṣaṇika*), he states its verbal nature (*śrautītva*) with the words: "Even where it is verbal (*śrautī*)."

In that case, since the communication of cessation is possible through the very power (śakti) of the negative particle (nañ) itself, there is no occurrence of the two faults—namely, the abandonment of its own meaning (svārthahāni) and the assumption of another's meaning (parārthakalpanā);
however, the state of being a sublation of what was previously established (prāptabādhatva) certainly exists, as he says: "Not that... (na tat).

It is not inconsistent [to say] that because the two [defects] are absent even when there is one [validity], the three defects do not arise; however, as for the example of verbal *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) shown by Pārthasārathi and others— namely, "only here do they pour"— that is untenable, because if the particle *eva* serves to exclude connection with anything else (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), then the contingency of optionality (*vikalpa*) would follow, just as in the case of the statement "he does not perform those two on the animal-sacrifice."
However, it will be explained in the tenth [book] that here, from the perspective of the result, there is indeed only a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*).
(1.1.29) Restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*) is, for example, as in "one should not speak untruth," and so forth;
yet even there, it is not that [restriction].
Therefore, a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*) is that scriptural rule whose object, whether by its verbal form or by its result, is the exclusion of something else.

In this context, it should be understood that in the absence of such an injunction, there is generally an application (prāpti) based on the general rule (autsargikī) both here and elsewhere; however, even that [general application] does not constitute a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇaghaṭikā).

For this very reason, although there is an optional application (pākṣikaprāpti) of untruth alongside truth regarding a single action, the statement "one should not speak untruth" is merely an exclusive specification (parisaṅkhyā), and not an injunction of occasion (nimittavidhi).
(B2) [Demonstration that the Vārttika concerning the determination of exclusivity (*parisaṅkhyātva*) in instances containing the particle *eva* aims at scriptural restriction (*śrautaniyama*):

As for the fact that in this Sūtra the Vārttika states— beginning with "For everywhere, either by the word 'exclusivity' (*parisaṅkhyā*) or by the particle 'only' (*eva*), exclusivity or restriction is expressed through direct statement" (*śrutyā*)— that there is scriptural exclusivity (*śrautaparisaṅkhyātva*) in instances where the particle *eva* occurs, that must be understood as referring to cases where the particle *eva* is co-occurrent with an object already established through desire (*rāga*).

As for what was stated in the *Nyāyasudhā*—on the basis of the very force of the *Vārttika*—that in instances where the particle *eva* occurs, there is a scriptural restriction (*śrauto niyama*), that is indeed true; however, this is with the intention that it serves to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) because there is a possibility of optional application (*pākṣikaprāpti*) in such cases.
But where the application is invariably established by scripture, [the particle *eva* serves to exclude connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).]
In that regard, however, it is clearly stated in the Kaustubha that this is indeed a restrictive injunction (parisaṅkhyā) by way of its result.
(An examination of the grounds for defining *parisaṅkhyā* when first explaining its definition):

Although the definitions of that [type of injunction] were stated in the Vārttika according to the sequence of the "newly introduced injunction" (*apūrvavidhi*) by means of the statement, "An injunction [applies] where there is absolute non-attainment," and so forth;

nevertheless, because both types of *parisaṅkhyā* are presented first through their investigation, or else because of the nature of an injunction whose fruit is distinct from restrictive injunction (*niyama*) and exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*), [it is called] *apūrva*.

Since the definition of *vidhi* (injunction) will be stated by [the author] himself, or because it is appropriate that it be done first for the sake of establishing the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
he sets aside the aforementioned order and states the definition of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) at the outset, beginning with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

(An explanation of how the phrases "there and elsewhere" and "that and the other where" serve as indicators for the two types of exclusion: that which does not include [the excluded] and that which is non-inclusive).

Here, although the Vārttika—"When there is the possibility of application both 'there' and 'elsewhere,' it is called a restrictive injunction (parisaṅkhyā)"—is applied to the illustrative examples with the intention of referring to the restriction of the primary element (śeṣin), it is nevertheless an indicator of the meaning "where that and the other are applicable," in order to include the restriction of other secondary elements (śeṣa).

Therefore, in the case of the restrictive injunction (parisaṅkhyā) "he offers the two portions of clarified butter," there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the attainment of the two remaining [acts]. Nevertheless, this is not intended as a definition of a restrictive injunction, because it lacks pervasion in the case of the Vedic restrictive injunction: "One should not speak untruth."
However, he states "here" [in the verse] to indicate that, as a general rule, the purpose is merely to describe the essential nature [of the object].

(An examination of the nature of restrictive injunctions (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*) in sentences containing the negative particle (*nañ*), even when [the action] is already established; and an examination of the status of examples such as "the initiated one does not give," etc., as objects of definition.

Regarding the phrase "even when established": [This means: Even though [the act of giving] is already established by other means, [injunctions] such as "the initiated one does not give" are determined to be restrictive injunctions (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*) because they are composed with the negative particle (*nañ*). Thus, these too are defined as the intended objects of this category.

Moreover, although a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) may be established when there is a possibility of simultaneous application through conjunction (*samuccaya*), here the status of the rule as a restrictive injunction is not otherwise possible because the prohibition operates even when [the alternative] is only optionally applicable (*pākṣika*).

By this very logic, it is also indicated that in the case of "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten," the status of the rule as a restrictive injunction remains faultless even though there is only occasional optional applicability.

By this illustration, it should be understood that the attempt by the authors of the *Vidhirasāyana* to establish that prohibitions such as "the initiated one does not offer oblations" (*dīkṣito na juhoti*) and "he does not perform those two [rites] at the animal sacrifice" (*na tau paśau karoti*)—

on the grounds that they result in cessation (*nivṛtti*) and thus lack the application of a contingent restrictive injunction (*pākṣika-niyama*)— is refuted. For, while these are shown to be exclusions (*parisaṅkhyā*), their status as original or restrictive injunctions (*apūrva-niyama-vidhi*) has been rejected due to the resulting over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of exclusion.

Nor is there an absence of conventional usage as a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification); for it has been demonstrated in the *Nyāyasudhā* itself that there is no deficiency even if there is no usage as such, provided that usage is established as being either an *aparyudāsa-pratiṣedha* (non-exclusionary negation) or a *paryudāsa* (exclusion).

(An exposition on how there is no fault even if the injunction for threshing is effectively a *parisaṅkhyā* [exclusive specification], by defining the counter-positive of the negation of non-existence):
And here, the counter-positive of the negation is intended not only as something of a positive nature (*bhāva-rūpa*), but also as something of a negative nature (*abhāva-rūpa*).

Therefore, it is consistent with the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) in the tenth [book] that the two prohibitions— "the Prāyaṇīyā concludes with the Patnīsaṃyājas" and "he does not perform the Anuyājas"— are redundant once the exclusion of all subsequent subsidiaries is established by the injunction for the performance of the Patnīsaṃyājas in the context of the Prāyaṇīyā and Ātithyā; thus, they serve the purpose of a restrictive exclusion (parisaṅkhyā) regarding the absence of other subsidiaries.

And thus, it should be noted that in the case of the illustration of a restrictive injunction (*niyama*)— which has as its fruit the cessation of the absence of threshing— even if the definition of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) is present because it has as its fruit the cessation of the counter-positive of the absence of threshing, there is no harm due to the lack of any sublation by overlap (*sāṅkarya*). For this very reason, where the purport of the scripture lies in the cessation of an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a particular property (*dharma*), that is a restrictive injunction (*niyama*).

But where it [the exclusion] exists as the cessation of that which is its counter-correlative, there it is a *parisaṅkhyā*; it is by this much alone that the distinction between the two is established.
(Regarding the view that a prohibitive injunction (*nivṛttividhi*) is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*), this is the rebuttal of the objections stated in the *Vidhirasāyana*:
Here, the meaning of the phrase "both verbally and as a result" is as follows:
where the cessation [of an action] is understood even without the recognition of its purposelessness (*vaiyarthyapratisandhāna*).

That [injunction] is so by virtue of its verbal form (*śabda*) where, through the connection of that [word], it becomes the object of the intended meaning (*tātparya*); it is so by virtue of its result (*phala*) where the result resides. And thus, the objection raised in the *Vidhirasāyana*—that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition "an injunction whose result is cessation is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*)" to the injunction regarding the *agnihotra*, because it has as its result the cessation of non-performance—is refuted.
This is because the non-performance [of an act] is not the intended meaning (tātparya-viṣaya) either through the word itself or by its result,
and because there is no pointlessness since it serves as an injunction for the performance of the Agnihotra.
Therefore, it should be understood that these two words are included within the definition precisely because of the intention to convey such a meaning.

Thus, when there is a possibility that something might occur in the absence of an injunction, the exclusion of that thing—whether by means of a word or as a result—is the intended scope of the verbal purport; therefore, because of this inclusion, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi), even though the exclusion of actions such as splitting [grains with the nails] is its result.

(An exposition on how the absence of this injunction, as a constituent of the definition of *parisaṅkhyā*, must be intended as having that alone as its counter-positive, or as having as its counter-positive this injunction accompanied by the non-application of other injunctions.

In this context, the "absence of this injunction" should be understood—just like the optional non-application (*pākṣikāyoga*) that constitutes a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) to be described later—as having either this alone as its counter-positive, or as having as its counter-positive this injunction accompanied by the non-application of other injunctions.

Otherwise, in the case of the injunction "he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings" occurring in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, which is the intended object of the definition of *parisaṅkhyā*, there would be an absence of the injunction for the *ājyabhāgas* alone.

By the re-enactment of archetypal (prakṛta) subsidiary elements such as "He cuts off [the portion] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" and "Invoke the Iḍā," there is obtained an exclusion (parisaṅkhyā) of other subsidiaries; since there would be no acquisition of those other subsidiaries due to their commonality with the two Ājyabhāga offerings, it would follow that the definition suffers from non-pervasion (avyāpti) because it would result in the cessation of those [other subsidiaries]. Therefore, the definition must be understood by taking into account the absence of the injunction for the two Ājyabhāgas together with the non-application of other injunctions, whereby the two Ājyabhāgas and the other subsidiaries are all acquired.
In this way, it should be inferred in other cases as well.
(Refutation of the *Vidhirasāyana*’s section on demonstrating the over-extension of the definition of *parisaṅkhyā* in the case of "the *prayāja*s [are] without the *barhis*"):

Furthermore, in this context, what is intended by another injunction (*vidhyantara*) is that which takes the form of an obstacle to the status of being an object of prescription (*vidheyatā*)—which is the intended fruit of the relevant injunction—and nothing else.
And since there exists such an injunction for barley (*yava-vidhi*), as well as this one for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt (*agnaye sviṣṭakṛte*), there is no inconsistency.

By this [it is meant]: in the commentary on the eighth verse, by means of the re-enactment of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, just as in the case of the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, there is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) regarding the *avabhṛtha* bath—namely, "he performs the *prayāja*s without the *barhis* grass; he performs the two *anūyāja*s without the *barhis* grass"—which serves to obtain the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s other than the *barhis*.

For, in the absence of this injunction, together with the non-operation of other injunctions, there would be no obtaining of those *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s other than the ones designated as *barhis*.

Furthermore, the objection raised in the *Vidhirasāyana*—that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of *parisaṃkhyā* because it results in the exclusion of something that is already established as necessarily obtained—is refuted.

This is because the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings does not obstruct the status of the *anūyāja* and *prayāja* offerings as things to be enjoined, and thus it is not included under the term "another injunction" (*vidhyantara*).
Therefore, since such another injunction does not exist here, this case is not an instance of that [definition].

However, in the absence of this specific rule alone, because [the sacrifice] is restricted by the rule for the *ājyabhāga* offerings, there is no fixed application of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s designated as *barhis*, nor of the *prayāja*s other than those;
thus, there is no entry into the scope of the definition (*lakṣaṇā*).

By this very logic, when the restrictive rule "The *pṛṣṭha* is the *bṛhat*" has been established, and prior to this rule, neither the original (*prakṛta*) rule nor the optional (*vikalpa*) rule for the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] operates.

By the force of the two statements, "By nature it has the *bṛhat* as its *pṛṣṭha*" and "The *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*," there is a simultaneous application (*samuccaya*) of both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*; therefore, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) that was previously raised must be refuted.
In this same manner, the defects such as over-extension and others raised against similar examples should likewise be refuted.
Even more than this should be seen in the Kaustubha.

(Refutation of the *Vidhirasāyana*’s argument regarding the induction of a confusion of ritual properties (*dharmasaṃkara*), by demonstrating that even when there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva* through the word ‘horse-bridle,’ the intention to denote the specific nature of a horse-bridle is nonetheless necessary.
Now, one might object: Let it be granted that the definition of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) applies equally to both cases;

nevertheless, in the injunction “He takes up the horse-bridle” (*aśvābhidhānīm ādatte*), where the taking up is enjoined as qualified by the mantra with reference to the horse-bridle (*aśvābhidhānī*), [how can there be an exclusion?]

Since it is necessary to resort to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being a means to the *apūrva*" in order to avoid the charge of meaninglessness regarding the nature of the horse's halter, and since that form [of being a means to the *apūrva*] exists in the donkey's halter as well— given that both are means to a single *apūrva*— the commingling of ritual properties (*dharmasaṃkara*) cannot be avoided, just as in the case of rice-grains and barley;
so how can the result of the exclusion of the mantra from the donkey's halter be obtained?
If it is argued that there is no escape from the refutation stated in the *Vidhirasāyana* regarding the objection to this example—[we reply:

since the confusion of properties (*dharmasaṃkara*) is already established by the very Vedic text inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the futility of the injunction cannot be avoided unless one asserts that it merely expresses the status of being a means to the *apūrva*;

and because that futility would otherwise be untenable, we must accept that even the cumbersome property of being "the horse-dedicator" (*aśvābhidhānītvam*) enters into the scope of the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). Thus, that [confusion] does not follow.

Therefore, even the specific designations found in the injunctions for those respective groups—such as "He addresses the horse, saying, 'Run swiftly, O conqueror! and "He causes the donkey to mount, saying, 'Yoke the two of you, O ass!'"—are thus rendered appropriate.

Regarding the statement in the *Vidhirasāyana* that—even if one were to enjoin the mantra with reference to the horse’s halter (*aśvābhidhānī*), or enjoin the taking [of the halter] as qualified by that [mantra], or enjoin [the taking] as qualified [by both]—since this would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the multiplicity of objects, the qualification "horse" would not be intended, and thus the application of the mantra to the donkey’s halter (*gardabhābhidhānī*) would be unavoidable; [This is the refutation of that argument. In the case of the expression “the horse’s halter” (*aśvābhidhānīm*), there is no intention to exclude the connection with the horse. This is because the word “horse” (*aśva*) functions as a restrictive qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for the object of the injunction, thereby precluding its application to other halters. Furthermore, since the word “horse” is not a subordinate element (*guṇa*) within the compound, it cannot be disregarded on the grounds of being unintended. Therefore, the mantra is restricted to the horse’s halter alone. Consequently, the objection raised in the *Vidhirasāyana* is untenable. Thus, the conclusion remains that the mantra is indeed enjoined with reference to the horse’s halter.

That is not so; for since a qualified entity is understood through the grammatical derivation of mutual connection within a compound, even if one accepts that such a qualified entity is the object of the injunction, that [undesired] consequence does not arise.

Indeed, it is clear that in the case of "The Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer restrain their speech," there is no plurality of objects of the injunction, nor is there a lack of intent to express the connection with the *prayāja* offerings when the remnant of the *prayāja* is to be consecrated.

Furthermore, for the very purpose of avoiding the futility of the injunction (*vidhi-vaiyarthyāparihāra*), one must accept—despite the lack of other recourse—the qualification of the restatement (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*) as in the case of "one shall not kill a Brāhmaṇa" (*na brāhmaṇaṃ hanyāt*).

Moreover, when there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva*, it is logical that the qualification itself is intended through that indication of the qualified whole, just as the qualification of the *apūrva* is intended.

Nor can it be argued that here, as in the case of "he spreads the sacrificial cake with the mantra 'O, spread yourself wide' (*uru prathasva*)," the injunction of taking [the grass] serves the purpose of establishing a restriction on the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) as the agent of the spreading—which is already established by the nature of the action.
It should not be said that "the futility [of the injunction] is easily avoided, therefore what you have stated is correct";
for according to the method you have proposed, even with that much, the restatement of a qualified entity (viśiṣṭānuvāda) remains untenable.
Indeed, you cannot avoid the restatement of a qualified entity merely by the fear that the injunction would otherwise be futile.
For just as in the case of seizing the horse's reins, the injunction is valid even for seizing the donkey's reins in order to establish the Adhvaryu as the performer;

and because it is improper to assume the status of a restatement (anuvāda) regarding the mantra portion—despite the possibility of an injunction—merely to secure the identity of the agent for both the mantra and the action.
Indeed, there is no evidence for a rule that the recollection of one's own ritual action occurs solely through the recitation of a mantra performed by oneself.

For even by the recitation of a mantra performed by the *hotṛ* priest, there arises a recollection (*smṛti*) of the sacrificial oblation (*yajñapraharaṇa*) to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the *adhvaryu* priest.

For this very reason, it is stated everywhere that, on account of the equality between mantras and *kalpasūtras*, the mention of "observers" (*upadraṣṭṛ*) and so forth is included as a means for remembering the matters to be performed.
And thus, when there is an injunction by means of a mantra, the result—namely, a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of equal alternatives—cannot be avoided at all.

In reality, however, since the mantra is recited specifically in the *Ādhvaryava-kāṇḍa*, and because there is an explicit injunction stating "one addresses the horse with the words, 'O steed, run swiftly! as well as an injunction for the act of binding at that very place, the restriction that the binding must be performed by the *adhvaryu* is established;

consequently, the restriction that the taking up [of the horse] for that purpose must also be performed by the *adhvaryu* is established. Thus, in no way does it result in the consequence of a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*).
That the injunction would be rendered futile has already been explained by the venerable [author] in the Kaustubha.

If, however, by this same reasoning, it is argued that since the injunction for the restriction of digging is necessary in the phrase "he digs with two [hands]" (*dvābhyāṃ khanati*), and since the Adhvaryu's status as the agent is established therein, his agency would consequently apply to the taking up of the spade (*abhryādāna*) as well— therefore, no further fruit exists in an explicit injunction for it—

then it should be understood that in both cases, the injunction is not heard to extend as far as the taking up, solely for the purpose of avoiding a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of a specific qualification.
Just as the application of the Yajurvedic expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) for a failure in the taking [of the grain] results in a specific fruit, so too should it be understood from the *Kaustubha*;
furthermore, this will be explained under the mantra for spreading [the grains]. Enough with this elaboration; let us follow the subject at hand.
(An attribution of the nature of *parisaṅkhyā* [exclusive specification] to certain rules of *upasaṃhāra* according to the opinion of some:

Now, an objection is raised: "In this way, this definition of *parisaṅkhyā* is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), because it would apply even to another rule studied independently or elsewhere that is combined with a given rule, since the exclusion of others is effectively the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the scripture in that case.
To this, some have replied by simply accepting the objection as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Therefore, in the introduction to the eighth verse, the Dīkṣitas have accepted that the statements occurring in the section concerning Mitravindā and others function as *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification).
(An exposition of how, according to the author of the *Prakāśa*, the injunctions of restrictive enumeration (*upasaṃhāra-vidhi*) are not cases of preclusion [*aparisaṅkhyā*]):
This very point the authors of the *Prakāśa* do not tolerate;
for they have established it in this manner in their refutation of the *Vidhirasāyana*.
If restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*) were the nature of an application (*upasaṃhāra*),
then the application would be rendered utterly futile, as it would result in the rule "one divides the cake dedicated to Agni into four parts" also being a restriction.
For this very reason, eight alternative views (*pakṣa*), which are accepted by all authorities such as the author of the Bhāṣya, are possible in the section concerning the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.

Otherwise, because the fifth [type of fallacy] would be a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), and because the seventh, which consists of the subsumption under the sixth, would also be included within the category of *parisaṃkhyā*, the impossibility of there being eight [types of fallacies] residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) would follow.

Furthermore, in the section concerning the statement "The [ṣoḍaśin] is taken because of the existence [of the rite] after the Atirātra," the Bhāṣya states: "Is the subsequent sentence regarding the ṣoḍaśin an *upasaṃhāra* (reiteration) or a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusion)? This would be untenable if there were no difference between the two;
therefore, there is indeed a distinction between *upasaṃhāra* and *parisaṅkhyā*.
If one asks how these two differ:
Listen: since the *Vārttika* states that "a general rule which is unclear may be restricted by a specific one,

but for a rule that is already clear, restriction by others is not desired," and by saying this it indicates— by implication— that restriction (*upasaṃhāra*) applies only to the subject matter of the first half [of the verse], whereas exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) applies only to the subject matter of the second half and never to the subject matter of the first half, the distinction between the two is indeed clear.

For example, because a whole (avayavin) exists distributively across its parts and lacks the nature of a universal (sāmānya), the injunction regarding the whole is not subsumed by the specific injunctions regarding the parts. Even if one were to accept that the unity of the *yāga* and *homa* is not the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, the subsequent half-verse [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*] addresses the fact that the injunction regarding the *āgneya* [cake] is not subsumed by the rule "one offers the four-fold portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*). Similarly, the general injunction that impels the group of eleven portions (*ekādaśāvadāna*)—namely, "one first cuts a portion from the heart"—is not subsumed; this is the domain of the restrictive exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of what has already been obtained.

Thus, it is first of all not included within the category of restriction of what is already obtained (*prāptaparisaṅkhyā*), nor even within the category of restriction of what is not yet obtained (*aprāptaparisaṅkhyā*);
for the general injunction is directly perceived.
Thus, regarding the two general rules—"That which one takes in the *juhū* is for the *prayāja*s;

that which one takes in the *upabhṛt* is for the *prayāja*s and *anūyāja*s"—the rule prescribing the time for the bringing together of the clarified butter in the *upabhṛt*, namely "Having passed over the *iḍā* and the *barhis*," is merely a restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*) based on what is implied by the purpose, and not an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*).

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* in the fourth book (*cāturthika-adhikaraṇa*): "The bringing together [of the butter] must be primary, because of the observation of the indicative mark."

By the passage stating that the unqualified scriptural hearing of "for the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s" is restricted to the subject of the latter two *prayāja*s by the force of the injunction regarding time— "having passed over the *iḍā* and the *barhis*"—

it is precisely stated to be a case of restriction (*upasaṃhāra*). Similarly, in cases such as "the *prāyaṇīyā* concludes with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s," because the general rule of extension (*atideśa*) is not explicit, there is a restriction obtained through the meaning of the injunction for *saṃsthā* (conclusion), which is the cessation of the denoted meaning of the verb *tiṣṭhati* preceded by the prefix *sam*.
Thus.
Therefore, the demonstration that such examples constitute *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) by the Dīkṣitas is indeed improper.
Be that as it may,
in every case, the exclusion of other [alternatives] is obtained from the injunction itself for the purpose of enjoining another matter.
However, that is not designated as a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusionary injunction);
for the designations *apūrva*, *niyama*, and *parisaṅkhyā* apply only to those injunctions directly heard in scripture (*śruta*).
Indeed, an exclusionary injunction does not have the result of producing a cognition of avoidance through a mediated process.
Otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*).

Therefore, in the case of injunctions such as threshing (*avaghāta*), since their result is the exclusion of other means through a mediated process, they are designated as restrictive injunctions because their direct result is merely restriction.

Similarly, in the case of injunctions regarding technical numbers ending in *ṣakāra* or *ḍakāra*, since they only bring about technical numbers that were not previously established, it is appropriate to designate them as original injunctions (*apūrvavidhi*).

Nor is another injunction postulated on the grounds that the present injunction would otherwise be inexplicable, such that it could be designated as a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) of what is already established;

rather, only a specific indication (*viśeṣalakṣaṇā*) is obtained through the word *prayāja*, which serves to provide the object of reference for the injunction enjoining the clarified butter (*ājya*) contained in the *aupabhṛta* ladle.
For this reason as well, it is not logical that they possess the nature of a restrictive enumeration (parisaṅkhyā).

(An exposition of the distinction from the view of the *Prakāśakāra* by demonstrating that, among the three types of results being understood, the fact that a sentence achieves its purposefulness through [one of them] constitutes the designation of "injunction" (*vidhi*), and by establishing that this general injunction (*sāmānyavidhi*) merely demonstrates the difference between itself and restrictive injunction (*upasaṃhāra*) or exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*).)

In this regard, the following should be noted: by this demonstration of the distinction between clear forms and objects, it is understood that what is intended in the definition of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) is its dependence upon a clear injunction and the attainment [of the object] through it.
Furthermore, it is your view that because of the absence of those two in the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition.
In that case, according to your own view, it must be stated whether the injunction of extended application (*atideśavidhi*) is clear or unclear.

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence that the concluding statement in passages such as "the Prāyaṇīyā ends with the Patnīsaṃyājas" would fail to apply; furthermore, there would be the failure of the conclusion regarding the seventh alternative concerning the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.
In the second case, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the exclusion (parisaṅkhyā) of what has already been established by the fifth alternative.
Furthermore, it is difficult to state with certainty what constitutes clarity or lack of clarity regarding a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*).

We do not perceive how the injunction for the *Āgneya* sacrifice is clear, while the injunction "he divides the sacrificial cake into four parts" (*puroḍāśaṃ caturdhā karoti*) is unclear. As for the argument that—even though the exclusion of others is obtained by implication—such an injunction is designated as an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) because it brings about what was previously unattained, and thus it cannot be classified as an exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*), [we reply:]...
That too is incorrect;

for if that were the case, since the object would already be obtained through the prior operation, even the injunction regarding the taking up of the horse's bridle (*aśvābhidhānī*)—by virtue of enjoining what was previously unobtained—would result in being an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction), and thus the designation of "exclusion" (*parisaṅkhyā*) as stated in the Sūtra would not apply.
Therefore, this must be resolved in the following manner.
Wherein, among those things perceived as consisting of two or three fruits, that by which their own redundancy is avoided is designated as an injunction for those fruits;
taking such a designation as the basis, these definitions [are formulated].
Whether that fruit is proximate or remote,
it is for this very reason that he demonstrates the non-possession of the fruit through its result, [stating] "herein."

The phrase "the restrictive particle *eva* indicates that the status of being an exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*) is not to be resorted to, but rather [it is] precisely a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
This is because it has the result of a restriction.

By this, the following arguments stated in the *Vidhirasāyana* are refuted: (1) that when a result residing in the thing to be enjoined is possible, it is more parsimonious (*laghu*) to accept the word *vrīhi* as having the purpose of excluding barley (*yava-parisaṅkhyā*) by means of entering into a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a means to the *apūrva*, rather than including even the quality of "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) which is superfluous (*guru*); and (2) that it has a purpose through the attainment of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*) as the performer.

Furthermore, because the restriction that those two [mantras] must be performed by the person perceived as the speaker— through the perception of the first-person endings in the two mantras, "May I slay the lower Rākṣasa from heaven" (*avarakṣo divaḥ*) and "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni" (*agnaye vo juṣṭaṃ prokṣāmi*)— is already established,
for this very reason there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantras to establish that they are to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest.

Just as in the case of *prathana*; the point is that even though the mantra belongs to the *adhvaryu* priest, it is indeed intended as an injunction (*vidhi*) because it serves to establish the restrictive rule for *prathana*.
(An objection regarding the lack of conformity of restrictive injunctions due to the non-conformity of their optional nature:
But surely, because the impossibility [of the injunction] differs according to the difference in their optional nature, there is a lack of conformity in the definition;
for if it refers to the optionality between two means to the effect, it would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to each individual restrictive injunction.

If the definition intends to refer to the optionality of either the *kārya* (the result) or the *upāya* (the means), it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) because one or the other is not necessarily restricted;

if it refers to the optionality of that which is included in the injunction (*vidhi*) after considering both the *kārya* and the *upāya*, it lacks pervasion regarding the restriction of that which is not included in the injunction;

and if it states the optionality of the object to be restricted (*niyamya*) after considering both what is included and what is not included in the injunction, it lacks pervasion in a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) where optionality belongs only to the opposites of the object to be restricted.
