If it is stated that [the definition applies] to anything whatsoever—whether the object to be restricted (*niyamya*) or another—that is subject to optionality (*pākṣikatva*), then there would be non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) that lack mere optionality.

Thus, since the example shown in the *Vidhirasāyana* for the verse "In some cases, the effect [is produced] by this cause" lacks pervasion, how can there be liberation [from this fault]? To this, he says: "Even though such a distinction exists..."
And the detailed exposition of this should be seen in the *Kostubha*.
(B1) Since [the requirement] regarding the existence of rice is already established as a prima facie position through implication (*ākṣepa*),
there is no fault whatsoever, because even when such a distinction exists, only the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyāvṛtti*) is included in the definition.
(B2) [The refutation of the *Vidhirasāyana*’s claim that "having a visible purpose" is the definition of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*):]

Thus, having himself demonstrated various instances of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and non-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) formulated by the Ācārya, and considering that definition to be untenable, [the author] established the definition of a restrictive injunction as being "that which has a visible purpose" (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). Although this [definition] is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), applying even to injunctions such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice which teach visible results;

Nevertheless, it has been established that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because of the qualification "provided it does not have the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as its medium. Repeating that point, he refutes it with the words "As for what... The meaning is clear.

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) in this passage, the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) is indicated even in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) within the modified ritual (*vaikṛta*), such as: "The *bṛhat* [sāman] is the *pṛṣṭha*."

Furthermore, if one intends to mean that the object of the injunction has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the injunction that restricts the use of mantras (*mantraparisaṅkhyāvidhi*).

If one intends to mean the result that constitutes the intended scope of the injunction’s purport (*tātparya*), this is impossible because a restrictive rule (*niyama*) has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); thus, this too should be understood as a refutation.
(The integration of the definition characterized by the result of excluding non-connection [ayogavyāvṛtti] into the injunction regarding the substitute [pratīka]:
Although this is not applicable to the injunction for a fixed substitute, namely, "If one does not find Soma," because—

by the logic of extreme similarity— there is never a possibility of non-connection with substitutes that are utterly dissimilar, and thus the contingency of occasional non-connection (*pākṣikāyoga*) does not arise;

Nevertheless, although there arises— due to the injunction for the ritual act— the contingency of employing any substance whatsoever in the absence of Soma, no fault occurs because, before a rule based on logical similarity (*nyāya*) can begin to restrict the choice to something very similar, it is accepted that the application of the *pratīka* (representative part) already functions; thus, at that stage, the application of the *pratīka* as a general rule is logically established.
(The reconciliation of the rule "The days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyājas," preceded by the removal of doubt:

Now, even if in all cases there is some kind of figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*), in the restrictive injunction "The days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyājas," there is no possibility of the conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyājas being merely optional.

For the sake of establishing the simultaneity of the twelve days, and because the twelvefold nature of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) must be observed up to the Hāriyojana cup, it follows that the [ritual] which is to be repeated must come to rest at that very point.

Alternatively, since it will be explained in the eleventh [book] that the performance of the iṣṭi-related animal rites (pāśukakarmāṇi), together with their ancillaries (sāṅga), on their respective days during the period of the Soma-pressing (sutyākāla) occurs separately, it follows that [the *udavasānīyeṣṭi*] is obtained only immediately after the complete conclusion of the iṣṭi and pāśuka rituals;
thus, there is no possibility whatsoever for the Patnīsaṃyājas and other subsequent rites to apply in this case.

If it is argued that, for this reason, there arises the contingency of this being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), as in the case of the statement "the Agniṣomīya sacrifice concludes with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings," this has already been refuted by the authors of the *Prakāśa* in their *Khaṇḍana* of the *Vidhirasāyana*.
For it is not the case that the repetition of all [rites] by virtue of occurring at the time of the *sutyā* is the subject matter of that section;

rather, it concerns only those rites included within the *sutyā*. Therefore, since the rule of separate performance applies only up to the *hāriyojana* [offering], and there is no rule for the repetition of the subsequent *saumika* and *aiṣṭika* rites, is it for the sake of establishing the simultaneity (*sahatva*) of everything that follows?

When the possibility of "tantratva" (common performance) arises through repetition in the ritual execution, and when there is the contingency of no fixed rule— such as whether the *tantratva* applies to ten, fifteen, or twenty [offerings]— the conclusion at the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is prescribed as a restrictive rule.

(An establishment of the status of this as an *apūrva-vidhi* by refuting the claim that the sentence "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartata" functions as a restrictive injunction [*niyama-vidhi*] as stated in the *Vidhirasāyana*:

For this very reason, in such passages as "With the mantra 'Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre,' he pours the *āghāra* libation," there is no possibility of the mantra revealing Hiraṇyagarbha being obtained for the *āghāra* to Indra and others in any way, because it lacks any indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Indra; even though [the mantra] exists there...

It should be observed in the *Kaustubha* that, because it produces an unseen merit (*adṛṣ�ṭa*) based on a restriction already established, the injunction of the mantra for the subsequent *āghāra* offering is indeed an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).

Thus, the conventional designation of it as a *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction) is merely figurative, based solely on its producing an unseen merit through a restriction that was already established.
By this same method, [the status of] injunctions such as "one places the whey (*vājina*) on the *utkara*" and "one should bind the animal to the *paridhi* [enclosing-stick]" is to be understood.

In the section concerning the *utkara* and the *paridhi*, since there is no possibility of [the mantra] being obtained through the rule of the "wing" (*pakṣaprāpti*), it must be accepted that this is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); thus, the avoidance of the charge of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) stated in the *Vidhirasāyana* should be observed.

As for the objection raised in the refutation of the fifteenth verse of the *Vidhirasāyana*—namely, that although the *Hiraṇyagarbha* mantra lacks the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) due to its indicative power (*liṅga*), it might nevertheless be used by chance through a secondary sense (*gauṇī*) or the like, as is common with worldly meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth, like the act of splitting (*vidalana*) and other such [optional] acts—[this is addressed as follows:]...
Having taken up the attainment [of the mantra], its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) was established; however,

while that might somehow be possible by taking into account the fact that the capacity to produce the removal of the husk is understood from common worldly experience in the case of threshing and so forth— where there is thus an accidental attainment— here, in the case of the Prajāpati-mantra, which lacks the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of Indra and whose capacity for the purpose of recollecting him has not been established, [the situation is different].

Since, when there is a certainty of sublation, a coincidental attainment is in no way possible, and [the attainment] must be postulated only after resorting to a secondary sense (gauṇī), this [position] is considered improper by the Venerable Master.

(An exposition on the acceptance of the definition of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—characterized by having the fulfillment of an unobtained portion as its fruit—as presented in the *Vidhirasāyana-khaṇḍana*: Furthermore, regarding the eighteenth verse of the *Vidhirasāyana*, the following definition of a restrictive injunction was proposed: "A restrictive injunction is an injunction whose fruit is the fulfillment of an unobtained portion that has not yet been determined."
That very [definition] was accepted in the *Vidhirasāyanakhaṇḍana* as being faultless by way of avoiding the aforementioned over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
However, if one intends to mean merely "having the result of fulfilling a portion not previously obtained," there is an over-extension to all sentences concerning optional rites (*kāmyavākya*);
for even in those cases, once heaven is attained through a sentence concerning heaven, they have the result of fulfilling other portions in the form of other results not previously obtained.

Furthermore, in the injunction for all desired results (*sarvakāmyavidhi*), the portion consisting of heaven is already established, whereas the portion other than that is not; thus, because there is a definite determination (*nirdhāraṇa*), there is no lack of determination.
In the case of rice and the like, since there is no determination of the unestablished portion—such as threshing—as "this very thing," there is no impossibility [of the definition].

As for the definition of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), which has been stated by some, that is disregarded because it is too narrow (*avyāpti*), failing to cover cases such as "the *dvirātra* sacrifice is to be performed with the *ṣoḍaśin* cup" and so forth;
for the repeated performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup sacrifice has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, the definition of an *apūrva-vidhi*—namely, that it is a prescription whose fruit exceeds both restrictive (*niyama*) and exclusive (*parisaṅkhyā*) prescriptions—is also well-established.
(B2) [The description in both the *Vidhirasāyana* and its critique of the impropriety of an *apūrva-vidhi* as a restrictive prescription (*niyamavidhi*) is incorrect.
That is improper.
In the *Upahavya* sacrifice, having prescribed the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as "a dark-brown horse," it is stated in the injunction, "That [horse] is to be given to the Brahman priest";

then, in the *Audumbara* sacrifice, having prescribed the sacrificial fee as "a cup made of Udumbara wood," it is stated in the injunction, "It is to be given to the dear Brahman priest of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Finally, in the context of the *Āyuṣkāmeṣṭi*, it is heard in the injunction: "He distributes everything to the Brahman priest."

Furthermore, there is over-extension [of the definition] to an injunction in the form of a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification), because it is impossible to determine—among the horse-cups, Soma, and sacrificial remnants common to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—that "this belongs to the Brahman priest" and "this belongs to the others," since the result of such a rule is to fulfill an undetermined and unobtained portion.
As for what was stated in the *Vidhirasāyana* regarding these being *apūrvavidhi*s (original injunctions): [that is incorrect].
As for the claim made in that refutation that it must necessarily be an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*),
both of those points are incorrect;

for, according to the definition stated by the Teacher exactly as heard, the connection with Brahman and the connection with the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are [both] delimited by what is to be enjoined.

Since [the rule] would merely result in a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*)—because it is already eternally established as occupying the place of the ordinary *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice—the definition of such an injunction cannot possibly apply.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that such cases constitute restrictive injunctions based solely on the popular maxim that "all rules concerning substances are restrictive injunctions," then even injunctions for optional accessories (*guṇakāmavidhi*) would incur the status of restrictive injunctions. Moreover, if one were to admit the status of various injunctions merely by their inclusion within one's own definition of them, there would be no obstacle to accepting that status even for all optional injunctions; consequently, the inclusion of the term "unrestricted" (*anirdhārita*) in the definition would become redundant.

Therefore, intending that this definition is not tenable, the venerable teacher has stated a definition of restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) formulated by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, it will be shown that the status of a preclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) applies to the statement, "That [gift] is to be given to a Brahmin."

(Definition of the Apūrva-vidhi) Having thus demonstrated the definitions of the *parisaṅkhyā* and *niyama* injunctions, he states the definition of the *apūrva-vidhi*, which is constituted by its distinctions from those two, beginning with the words "ata eva" (for this very reason).

Due to the qualification "being distinct from a restrictive injunction" (niyama), there is no over-extension to the statement concerning *pūtīka* plants; nor, due to the qualification "being distinct from an exclusive specification" (parisaṅkhyā), is there over-extension to the injunction regarding the two *ājyabhāga* offerings in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice.
The application of this definition to the *agnihotra* and other such statements is indeed clear.
(An exposition of the refutation of the view that the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings for the horse-sacrifice priest is not a restrictive injunction [*parisaṅkhyā*]):

As for what was stated here by the authors of the *Khaṇḍana*— that, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings does not possess the nature of a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*),
because no such usage as a restrictive injunction is observed in any Mīmāṃsā treatise—
Furthermore, because such [a restrictive function] is not observed even in the Vedānta texts,

it is indeed an *apūrvavidhi* (injunction of what is previously unknown), as evidenced by the conventional usage that "novelty" (*apūrvatā*) constitutes the sublation of the general rule (*codakalopa*). However,

in the case of the mantra "imāmagṛbhṇan," since there is no prior attainment of anything else, the initiates (*dīkṣitānām*) mistakenly believe it to be a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) due to the similarity of its object with the two [other types of injunctions].

And for this very reason, regarding the locative case in the phrase "tatra cānyatra ca" (in that [case] and elsewhere), when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the locative in the sense of "is obtained," the author of the Vārttika stated that it constitutes an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) according to the fifth alternative, and not according to the eighth.

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) also, while explaining the example "like the Ājyabhāgas" in the sūtra *ājyabhāgavad vā* under the seventh pāda of the tenth book, stated that this is "as in the fifth alternative regarding the Gṛhamedhīya," and not "as in the eighth alternative. Furthermore, if the hearing of the Ājyabhāgas in the Gṛhamedhīya were a *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), [it would follow] from the section on the Gṛhamedhīya in the subsequent section separated by one [topic].

Regarding the statement, "There would be a prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt*," the claim in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that this is a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation) because the restatement of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries occurs specifically in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice would be incorrect;
for such a deliberation is only logically possible within the context of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

And it should not be said: "If the definition of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) is present here, why is it not a case of *parisaṅkhyā*?"—for there is no possibility of [the action] being established elsewhere or otherwise.

And on this point is the following passage from the works of the ancients: "For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), in addition to the form of the sacrifice explicitly heard in the case of the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, there exists a function belonging to the sacrifice, which is to be inferred from its mention in the context (*prakaraṇa*) and which operates through its own unique transcendental result (*apūrva*)."
This re-enunciation of the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of defining their specific form;
otherwise, it would be purposeless.
And by virtue of this necessity to avoid purposelessness, the assistance rendered through the performance (*karaṇopakāra*) is indeed that of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite.

In that case, although [the term] is produced by many constituent parts, it is taught here as referring— through a *jahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (denotation where the primary sense is abandoned) based on a possible connection— to that which is qualified solely by the *ājyabhāga* offerings; thus, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established that the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, being dependent on the assistance of the performance (*karaṇopakāra*), is a new rite (*apūrva*).

Therefore, since it is the very archetypal (*prākṛta*) benefit, qualified by the *ājyabhāga* offerings, that is enjoined, there is no definition of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) involving a distinction between the thing to be enjoined and the thing to be excluded—both of which would apply here and elsewhere. Thus, it has been stated that this is indeed an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).
(This refers to the refutation of the argument supporting the status of the *ājyabhāga* injunction as a *parisaṅkhyā*, following its initial presentation.
Here, this should be noted: your recourse to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is indeed due to the force of [avoiding] meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).

Since that [prohibition] occurs by functioning prior to the extension (atideśa) of the rule, its purposefulness is established through the injunction of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, which effectively results in the exclusion of other subsidiary elements; thus, we do not understand how it could otherwise be [meaningless].

Furthermore, as for the statement by the ancients that it is "figurative" (*lakṣaṇā*) due to meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), that too is not rooted in the meaninglessness of the injunction itself, but rather is understood in their works to be rooted in the meaninglessness of enjoining the mere performance of the *ājyabhāga* ritual.
For instance: first of all, this definition is not established in the Bhāṣya;

however, in the Tantraratna, it is stated that through an implied archetype (*prakṛti*), the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice enters into syntactic unity with the two Ājyabhāga offerings obtained from another injunction by means of *lakṣaṇā*.
Therefore, the Gṛhamedhīya is not connected with the archetypal word which is merely inferential; thus, having established its novelty (*apūrvatā*) by means of its being "new" (*apūrva*).

Now, one might raise the objection that, because there is no further expectancy once the requirements are satisfied by the directly perceived subsidiary offerings (upahoma) and so forth, sacrifices such as the Nakṣatreṣṭi would lack originality (apūrvatva); it is with this objection in mind that the following text is written to explain the Bhāṣya.
The intended meaning is as follows: "How" (katham) requires a specific type of ritual activity belonging to the sacrifice;
therefore, only that word which provides the specific mode [of performance] is capable of attaining syntactic unity by fulfilling that expectancy, and nothing else.
Furthermore, another action does not, by its very nature, become an activity included within [the primary] action.
The accomplishment of the mode, however, must be the operation directed toward that [result],
for a connection between two actions is not possible by their own nature, but rather by depending on a specific intermediary.

Furthermore, in the case of the subsidiary offerings (upahoma) and so forth, no established means (dvāra) exists by which they could be understood as performing the function inherent in the primary sacrifice.

However, the term "according to the model" (prakṛtivat), by conveying the manner consisting in the accomplishment of the intermediate effects along with all their constituent parts belonging to the archetype, easily achieves syntactic unity.

However, because the subsequent recitation would otherwise be purposeless, those [elements] also achieve syntactic unity with the main injunction through the postulation of a mediating function (*dvārakalpanā*).
As for the archetypal subsidiaries such as the *ājyabhāga* offerings,

since they have already obtained their intermediate benefit (*avāntaropakāra*) within the archetype itself, and thus already established their connection to the primary rite, when they are heard of in a modified rite (*vikṛti*), they bring to mind— by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— the archetypal procedure known as the accomplishment of its own specific intermediate effect.
This statement, "he offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations," is for the purpose of indicating that [the *ājyabhāgas*] are subordinate (*tallakṣaṇārtham*);
for if it were intended to convey their own essential form (*svarūpaparatve*), it would result in meaninglessness (*ānarthakyāpatteḥ*).

By means of such indication, however, it is able to achieve syntactic unity with the principal injunction by fulfilling the requirement of the "manner of performance" (*kathaṃbhāva*) of that principal act.

And because that [requirement] is fulfilled, the injunction (*codaka*)—which acquires its own existence dependent upon the absence of further expectancy—is set aside; thus, there is "novelty" (*apūrvatva*).

By demonstrating through this the distinction from the *upahoma* offerings, and for the purpose of establishing the possibility of syntactic unity with the primary injunction by means of a word capable of fulfilling the expectancy regarding the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*), it is shown that the term *ājyabhāga* does not merely enjoin the essential nature of the action itself.

Furthermore, it is the injunction of a specific operation known as "the accomplishment of a particular mode," which is understood in the primary sacrifice (prakṛti) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). However, in the case of the subsidiary offerings (upahoma), since such an accomplishment of a mode was not previously understood, secondary indication is simply not possible. Thus, it has been stated that even through secondary indication, the injunction of the subsidiary offerings is unable to achieve syntactic unity; for where, then, could there be a secondary indication of the assistance rendered by other auxiliary parts to the performance?

Even in the previously cited *Śāstradīpikā* text, it is understood that the definition applies only to that which exists in the form of an operation belonging to the sacrifice, by way of its own unique apūrva (*svāpūrva*) residing in the *ājyabhāga* offerings;

thus, if one is not troubled by the error in the explanation of that text— namely, that [the definition] would apply even to what is related to me (*madgata*)— then, regarding the prescription of the specific mode produced by the *ājyabhāga*,
as for the alleged futility of the injunction (*vidhivaiyarthyam*), [it is not so].
However, that [objection] was already refuted in the *Tantraratna* by accepting a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*) based on the preceding text which establishes its novelty (*apūrvatā*).

Furthermore, in such a case where there is a definition of "benefit for another" (*parārtha*), how could the loss of one's own purpose (*svārthahāni*) and the assumption of benefit for another (*parārthakalpanā*) not result, as they do in the fifth position?

Moreover, if the two *ājyabhāga* offerings were intended merely for the sake of the assistance produced by other subsidiaries, they would fall into the error of having a non-original function (*aprākṛtakārya*).

Therefore, rather than accepting that [status] and relying on an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), it is more appropriate to accept an injunction of those very [offerings] characterized by their own specific assistance, and thus to rely on what is effectively a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*).

Furthermore, even if the *ājyabhāga* offerings are enjoined for the purpose of providing assistance generated by other auxiliary elements (*itarāṅga*), the cessation of the *codaka* (the rule that extends the archetype) must be stated as resulting precisely from the destruction of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), since its own existence depends upon expectancy. Otherwise, it would be unavoidable that the other auxiliaries would have to be performed in conjunction [with the *ājyabhāgas*]. Since such a destruction of expectancy is already established by the injunction of the *ājyabhāga* itself as qualified by its own specific assistance, resorting to an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) extending that far is entirely redundant.

For this very reason, in the subsequent section [of the *Tantravārttika*], regarding the statement "only as much as has been mentioned," it is held that when many archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements are heard, there is an option (*vikalpa*), because each one alone possesses the capacity to fulfill the requirement of the primary element (*pradhāna*) by virtue of having its contribution already established (*kḷptopakārakatva*). Thus, in the *Tantraratna* and other treatises,
the state of having a pre-established contribution is made the reason for the capacity to fulfill the requirement.

As for the objection raised regarding the contradiction between the Bhāṣya and the Vārtika texts: the intention behind the Bhāṣyakāra’s statement in the *Sviṣṭakṛt* section—where he adopts the fifth position (*pañcamapakṣa*) and speaks of a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation)—has been demonstrated in the *Tantraratna* itself.

For in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, because the two *ājyabhāga* offerings bring to mind other sacrifices of the same class, there is indeed the exclusion [of those others]; thus, for all the remaining duties that are to be enjoined...

It is stated in the *Tantraratna* that, given their non-cessation, it is considered whether the injunction for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is intended as an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of other subsidiary rites or not;
however, this deliberation is not appropriate in the eighth alternative,
because at that time, due to the omission of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), all [subsidiaries] would cease, making such a deliberation impossible.

Therefore, this statement—that "this investigation serves as the basis for the non-cessation of the remaining operations; and since the fifth position is established merely by way of a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvā-cintā*), it follows that the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) itself is logically consistent with such a consideration"—is incorrect.

Furthermore, regarding the presentation of the fifth position as an example in the *Vārttika*, that was intended precisely for the sake of clarity, because in the case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two locative endings in the phrase *tatra ca anyatra ca* (in that [case] and in another), the example must be shown in order to demonstrate the cessation of others preceded by their prior occurrence (*prāpti*).

The clarity of the reason is established through logic (*tarka*) and with respect to attainment through scripture (*śāstra*); since it is easily obtained upon attainment [through scripture], it is not a proving factor.

Furthermore, the objection raised regarding the contradiction with the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—which aims to explain the example "like the *ājyabhāga*" found in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the seventh chapter of the tenth book—is also weak.

In this regard, the statement in the Sūtra, "Because of the specific mention, there would be an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) as in the case of the *ājyabhāga* offerings," declares that it is an exclusive specification due to such a mention; and this mention—namely, "There are indeed eleven cuttings of the animal"—is stated in the Bhāṣya and explained therein.
Since these [cuttings] are already established by other means, an injunction (*vidhi*) for them alone is not possible.

Because it would be purposeless, it is not a mere restatement; furthermore, since the repeated hearing of that which is devoid of qualities serves as an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of other [parts] not mentioned [in the injunction], there can be no cessation [of expectation] here based on the satisfaction of expectancy, according to the logic of the eighth alternative,
because the expectancy for the cutting out of the other parts does not cease by the injunction to cut out the eleven [parts].
Therefore, the citation of the example "like the *ājyabhāga*" by the author of the *Bhāṣya* has been explained as being directed toward the fifth position (*pakṣa*).

Since that very position yields the sense that there are no [additional offerings] other than the eleven, the subsequent sūtra establishes that the three-fold fault (*traidoṣya*) applies to it and demonstrates that the injunction can be accounted for otherwise.
Thus, although an explanation was made there as being directed toward the fifth position because there was no other way, this does not affect the status of the *ājyabhāga* sentence.

Intending precisely that the status of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) as a result [of the injunction] would be faulty in the eighth alternative (*pakṣa*), the venerable teachers will explicitly state the nature of *parisaṅkhyā* in the eighth alternative in the section concerning the *Gṛhamedhīya*.
This has also been stated by the Dīkṣitas.

As for that which was stated by the Dīkṣitas in the *Siddhāntaleśagrantha*, where the example of *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification) was presented as "one performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings," and it was remarked that this is an example according to the method of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the *Gṛhamedhīyādhikaraṇa*: [that is the case] when there is a constant application (*nityaprāpti*) of two subsidiaries to one principal, or of one subsidiary to two principals, or of two subsidiaries to one principal, [and then one seeks to exclude] another principal...

Alternatively, the third [type of injunction] has as its fruit the exclusion of what remains; this is for the purpose of demonstrating an "inclusionary exclusion" (*prāptaparisaṅkhyā*)—intended to show that the previously stated definition of exclusionary restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*) implies constant necessity—and it is not contradictory to accept it as an inclusionary exclusion merely on that account. Therefore, the definition of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) does not apply there.
As for the objection that the term "parisaṅkhyā" (exclusive specification) is not observed as a technical usage in the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta treatises, the reply is this:

it must be stated where, in a statement concerning the established doctrine of ritual action (*karma-siddhānta*), the usage of "upasaṃhāra" (subsumption) as explained by you is observed; or likewise, where, in a statement concerning Brahman, the usage of "niyamavidhi" (restrictive injunction) as explained by you is found.

If it is argued that even when a transaction is generally carried out in some form or another, the specific character of each particular injunction attained through logical necessity cannot be denied, then here too, although the transaction is established by the very words such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so forth, its status as a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*) cannot be denied; thus, the two cases are equal.

For here, by the term *apūrvatā* (novelty), what is intended is not the status of being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), but rather the absence of a prior archetype (*prakṛti*); thus, this point is of no consequence.
Let us proceed with the subject at hand.

(Refutation of the view that "having an unseen purpose" constitutes an *apūrva-vidhi*): As for the claim that the definition of a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*) provided by the Dīkṣitas— that an injunction whose purpose is visible is a restrictive injunction— implies that the intended definition of an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) is "an injunction whose purpose is unseen," so they explain.
That is not so; for there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of the statement: "On the subsequent day of the Dvirātra, [the Soma] is taken."

Furthermore, regarding the state of having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*): does it take as its intended result a fruit that is itself of an unseen nature, or does it take as its means an unseen intermediary?
Not the first; for there would be no over-extension (*avyāpti*) to injunctions such as the *Kārīrī*, which have a visible fruit.

Nor is the latter [definition] correct; for it fails to apply (avyāpti) to the injunction "one should praise with the Sāman" (*sāmnā stuvīta*), which establishes that the Sāman serves the purpose of praise.
In that case, the door consisting of the manifestation of the syllables of the Ṛk is not something other than a visible result; therefore, this definition is not tenable.

Furthermore, even if there is an overlap (*sāṅkarya*) among these limiting conditions (*upādhi*) in certain examples, it does not constitute a fault; thus, there is no room for the criticism of the definition stated in the *Vidhirasāyana*.
This should be seen in detail in our own work, the *Mīmāṃsākaustubha*.
Therefore, even though mantras serve as reminders of meaning, their application (*viniyoga*) is not rendered purposeless.
(B2) (The definition of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) according to the *Khaṇḍana* author, and the purpose of its constituent members:

As for that which—according to the *Khaṇḍana* authors—is [the definition of] an original injunction (*prakṛtavidhi*): whatever is the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of the present injunction, other than being "that which pertains to an original injunction" (*apūrvīyatva*), by that form, in the case of the object (*uddeśya*), [there arises] from an injunction belonging to the same recensional branch (*samāna-śākhīya*) as the present injunction—other than an extended injunction (*atideśa*)—in the absence of the present injunction...

The definition of an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) is: an injunction whose object is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) that is to be performed (*vidheya*) and which has not been previously established (*saṃbhavatprāptika*).

In this context, the qualification "other than being for the sake of an *apūrva*" is added to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the injunction regarding threshing (*avaghāta*), which brings about threshing in rice-grains (*vrīhi*)—where it is absolutely unestablished—in its capacity as something "for the sake of an *apūrva*.
That other [qualification] is the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*); in the case of the injunction regarding threshing and the like, it is "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*).
Furthermore, because threshing (*avaghāta*) can be understood as already established by the injunction for such sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

By specifying "in the form of that which delimits the objective status (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka-rūpa*)," there is no non-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of the two injunctions regarding the precedence of the *vāyu* cup in the *gavāmayana* and other sacrifices, nor in the injunction for heaven-desiring [rites] in the *darśa-pūrṇamāsa*;
for in those cases, the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup is already established by the injunction for the *tryanīkā* sequence in its capacity as the first portion.

Furthermore, since there is no prior attainment [of heaven] under the form of being the specific object of the injunction (svoddeśyatāvacchedaka), even though attainment is possible for heaven as the object under the form of being desired by the *sārvakāmya* injunction, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because such attainment does not exist under the form of "heaven-ness" (*svargatva*).

Because it is intended that the term be qualified by "other than those [injunctions] involving extension" (*atideśabhinnā*), there is no lack of pervasion in the case of modified (*vaikṛta*) injunctions regarding recipients (*pratigrāhya*), nor in the two injunctions regarding precedence (*agratā*) within the *nyanīkā* of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), since attainment through extension is possible in those cases.

Due to the qualification "belonging to the same branch" (*samānaśākhīya*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites found in other branches, which could potentially be obtained through the injunctions of those other branches. Where a particular injunction exists as the generator of a specific benefit, that [injunction] is intended to exclude the absence of its attainment—which is synonymous with the possibility of performing it by mere chance—rather than its non-existence; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the injunctions for the *hiraṇyagarbha-mantra* or the restriction regarding *pūtīka* plants.

Because of the inclusion of the term "bhāva" (the state of being), there is no over-extension [of the definition] to a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) which brings about the cessation of what has not yet been attained.
In this very manner, by avoiding both under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*) as established in the *Vidhirasāyana*, the wise should apply this definition everywhere.

(Refutation of the definition of an *apūrva-vidhi* as accepted by the author of the *Khaṇḍana*) That is incorrect; for there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of that definition to the restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) regarding Hiraṇyagarbha and Pūtīka grass— which you have established by taking recourse to their incidental occurrence (*yādṛcchika-prāpti*) through secondary usage (*gauṇī*), even though they are cases where the [injunction’s] application is otherwise impossible (*asaṃbhavat-prāptika*).

If, however, the absence of accidental attainment (*yādṛcchikaprāpti*) is also intended as a separate characteristic [of an object], then there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the injunction for one desiring heaven (*svargakāmavidhi*).

According to the principle of the accomplishment through yoga (*yogasiddhiniyāya*), even without depending on the injunction for one desiring heaven, a person necessarily engages in action directed toward heaven in its form as "heaven" by the force of the injunction for all desires (*sārvakāmyavidhi*).

Furthermore, since the attainment of such fitness for performance in the manner described by you could occur even without the present injunction—just as in the case of the *pūtīka* plant—there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Moreover, according to the view that there are two types of *pṛṣṭha* chants, even though the possibility of obtaining [the *rathantara*] through extended application (*atideśa*) exists in a restrictive injunction such as "the *rathantara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha* in the modified sacrifice," it is nevertheless impossible to obtain it from an injunction belonging to another identical branch; thus, there is an over-extension. In reality, however, the injunction regarding the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth, being untenable without the dehusking of the primary substance, intends to exclude ordinary (*laukika*) rice.

The venerable teachers have disregarded this [criticism], as it has already been refuted by those very same authors in the *Bhaṭṭālaṅkāra*, on the grounds that this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) even in the well-known example [of the *vrīhi* injunction]. This was because they sought to avoid the complexity of the delimiting factor of the intended object (*uddeśyatvāvacchedaka-gaurava*) as well as the complexity of the internal implication regarding barley (*yava*). They argue that [the injunction] brings about the application precisely by way of the delimiting factor of being the material substance for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa-prakṛtidravyatva*). Thus, it is incorrect to claim that this definition is over-extensive.
(An exposition on how there is no fault even when two types of injunctions are accepted as applicable in certain specific examples:

When the threefold definitions of injunction have been thus established, in cases where the purposelessness [of an injunction] can be easily avoided even by means of two or three results of injunction,
by which [definition] should it be designated?
In response to this inquiry, he says: "And of these..."
"In some examples" means as follows.
And those examples have been stated in the introduction to the ninth verse of the *Vidhirasāyana*; they should be consulted there.
As stated in the Vārttika regarding the two examples, "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and "He threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*):
in the first case, because it precedes the injunction inferred from the mantra "I sprinkle you, who are dear to Agni," it serves to bring about the sprinkling that was previously unestablished.

Following the observation of that inferred attainment, it is further inferred that [the act] possesses a reward as its culmination, that there is an occasion for expiation, and that it results in the restriction that the Adhvaryu priest alone is the performer.

In the second [case], by considering the attainment of the restrictive rule of threshing—which is to be determined through reasoning and its associated mantras—one must determine whether it brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*), whether it necessitates an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), or whether it is intended to establish the restriction that the *adhvaryu* priest alone performs it.
In this way, one should provide examples even when there is a confusion of the three types of results.

Even though such results and other factors may be present, wherever there is no fault such as excessive complexity (*gaurava*) and so forth, the scripture (*śāstra*) certainly possesses its intended meaning (*tātparya*) in every instance.
Otherwise, there would be no occurrence of deficiency (vaiguṇya) in the performance of that purpose,
as in the case of accepting a restrictive exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) in the injunction regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

However, where a fault such as prolixity (*gaurava*) exists— as in the sentences concerning sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, if the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*) and the like were to be included— [then such an exclusion is not accepted].
In that regard, it has been stated that there is no result consisting in a mere enumeration of barley.

For this very reason, when the status of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible in certain cases, the status of an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is not accepted where it would entail the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

This is as in the case of the *hīṣ* and other syllables, where, since a restriction for the sake of systematic arrangement is possible, one does not accept a connection between a quality and a fruit that would necessitate the postulation of another unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

But where there is no such contingency— as in cases like "he spreads the sacrificial cake" (puroḍāśaṃ prathayati)— there, even though the result is the restriction of the Adhvaryu as the performer, it is indeed accepted as being an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) because its result is the [prescription of] a Yajurvedic expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*).

And thus, in all these statements—whether through a difference of objects or an identity of objects, whether sequentially or simultaneously—the meaning is that there is no fault because, although there is a commingling of the things to be enjoined (*upādeya*) due to their having a single intended fruit, the designations (*lakṣaṇā*) of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) remain unconfused; for since the practical usage by one or another [condition] in a particular case is optional, it is based on internal factors (*antaraṅga*). [Objection: But if such a commingling is admitted, then even a staff other than the one belonging to the *daikṣa* (sacrificial) ritual would, in some cases, be liable to be employed for the task of the *praiṣa* (command).

Since the statement that the singing of the *stotra-sāmans* belonging to the various sacrifices occurs only in the *uttara* verses would contradict the latter half of the ninth verse in the *Vidhirasāyana*, he says: "And in detail... (*vistareṇa ca*).

For, in the absence of both the injunctions "tataḥ hi krīte some" and "daṇḍī," since the consecrated sacrificer's staff (*dīkṣitadaṇḍa*) is already enjoined for the purpose of being held by the sacrificer, the rule "daṇḍī" would be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding a secular staff.

However, in the absence of the rule "daṇḍī" alone, when the consecrated staff— having been given to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest— is in need of a purpose and thus applies to all tasks collectively as a support, the rule "daṇḍī" becomes an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) that restricts its application to other tasks besides the formal commands (*praiṣa*).
And for this reason, the objection has been stated that if such a confusion were admitted, it would follow that even the ordinary worldly staff would have to be included.

For indeed, even though multiple results might be conjectured, it is not logical—given that the staff is actually enjoined by the *krīta* formula as being for the sake of the Maitrāvaruṇa—to enjoin its function by means of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍī*) when there is a need for a purpose; because, in that case, nothing else could possibly apply. Thus it is stated in the *Kaustubha*.
This is the meaning of "it should be seen.
In reality, however, because the definition is formulated as "accompanied by the non-activation of another injunction," and because the non-activation of multiple injunctions is not included therein,

and because "the state of being another injunction" is intended in the manner previously stated, there is no overlap with those respective definitions by taking the non-activation of just any injunction whatsoever.
It should be understood that there is no risk of confusion with *pīti*.
(B3) (1) Furthermore, all these other topics will become perfectly clear by examining the commentary on the second verse of the *Vidhirasāyana*; therefore, they are not elaborated upon here by us.
The meaning of this term is clear on page twelve of the *Vidhirasāyana* manuscript.
(B1) Nor does this result in an impossibility of validity; for that [validity] characterized by correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*) remains unimpaired.
However, by way of being the referent of a word (*padārtha-vidhayā*), it is common to all mantras beginning with *sāma*.

For just as it is accepted by all schools of thought that "the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)" because it is the object of the knowledge that serves as the cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*),
so too can it be said that the referent of a word is likewise [a means of valid cognition], since it is also a cause for the knowledge of the referent of a word.
And therefore, since mantras are also constituent elements (*padārtha*) in the injunctions regarding their application (*viniyoga*), it is logical that they possess authority (*prāmāṇya*).
Alternatively, even if they lack authority, let there be merely their purposefulness (*prayojanavattva*); for by that much alone, the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is justified.
The purpose is as clear as that of an explanatory passage (arthavāda). // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth section, concerning the authority of mantras.
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* composed by Khaṇḍadeva. (B2) (The conclusion of the refutation of the futility of the injunctions of application.)
Thus, he concludes the demonstration of how the futility of the injunction of application (viniyoga-vidhi) has been avoided, saying: "tadevam" (thus, therefore).

As for the objection that the application of the mantra to the act of spreading [the sacrificial cake] would result in its purposelessness—that is intended to establish a basis for the praise expressed in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), which states that "it causes the lord of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*) himself to expand through progeny and cattle.
For in the mantra, the Adhvaryu priest says with regard to the sacrificial cake: "May the lord of the sacrifice expand widely for you."
And whoever speaks thus indeed spreads [the cake].

Therefore, the act of the Adhvaryu priest in bestowing the blessing (*āśīḥ*) is figuratively treated as the act of producing the spreading of the master of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*); thus, it is a praise of the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

Consequently, the mantra is employed to praise the spreading of the cake by way of its resulting in the spreading of the master of the sacrifice. This is included under the phrase "for the sake of [indicating] a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), and so forth."

Nor should it be argued that—since spreading [the cake] is already established by the sense of the injunction and is therefore not something to be enjoined—it is impossible for it to be an *arthavāda* due to the absence of its status as a supplement to an injunction;
for even though it is already established, its enjoinment is justified as being for the purpose of securing the Adhvaryu priest as the performer.

Furthermore, in this case, unlike the *Rātrisatra*, there is no inconsistency in the inclusion of the mantra, because the *arthavāda* serves to make known that the spreading of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is the fruit [of the action]; this should be understood from the *Kaustubha*.

(On the validity of mantras characterized by their correspondence to reality): Even so, he restates what was said regarding the impossibility of validity in the form of apprehending an object not previously known—namely, "And it is not thus."

Even though mantras are restatements of what has already been prescribed, their validity consists precisely in their correspondence with reality regarding the nature of the act—such as cutting and so forth—which constitutes their intended meaning (tātparya), just like the case of Smṛti texts.
And this intended meaning is to be known through the means of application, such as direct Vedic statement (śruti) and others;
for example, the case of the *aindrī* verse with respect to the Gārhapatya fire.

He refutes the argument of certain [opponents]— who have established that the Sāman texts, being essentially musical chants, lack direct cognitive power and thus possess authority only indirectly by way of manifesting the syllables which in turn convey the meaning— by stating: "of that which is characterized by correspondence to reality" (*yāthārthya-lakṣaṇasya*).

Since even the characteristic of being in accordance with reality is impossible through a traditional succession among those who do not know the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda, he states another alternative: "sāmādīti" (beginning with the Sāmaveda).
"And either the word 'atha' itself is established as the means of valid cognition, or its manifestation [as such] is being examined."
As stated in the *Kārikāvārtika* on the *Codanāsūtra*: "The cognition [of the sentence] may consist of the word-meanings, or it may be [the cognition] of the sentence-meaning itself.

Likewise: "In this regard, it is replied: although the mind has another basis [in the form of the sense organs], the word-meanings possess the status of being the primary cause, because no other instance can be produced as a corroborative example."
Although the phonemes directly effect the communication of word-meanings, they do not terminate in that fruitless end;
for their activity is necessarily directed toward the measurement of the sentence-meaning.

And taking recourse to another view—that the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is the knowledge of word-meanings as stated in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning sentences (vākya-adhikaraṇa), namely, "the presentation of word-meanings is like the kindling of wood for cooking," and that by means of that [intermediate operation], word-meanings alone possess the status of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) of verbal valid cognition—he says: "Just as... and so forth.

(Examination of the Validity of Word-Meanings as Objects of Cognition): Even though past and future objects do not exist by way of their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), they possess existence (*sattva*) as objects of cognition (*jñānaviṣayatvena*). Therefore, just as in the case of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), it is logically consistent for them to serve as causes for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*); thus, there is no fault.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and the like would also possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) as word-meanings; for such a consequence is accepted.

Nor does this violate the restrictive rule that "injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge" (*codanaiva pramāṇam*); for since that rule is intended to establish the primacy [of injunction], it does not preclude the validity of other means of knowledge—this is the meaning. For this very reason, in the aphorism *tadbhūtānāṃ kriyārthena samāmnāyo 'rthasya tannimittatvāt*, there is the explanation of the constituent parts beginning with the word *arthasya*.
The commentator, while composing [the work], stated: "For words, having denoted their respective individual meanings, cease their operation;
then, the word-meanings, being thus understood, bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning."
(Regarding the doubt concerning the impossibility of validity characterized by correspondence with reality [yāthārthya] according to the view of the *Prakāśakāra*, and its refutation:
As for that which the *Prakāśakāras* state in the section establishing the authority of the *Kalpasūtras*—

namely, that if validity were accepted as being defined by correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), then since that would apply even to worldly statements such as "The Jyotiṣṭoma is the means to heaven" and to the words of Śākyamuni and others which teach non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, they could not be authoritative in that manner.
Moreover, since it is from that [source] that an action understood as a means to the highest good called dharma is known,
that alone is the authority for dharma; the very cognition of that is called the "authority regarding dharma" (dharmapramā).
Such is the authoritative status of Dharma for the Smṛtis and other texts:
because the author of Manu and others is authorized as a promulgator of Dharma,
and because even the Vedic mantras are regulated by virtue of their function as reminders.
This is because only the recollection (*smṛti*) produced by that [Veda] is useful as a means to attain the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).

Even though other means such as meditation (*dhyāna*) may be useful in the absence of a mantra, there is no risk of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because they lack the status of being a means to the highest good characterized by being an enjoined auxiliary (*aṅga*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "Therefore, those very scriptures which do not transgress the root of the Veda..."
"By those very [means] established [by tradition], the Dharma is known to be the bestower of fruit.
Likewise: "Those alone who possess the authority to proclaim it are authorized by the Veda itself."

It is the settled conclusion that the words of those eternal beings who, throughout the transitions of Manvantaras and Yugas, compose compendiums of Dharma, are authoritative, and not those of others.
The phrase "iti" [refers to] that which has already been refuted in the *Kaustubha* on those respective topics;
here, the rejection of other views should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.
Because there is no confidence in that previously mentioned view, he states another position, beginning with "astu tu" (let it be so).
And it is not the case that there is a lack of consistency with the chapter (*adhyāya*) due to this absence of authority (*prāmāṇya*);

for there is no obstacle to investigating even a matter that is inconsistent with the chapter if it arises as a consequence of the utility of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Alternatively, since the utility of the Veda along with its ancillaries (*sāṅgaveda*) is precisely what is sought to be known, it is accepted as the subject matter of the chapter;
thus, it is appropriate that the section on Mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*) concerns itself with an investigation into mere utility. This is the meaning.
The purpose is as follows.

The meaning is as follows: just as the excellence (*prāśastya*) understood from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is conducive to the performance of dharma and thus brings about prosperity (*abhyudaya*), so too here, the very memory produced by the mantra is what brings about prosperity; this is the purpose.
Likewise: "The word 'Agnihotra' is the name [of the rite], while the 'Āghāra' is the conceptualization of a sacrifice."
This application to the primary sense [is established]; other purposes stated in such passages as "āmikṣā and milk indeed" should be consulted in the Kaustubha.

Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī*, composed by Śambhubhaṭṭa, son of Bālakṛṣṇa— known as Kavi-maṇḍana— who was a disciple of the illustrious Khaṇḍadeva, who himself stood at the forefront of those who have crossed the ocean of the glorious Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā.
